World.title: Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film
World.content:
An Al Jazeera data investigation raises questions about claims that an Israeli counter-documentary to NAZA got 40mn views.

An Al Jazeera investigation has exposed holes in claims that an Israeli counter-film to the acclaimed documentary NAZA achieved more than 44 million views. By examining domain registries, web archives, source code, and three independent traffic tools, the investigation exposed the fabricated numbers adopted by official Israeli entities to promote the film.

The original award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers, accusing the army of using artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems to kill numerous civilians in Gaza. The documentary takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes. After winning the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the film was scheduled to screen in 56 countries.

Official backlash

The success of the original documentary triggered a political storm in Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants and prosecute them for information security violations.

The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, were accused of treason, and Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.

Network of domains

To counter the film’s global resonance, opponents created a counter-film. On September 16, just days after NAZA premiered, the domain nazadocumentary.com was registered via Cloudflare, with the owner’s details hidden.



The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine revealed the site initially disguised itself as the official NAZA website, listing the directors’ names and information on screenings and press. However, it described the film as exposing the systems behind the calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza. By September 30, this deceptive page vanished, replaced by a new title, “NAZA: The Real Story”.

The individuals behind the 49-minute counter-film are Ariel Averbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman, who claimed the work was self-funded. Later, two more domains, whatisnaza.com and watchnaza.com, were registered to redirect users to the counter-film.

The fake counter

By the morning of October 14, the nazadocumentary.com website’s counter displayed 43,758,421 views, without disclosing the source of the number or how it was calculated.

Public platforms told a drastically different story. The full 49-minute version of the film on its official YouTube channel had not exceeded 130,000 views by the same date. This means the website’s counter displayed roughly 336 times the actual viewership. The YouTube channel had fewer than 2,000 subscribers, and the film’s account on X had only 170 followers.

Independent traffic analysis platforms confirmed the discrepancy. The US-based platform Semrush estimated the site’s total visits by October 8 at about half a million. Israeli-founded Similarweb estimated only 326 visits for September. Furthermore, the film’s domains were absent from the Tranco list of the world’s top one million visited domains.

Discrepancies and code

An examination of the page’s source code revealed that the element displaying the huge number was internally tagged as “visitors” but displayed to users as “views”. The number is delivered directly from the site’s server, making its calculation method invisible from the outside. Upon opening the page, the counter begins at 97 percent of its value and counts up for three seconds, creating the illusion of a live counter.

Additionally, the site collects actual viewing data without publishing it, sending a “watch-tracker” file after about 25 seconds of video playback to identify the viewing session and parts watched, leaving it unknown whether the counter is based on this data.



State promotion

Despite the seemingly fabricated metrics, official Israeli accounts spearheaded the promotion of the counter-film. The Israeli Embassy in Washington promoted it on October 3 on social media.

Tzipi Hotovely, head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, awarded the three creators certificates of recognition for countering the original film. Hotovely said the film had garnered tens of millions of views, transforming an unsupported, fabricated number into an official talking point.

This elaborate digital campaign unfolds against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Since the conflict started, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

World.title: What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
World.content:
Share What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it? on social media

Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service.

The Reuters news agency, quoting a source, reported that Kyiv is still seeking clarifications from Starshield’s parent company, SpaceX, as to why its service was disrupted between Tuesday and Wednesday.

Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has denied the company’s involvement and suggested only the US government could have disrupted it, despite President Donald Trump’s insistence that Washington is still sharing intelligence with Kyiv.

Here’s what we know:

What is Starshield?

Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, an array of 11,000 satellites placed by SpaceX into Earth’s low orbit to provide high-speed internet connectivity even in remote areas.

Starshield, launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.

Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.

What happened to Ukraine’s access to Starshield?

On Tuesday, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian strikes, which hit the country with more than 100 drones and five ballistic missiles, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.



“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X. “Regarding this strike, unfortunately, there was no warning from partners.”

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (160km/h).

That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.

Officials said the restrictions also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

Who controls Starshield?

On Wednesday, Musk denied any involvement in the incident, insisting that the service is “controlled by the US government”.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.

Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

Last year, Starlink cut off access for Russian troops who were covertly using the service on the battlefront in Ukraine.

Is Musk supportive of Ukraine?

The SpaceX boss has shown an active interest in the Russia-Ukraine war since it began, but has not been particularly favourable towards Kyiv. In 2022 – just after Russia invaded Ukraine – he proposed a “peace plan” under which Kyiv would end its claim to Russia-occupied Crimea and would drop hopes for joining NATO. Zelenskyy criticised Musk’s comments, and tensions between the two have remained.

On Sunday, the billionaire, who is also the CEO of Tesla and owns X, said Zelenskyy “has gone too far”, in a response to Trump’s comments that the Ukrainian president should leave office.



On Wednesday, Musk appeared to blame Zelenskyy for deaths in the war. “And so the slaughter continues,” he wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”

Does Ukraine blame the US for restricting intelligence?

Ukrainian officials have complained that the country received no warning in advance of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday. Usually, the US provides crucial early-warning alerts that allow Kyiv to issue evacuation orders.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.

The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.

Why might the US restrict intelligence from Ukraine?

Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Trump took office last year over a host of issues, including weapons transfers and the US’s increasing closeness to Russia.

In recent weeks, Washington has pressured Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries to allow more oil into global markets. In particular, Trump has sought to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel facilities for the rising price of the fuel globally ahead of November midterm elections.

Trump said last week he had agreed to a deal with President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel stocks into the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions on Russian oil.

Zelenskyy criticised the move and said it would embolden Putin.

Over the weekend, Trump unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, apparently without consulting Zelenskyy, who told reporters the deal was “news to me”. Russia also did not confirm it. Angered, Trump called for Ukraine to replace its president and blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for global energy disruptions.

Ukraine said it had, in fact, refrained from attacking Russian refineries and would continue to do so if Russia did the same. However, Russian strikes have continued. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure had caused blackouts affecting 600,000 people.

“We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in the FT interview, confirming that Kyiv had subsequently resumed attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure.

World.title: Russia accuses Ukraine of contradicting US brokered deal
World.content:
NewsFeed Russia accuses Ukraine of contradicting US brokered deal

Russia has accused Ukraine of going against US peace efforts, after an overnight Ukrainian drone strike on an oil refinery in a region south of Moscow. Russia added its diesel had begun to reach global markets after a deal with US President Donald Trump.

World.title: Real Madrid’s Vinicius says he’s being targeted by referees
World.content:
Vinicius wants protection for players like himself, Yamal and Alvarez ‘who bring something different to the game.’

Vinicius Junior is not happy with how he is being treated by referees and wants more protection for talented players like him, Lamine Yamal and Julian Alvarez.

The Brazil forward spoke out after Real Madrid’s 4-3 come-from-behind win at Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday.

He acknowledged that he is going through a slump, but said he had “no doubt” he will regain his best form soon.

The match against Roma came hours after he was handed a four-game suspension in the Spanish league after being sent off for pulling the hair of an opponent and for protesting against the referee.

“I don’t recall any other player receiving a four-match suspension. I tried to move the player in front of me out of the way and I ended up getting caught in his hair,” Vinicius said.

“That was it – a red card – which is why I was so surprised. I didn’t say a single offensive word to the referee that would warrant a four-match ban. But when it comes to Vini, it’s all too easy.

“The opposing team will always say it’s justified and the press will say the same. I understand that. I’m here to keep evolving and improving, because I know where I’ve come from and what I’m capable of achieving,” Vinicius added.

“It’s understandable for the opposing fans to jeer me, because my job is to score goals against their team, but I don’t get the referees.

“I’ve seen the stats: I’ve been on the receiving end of 500 fouls, yet that has only resulted in five red cards. In the end, the yellow cards always seem to go to Vini, to the attacking players. We need to protect the players who bring something different to the game, like Lamine at Barcelona or Julian at Atleti. Defenders are allowed to foul me the entire match but in the end it’s me who gets the card.”

Madrid coach Jose Mourinho complained about the timing of the announcement of the suspension.



“Do you think it’s normal for a player from a Spanish team, preparing for an important match that’s also crucial for Spanish football, to find out about his four-match suspension just two hours before kickoff?” Mourinho said.

“We were on the bus about to arrive at the stadium when we found out … they’ve started doing things without any shame.”

Vinicius, who hasn’t scored for Madrid since August, was replaced in the 59th minute of Madrid’s victory before the team rallied from 3-1 down.

“I’m working to get back to my best as soon as possible,” Vinicius said. “I know I’m not at my peak right now, but I’ve been through worse and even when people have doubted me, I’ve always stood up for this club. That’s why I signed a six-year contract extension.

“The good run of form will return and the goals will come back, too. I’m certain of that. I have no doubt. I’m here to help the team.”

The 26-year-old Vinicius has scored only two goals for club and country this season, one for Madrid in the team’s second league match and another with Brazil in a friendly against Australia in September.

He downplayed his frustration after Mourinho substituted him on Wednesday.

“It’s natural for me to get upset when I’m substituted because I always want to play every single match. I’m well aware of my current form and how I’m playing. I’m here to help the team and sometimes you have to come off so that other players can get on and change the dynamic,” he said.

“Mourinho and I have a great relationship. He’s always straight with me. Of course I got a little annoyed when I came off today, but that’s normal. In the end he was right, the team improved and that’s what matters most.”

Vinícius was replaced by Endrick, who scored an 85th-minute equaliser before Antonio Rudiger gave Madrid the win in the 90th.

“This is Real Madrid. We needed a match like this to shift the dynamic and turn the season around a bit,” Vinicius said. “It’s going to help and give us a boost because the younger players stepped up. They played a great game.

“Endrick played an incredible match. He scored and really helped us out. That’s why he was named man of the match.”

Because of his suspension, Vinicius will miss Sunday’s home match against Sevilla and the following week’s trip for “el Clasico” against Barcelona. He will also miss away matches at Racing Santander and Valencia.

World.title: Argentina’s President Has a Dog Psychic. Meet Celia Melamed.
World.content:
But in that first encounter about a decade ago, Conan was on his deathbed, and Ms. Melamed said she was communicating with him via an energy she felt in her chest. She said she relayed Mr. Milei’s message that he was desperately trying to save the dog.

“What I remember is that he felt better afterward,” she said of Mr. Milei. “Few people have such an intense connection with their animals.”

Ms. Melamed then became his dedicated pet psychic. He kept hiring her for the next two years, she said, including to talk to Conan in the afterlife and to the five clones made with Conan’s DNA. They stopped working together a few years before Mr. Milei was elected president in 2023.

Mr. Milei and his spokesmen did not respond to requests for comment. He has long made clear that he views his dogs as more than just pets. Mr. Milei, who is unmarried and childless, refers to them as his children, and his press secretary has admonished reporters who ask about the animals, saying it is equivalent to snooping into his family.

World.title: Trump Hands Victories to Putin, Who Offers More War in Return
World.content:
The wins for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia came in rapid succession from Washington.

President Trump proffered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel. He publicly called for Ukraine to get a new leader. And he pressured Kyiv to stop a strike campaign against Russian oil facilities that has damaged the Russian economy.

Mr. Putin, in return, offered more war.

Minutes after Mr. Trump announced the diesel deal, the Kremlin reiterated Mr. Putin’s stance that he would not negotiate with Ukraine at the moment, because he remained angry about Ukrainian strikes during last month’s Russian parliamentary election.

The next day, Russia launched an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 22 people, including four children. It was the latest in a near daily drumbeat of devastating Russian strikes, which have dramatically increased the civilian toll in Ukraine as Kyiv sorely lacks air-defense missiles.

And Mr. Putin has signaled that he plans to escalate further, aiming to knock out Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure in what Ukrainians expect to be the worst winter of the war.

World.title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
World.content:
The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.

According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.

Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.

He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.

Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.

European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".

"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."

He added: "Peace will be achieved when [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."

Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.

Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.

World.title: Trump calls off livestream for Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.

Trump had previously said he approved of showing online the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.

As criticism over the public display mounted, Trump said on Thursday that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.

"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added.

Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Trump said the execution can be viewed in person by the families of the victims.

"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Trump said.

World.title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
World.content:
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.

More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Several children are feared to be trapped under the rubble.

Emergency services were alerted to the incident at the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, a rescue official said.

He told the BBC the roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, causing ceilings below to cave in as well.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

"The children in the affected [classrooms] were trapped under the debris," the official, Bilal Faizi, said.

The school is located in a building that had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.

Earlier reports suggested the affected classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.

It appears that when the roof of the upper-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.

Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.

World.title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
World.content:
Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.

A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.

Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.

Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut GÃ¼l to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.

The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.

Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.

"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.

He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.

The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.

More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

World.title: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
World.content:
Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say.

The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire.

Romanian President NicuÈor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday.

The Wine Trader was empty of cargo at the time.

Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels.

Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.

The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks.

On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.

Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.

A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.

The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.

The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.

The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT).

Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones.

The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked.

This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.

The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."

Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.

The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.

Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports.

On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".

Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.

A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves.

Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.

Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports.

Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.

Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.

Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

World.title: White House defends new press secretary over her legal credentials
World.content:
The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.

President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week. She has referred to herself as a lawyer.

But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".

Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.

It is seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".

The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.

A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.

The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.

She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

The new press secretary also told the paper that when she answered China to a question about her bar exam, it was a misunderstanding. She had mistakenly thought, above the din of Marine One, the reporter had asked: "Where were you after law school?"

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.

A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.

World.title: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
World.content:
Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope

But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.

He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill".

"It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said.

"So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."

But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".

He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler.

"We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'."

"We have not chosen to do that."

World.title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
World.content:
Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.

The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.

Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.

Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.

The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.

FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.

Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers âwant to â see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."

The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.

Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.

Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.

"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.

World.title: Nigeria’s inflation eases to 14.63% in September
World.content:
Nigeria’s headline inflation rate edged down to 14.63 per cent in September, from 15.39 per cent a month earlier, official data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Thursday, as the pace of increase in price levels continues to slow in Africa’s most populous country.

The development extends the downward trend in annual consumer inflation recorded in recent months, with inflation dropping marginally to 15.39 per cent in August from 15.43 per cent in July.

Food inflation stood at 19.59 per cent year-on-year in September, slightly higher than the 19.57 per cent recorded in August, but lower than the 20.16 per cent reported in September 2025.

Food accounts for a substantial share of household expenditure, particularly among lower-income households.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile items like agricultural produce and energy prices, stood at 12.95 per cent year-on-year in September, down from 13.29 per cent in August and 22.11 per cent in September 2025.

The annual figure indicates a continued slowdown in price increases outside the more volatile food and energy components.

The divergence between the annual and monthly figures suggests that, although underlying inflation has moderated considerably over the past year, some price pressures persisted during September.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Despite the slowdown in inflationary pressures, Nigeria continues to face a cost-of-living crisis, principally on account of elevated food prices and energy costs, which have hammered the disposable income of many households.

The drop in living standards has been fuelled by tough economic reforms introduced by the current administration, including the removal of fuel subsidies, devaluation of the naira and a prolonged hawkish monetary policy stance.

The statistics office’s data also reflected differences between inflation in urban and rural areas.

Urban inflation stood at 15.64 per cent year-on-year in September, down from 20.63 per cent in the corresponding month of 2025. Rural inflation was lower at 12.46 per cent year-on-year, compared with 21.06 per cent in September 2025.

What the figures mean

The September data point to a further slowdown in Nigeria’s inflation rate, with annual headline inflation falling for another month.

A fall in annual inflation means that prices are rising more slowly than they did over the corresponding period a year earlier. A negative monthly rate, such as the September food inflation figure, means that average prices in the measured basket declined compared with the previous month.

With annual food inflation still at 19.59 per cent, the September figures show that the pace of food price increases has moderated over the past year, while the average cost of food remains higher than it was a year ago.

World.title: Presco Plc and SIAT Academy celebrate first cohort of graduate trainees
World.content:
Presco Plc, Nigeria’s leading fully integrated agro-industrial company and a member of SIAT Group, has celebrated the graduation of 33 young professionals from the inaugural SIAT Academy Graduate Trainee Programme. At the graduation ceremony in Benin City, the company also announced an expanded second cohort of 70 trainees, representing a 40% increase in intake and reinforcing its commitment to developing future leaders in agribusiness.

Established in 2025, SIAT Academy is a strategic training and development platform designed to strengthen technical, professional and leadership capabilities across SIAT Group and the wider palm oil industry. Its one-year Graduate Trainee Programme combines classroom learning, practical experience and mentorship, with training opportunities across the Group’s operations in Edo, Delta and Rivers States, as well as Ghana.

The inaugural cohort welcomed 50 graduates in July and September 2025. Following a year of structured training, practical assignments and performance assessments, 33 participants successfully completed the programme. They will now progress to the Management Trainee Programme, taking on greater responsibilities as they develop towards future management roles.

Speaking at the ceremony, Adewale Arikawe, Group Chief Executive Officer, emphasised the importance of investing in people alongside the Group’s expansion.

“Our growth ambitions require us to invest as deliberately in people as we do in plantations, factories, technology and markets. The graduation of our first cohort is an important milestone in building the talent pipeline needed to support our future. These young professionals have completed the first stage of their development, and we are committed to supporting their continued growth. Our ambition is not simply to build a bigger SIAT, but to develop the people who will build and lead it. The expansion of our second cohort to 70 trainees demonstrates that commitment.”

Reinout Impens, Director of SIAT Academy, highlighted the programme’s focus on practical experience and performance-based progression.

“We began with 50 young graduates, exposing them to real operations, workplace responsibilities and clear performance expectations. Today, 33 have demonstrated their readiness to progress to the next stage. Their graduation marks an important step towards greater professional and management responsibility. With 70 new trainees joining our second cohort, we are building on this foundation to develop the capabilities needed to support the Group’s strategic ambitions.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Reflecting on his experience, Michael Omi, a graduate of the inaugural cohort, described how the programme strengthened his understanding of industrial operations and plant maintenance.

“Before joining SIAT, I knew very little about the agro-industrial sector. The programme has given me valuable technical experienceand a deeper understanding of how the industry operates. Progressing to the Management Trainee Programme is an exciting opportunity to build on that experience and pursue my ambition of combining engineering expertise with business management.”

The ceremony brought together senior leadership, Academy representatives and trainees to celebrate the graduates’ achievements and recognise outstanding performance and project delivery.

The SIAT Academy programme also aligns with Nigeria’s National Agricultural Technology and Innovation Policy (NATIP) 2022–2027 and supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly quality education, decent work and sustainable industrial development.

Through the Academy, Presco and SIAT Group continue to invest in the skills, expertise and leadership capabilities needed to support their long-term growth and strengthen Africa’s agro-industrial workforce

World.title: Malnutrition admissions rise at ICRC-backed facilities in North-east Nigeria
World.content:
Malnutrition admissions at 10 health facilities supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in north-eastern Nigeria rose 18 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.

The facilities recorded nearly 20,000 admissions between January and September, up from about 17,000 in the same period of 2025, the ICRC said in a statement on Thursday.

The figures cover six health centres and four hospitals. Young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers were among those most affected.

Mubi in Adamawa State saw the sharpest rise, from about 4,600 admissions in the first nine months of 2025 to approximately 5,700 this year, an increase of nearly 24 per cent.

The latest numbers follow earlier ICRC warnings about rising demand for nutritional treatment in conflict-affected areas.

In October 2024, the organisation reported a 24 per cent increase in severe acute malnutrition admissions between the third quarters of 2023 and 2024, from 6,824 to 8,470.

Admissions of children under five with severe acute malnutrition and medical complications also rose from 1,212 to 1,691 in the same period.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

These figures cover different reporting periods and patient categories and cannot establish a continuous three-year trend.

They do, however, show repeated increases in demand for nutritional treatment.

Mothers struggle

At the Mubi Stabilisation Centre, Zulaihatu Mohammed brought her six-month-old daughter, Huseina, one of her twins, for nutritional support.

“When I gave birth to them, this one was tiny,” she told the ICRC. “I came today for the routine collection of children’s food. She is not feeling well. Since I gave birth to her, she has been unwell.”

Armed violence, climate shocks and economic pressures have disrupted livelihoods and limited access to food.

According to the ICRC’s video report, farmer Saminu Ijaduwa cultivates a small plot near his home because explosive devices have made more distant fields dangerous.

“Due to the conflict, going one kilometre out of town to farm could be highly risky. You might not return!” he said in the ICRC report.

Restrictions on farming and disrupted markets have made it harder for families to produce or buy enough food, particularly affecting young children and pregnant and breastfeeding women.

Humanitarian response

In a March 2026 report, the ICRC said more than 36,000 people received treatment for severe acute malnutrition at its supported facilities in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states during 2025.

The total included more than 16,000 children under five and more than 19,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women.

The organisation also provided cash assistance to more than 17,000 vulnerable families during the 2025 lean season.

Those annual treatment figures are not directly comparable with the new nine-month admission totals.

The ICRC said it is working with the Nigerian Red Cross Society to support 15 primary healthcare centres and four hospitals and to assist more than 200 communities with malnutrition treatment and food-security programmes.

Interventions include supplying farmers with seeds adapted to drought and flooding, promoting crop diversification and teaching mothers to prepare nutritious meals from local ingredients.

One such mixture of sorghum, millet, soybeans, groundnuts and moringa, known as Tom Brown, has helped more than 13,000 young children recover from moderate acute malnutrition, according to the ICRC. Mothers are also taught how to prepare it at home.

Wider food insecurity

The rise in admissions comes as the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) identify Nigeria among the world’s hunger hotspots of highest concern in their June to November 2026 outlook.

Citing United Nations analysis, the ICRC said more than 34 million people in Nigeria were expected to face insufficient access to food in 2026, the highest figure in six years.

In the North-east, prolonged conflict continues to restrict access to farmland and undermine household livelihoods, according to the ICRC.

World.title: Nigeria’s fiscal crisis forced us to be creative, look beyond oil revenues – Cardoso
World.content:
Olayemi Cardoso, the governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, said on Thursday that Nigeria’s fiscal crisis forced the monetary and fiscal authorities to be creative in revenue generation and stabilisation efforts.

Mr Cardoso spoke on Thursday while featuring on a high-level panel themed “Debate on the Global Economy: Forging Resilient and Dynamic Economies for the Future”, held on the sidelines of the World Bank/IMF meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

Moderated by Lisa Abramowicz, co-host of “Bloomberg Surveillance”, the debate was put together to explore how countries can build resilient and dynamic economies in an increasingly fragmented and uneven global landscape, using resilience as the common thread across the three segments.

Speaking on the panel, Mr Cardoso said the fiscal reality of the Nigerian state when the new administration came into power forced policy makers to be creative in their solution ideas.

“When you are going through a crisis, it forces you to be creative,” Mr Cardoso said.

Nigeria’s gross external reserves stand at $55.1 billion, with net foreign reserves at about $46 billion, according to recent updates from the Central Bank of Nigeria, amid relative stability in the foreign exchange market.

The CBN governor explained that the government inherited a situation where external reserves dropped to about $3 billion and the nation was owing about $7 billion in sundry obligations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The orthodox monetary policy helped to pay the debt and stabilise the economy, Mr Cardoso said, adding that it was clear to the CBN that reliance on oil revenue was not a sustainable model.

“We had to be creative as to how we diversify,” he said, adding that the apex bank looked at the diaspora and international remittances to remove all the bottlenecks and ease capital flow.

Mr Cardoso said the CBN embraced how to do things differently, and changed from ways that were not sustainable, as part of measures needed to create value.

“It seemed impossible to everybody and people laughed,” he said of the degree of scepticism the CBN leadership faced, adding that the policy decisions paid off.

The Central Bank Governor added that the nation is now looking in the direction of value addition, while making reference to the Dangote Refinery and its potential contributions to growth and foreign exchange stability.

Participants looked at how economies, firms, and institutions can preserve stability and withstand recurrent shocks despite more limited policy space, how they can sustain balanced growth amid widening global divergences, and how they can harness AI, innovation, and productivity-enhancing reforms to expand opportunity and growth.

The debate featured Kristalina Georgieva, Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kyriakos Pierrakakis, the Minister of Economy and Finance of the Hellenic Republic, and other experts.

World.title: How Toluwanisings died – Singer’s PA
World.content:
Babadunni Gbolabo, the personal assistant (PA) to late gospel singer Olayemi “Toluwanisings” Bolaji, has revealed that efforts to save the singer’s life took them to between seven and eight hospitals.

The revelation offers further details about the singer’s final hours after his family confirmed his death on Wednesday.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the singer’s family didn’t state the cause of death or explain the circumstances surrounding it.

Speaking to the BBC at the late singer’s residence in Alakia, Ibadan, Oyo State, on Thursday, Mr Gbolabo said Toluwanisings slumped in the early hours of Wednesday.

He said he was away when the incident occurred but received a call about the singer’s condition. He later arrived at the residence and joined others who tried to rescue him.

He said: “They carried him and tried everything to save him. At every hospital he was taken to, some said the doctors were on strike, some said the doctors weren’t on the ground, and some said they couldn’t admit him.

“That is what happened. We tried our best to save him, with prayers and everything. We took him to seven to eight hospitals in Ibadan, Oyo State. But God said it was his time.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He’s fine

Mr Gbolabo further said Toluwanisings showed no signs of illness before he suddenly slumped, adding that the singer was in good health.

He said the singer’s band members and others were waiting for his family to arrive before deciding on the next course of action.

“The next step is for the family members who are already here, so we are doing everything together. He is in the mortuary once the family finishes its meeting.

“We will do whatever they agree on. Some of them are not here yet, and they have not done the necessary things,” said Mr Gbolabo.

Backstory

This newspaper earlier reported that news of Toluwanisings’ death emerged on social media on Wednesday afternoon, leaving fans worried and uncertain until his family confirmed the reports.

Following the confirmation, colleagues, friends and fans took to social media to express their grief and pay tribute to the late singer.

READ ALSO: Gospel singer Toluwanisings is dead

Toluwanisings was a gospel singer, songwriter and music minister known for his energetic praise sessions and worship songs infused with Yoruba influences.

Some of his well-known songs include “Kabiyesi Olorun Ayo”, “Unreserved Praise”, “A Very Big God”, “Onibuore”, “Eleda” and “I’m Not Alone”.

He developed a passion for music early on and began singing in church choirs before taking further steps toward a career in gospel music.

Throughout his career, he collaborated with gospel artistes, including Tosin Bee and Adeyinka Alaseyori.

World.title: How ex-SUG president died at NYSC camp – Official
World.content:
A member of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), Etimbuk Daniel, has been confirmed dead while undergoing his compulsory three-week orientation course at the NYSC camp in Enugu State.

PREMIUM TIMES learnt that Mr Daniel was the immediate past president of the Students’ Union Government (SUG) of the Akwa Ibom State University.

The deceased hailed from Akwa Ibom State, South-south Nigeria.

Governor Umo Eno of Akwa Ibom announced this in a statement by his spokesperson, Ekerete Udo, which was posted on Facebook on Wednesday.

Mr Eno described the death of the former SUG president as a painful and devastating loss, not only to his family but to the entire student community of Akwa Ibom State.

“I received with sadness the news of the tragic passing of Comrade Etimbuk Daniel, a promising young leader whose life was cut short while answering the call to serve our nation,” the governor was quoted as saying in the statement.

He condoled with the bereaved family, leadership and members of the National Association of Akwa Ibom State Students, as well as the entire student community of Akwa Ibom extraction across the world over the loss.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Our youths are our future, and losing such a brilliant young man, with a bright future ahead of him, is deeply painful. His passing represents a huge loss to our State and the student community he served with dedication.

“At this difficult moment, I pray that God Almighty grants his family, friends, colleagues and the entire student community the fortitude to bear this painful loss,” the governor stated.

He did not specifically mention when the former SUG president died in the NYSC camp.

Allegations of fake drug

Meanwhile, the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) earlier alleged that fake drugs and delayed medical attention might have contributed to the death of the former students’ leader at the NYSC camp.

NANS President Akinteye Afeez, in a statement posted on Facebook on Sunday, said he received a report of Mr Daniel’s death with “a rude shock.”

Mr Afeez said the information available to the students’ indicated that the late Daniel complained of a headache and was administered some medication while at the NYSC camp.

“Unfortunately, his condition reportedly worsened after taking the drugs. He requested to be taken to the hospital, but the necessary approval allegedly came too late, and he passed away before he could be taken for medical attention,” he said.

The NANS president continued: “We were further informed that the doctor later identified the drugs administered to him as fake.

“These are deeply troubling allegations that require a thorough investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding his tragic death.”

Mr Afeez stressed that the student community had now entered into mourning even as he condoled with the family, friends, colleagues, and the entire Akwa Ibom State University community over the loss.

“The menace of fake drugs continues to pose a grave threat to lives in our society, and this tragic incident underscores the urgent need for accountability, proper medical care, and stronger measures to protect the lives of our young people,” he said.

“NANS is mourning this painful loss, and our further actions and official position on the matter will be communicated in due course.”

PREMIUM TIMES could not independently verify the claim that the NYSC member died after a fake drug was administered on him.

Also the paper could not immediately confirm that the former SUG president passed after approval to transfer him to the hospital came late.

Like Governor Eno, Mr Afeez did not specifically mention when Mr Daniel died at the NYSC camp.

However, there are indications that the former students’ leader died in the first week of October given that he posted last on Facebook on 4 October, about six days before the report of his death surfaced.

READ ALSO: Police chief speaks on alleged ransom payment for freed 20 NYSC members

NYSC authorities yet to speak

PREMIUM TIMES attempted to contact the NYSC Enugu State Secretariat on Wednesday to respond to allegations that a fake drug was administered on him and that the approval to move to the hospital came late.

A mobile phone number belonging to the NYSC Enugu State Secretariat was unreachable when our reporter dialled the phone line.

The secretariat was also yet to respond to a text message sent through the mobile number on Wednesday.

This newspaper also sent the same enquiry to the secretariat’s email address on Wednesday. But the secretariat was yet to respond as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Soldiers, terrorists killed in midnight terror attack on Borno military base
World.content:
About 20 security officers and an unspecified number of terrorists were killed during a Tuesday midnight terror attack on a military base in Borno State.

Security sources told PREMIUM TIMES that the attack, by jihadists either belonging to Boko Haram or the rival Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), targeted the military base in Mairari, Guzamala Local Government Area (LGA).

Corroborating one another, the sources said 15 soldiers and five members of the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF) were killed in the encounter.

The LG chairperson, Umar Sheriff, confirmed the attack to Punch, saying military operatives repelled it. Locals also told the newspaper that many terrorists were killed.

However, the military has not released any official statement about the attack. The spokesperson for Operation Hadin Kai, a joint task force in the North-east, Mohammed Goni, has not responded to a PREMIUM TIMES enquiry into the incident.

READ ALSO: Eight soldiers reported dead as troops foil terror attack in Borno

Last month, an ISWAP attack on a military position in Mairari was repelled by military forces with aerial support. Four ISWAP terrorists were killed in the attack, and a cache of weapons including a camera was recovered.

Boko Haram insurgency has lingered for more than a decade, with experts warning that the war is not close to its end as a new generation of fighters now dominates the battlefield amid challenges posed by the increasing use of new technologies.
