World.title: Africa: New TB Vaccines Could Save Millions, but Africa Must Prepare Now
World.content:
interview

More than a century after the BCG vaccine was licensed, new tuberculosis vaccines could arrive in 2029. Gavi says the groundwork has to start now.

TB remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, causing around 1.2 million deaths every year - equivalent to roughly one death every 26 seconds. Africa still records the highest rates of cases and deaths of any region. The burden remains substantial despite progress in diagnosis, treatment and prevention.

For more than 100 years, the only licensed defence has been the Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.

But now, a new generation of vaccines could offer a major breakthrough in the fight against the disease, potentially saving 7.3 million lives between 2030 and 2050, according to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance. The opportunity, however, will depend on more than scientific progress. This will include ensuring that vaccines reach the countries and communities that need them most, which will require early planning, sufficient manufacturing capacity, sustainable financing and equitable access.

The next-generation TB vaccines will potentially become available from 2029. Gavi is urging governments and global health partners to prepare now, before the first products are approved.

Closing the gaps in TB prevention

Africa has made significant progress in expanding access to diagnosis, treatment and prevention. However, significant gaps remain, with many people diagnosed late or not at all, while others struggle to access treatment.

Emily Kobayashi, Director of Vaccine Programmes at Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, said these gaps allow TB to continue spreading within communities, particularly among people living in poverty, overcrowded environments and areas with fragile health systems.

"Too many people with TB are diagnosed too late, or not at all, and others fail to access treatment," she said.

Closing those gaps, Kobayashi said, will take both stronger delivery of proven interventions and new tools. She said that the existing BCG vaccine remains vital in protecting infants and young children against severe forms of TB. However, it has limited impact on pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults, who account for most TB transmission.

"New vaccine candidates are being developed specifically to address this gap," she said. "If successful, they could represent the first major breakthrough in TB prevention in more than a century."

She said that the vaccines could offer a real opportunity to dramatically reduce transmission, save millions of lives and accelerate progress towards ending one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases.

Next-generation vaccines, if proven safe and effective, could complement existing prevention, diagnosis and treatment efforts by reducing the number of people who develop infectious TB.

"Next-generation TB vaccines can help to further bend the curve, meaningfully reducing the number of people getting sick with TB," she said. "In practical terms, it means millions of families being spared the devastating consequences of TB, with fewer parents, teenagers and breadwinners becoming seriously ill or dying from a disease that remains one of the world's leading infectious killers."

GAVI Emily Kobayashi, Director of Vaccine Programmes at Gavi.

For countries with a high TB burden, she said, a successful vaccine could also reduce pressure on health systems, lower treatment costs and boost economic productivity by helping adolescents and adults stay healthy during their most productive years. However, Kobayashi cautioned that the ultimate impact would depend on the characteristics of the vaccines approved and how quickly countries could introduce them.

She said the projected 7.3 million lives saved highlights why new TB vaccines are considered one of the most significant public health opportunities in decades.

Preparing for demand and securing supply

For Africa, where TB continues to cause significant illness and death, the question is not only whether new vaccines will work, but whether they will be accessible and affordable when they become available.

Kobayashi said that figure shows where the new vaccines must be prioritised. "The greatest health impact will come from reaching the communities where the disease continues to cause the most illness and death," she said.

That is why Gavi's focus from the outset has been on readiness. If a vaccine is successfully developed and approved, the countries carrying the heaviest burden need to be able to access and introduce it as quickly as possible. "Working with governments and partners," she said, "we want those most affected by TB to benefit first."

Gavi's Early Market Shaping Roadmap for Novel TB Vaccines suggests demand could average 86 million vaccination courses a year, with high-burden countries needing substantial supplies during the initial rollout.

The roadmap estimates that global demand could average 86 million vaccination courses annually. The vaccines could also generate up to US$135 billion in economic benefits for low- and middle-income countries, according to Gavi analysis.

One of the principal risks, said Kobayashi, is uncertainty over future demand. Manufacturers must be confident that sufficient demand will exist to justify investing in production capacity before a vaccine receives regulatory approval.

Manufacturers need confidence that there will be sufficient demand for the vaccine to justify investments in production capacity before a vaccine is licensed. Without that confidence, there is a risk that supply may not increase quickly enough to roll out the vaccine broadly after the evidence comes from the ongoing trials. That is why early planning is so important, she said. Working with countries, manufacturers and partners to describe future demand and likely introduction timelines, which she said can help reduce uncertainty and encourage investments that then support adequate supply.

Between now and 2029, Kobayashi said, several things must happen in parallel.

First, vaccine candidates must successfully complete clinical trials and demonstrate that they are safe and effective. At the same time, country governments, manufacturers and global health partners need to prepare for widespread access to the vaccine. This includes understanding future demand for the vaccine, planning how it will be delivered to communities, assessing manufacturing needs, developing policy recommendations and ensuring financing is available the moment a vaccine is licensed.

Simi Vijay/WHO Low funding, COVID-19 curtail tuberculosis fight in Africa.

"The key lesson from previous vaccine introductions is that preparation cannot start after approval," she said. "It needs to begin well in advance."

Kobayashi pointed to the malaria vaccine rollout as an example of how early coordination among partners can support rapid scale-up, with preparations taking place while vaccines were still undergoing trials. It resulted in one of the fastest rollouts in Gavi's history.

For African countries, this means considering how potential vaccines would be integrated into existing immunisation and TB programmes, which populations should be prioritised and what resources would be needed to deliver doses effectively.

Beyond preventing illness and death, next-generation TB vaccines could also contribute to efforts to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR), including drug-resistant TB.

Drug-resistant TB is one of the most challenging forms of the disease because it is difficult, lengthy and expensive to treat. It can take a significant toll on individuals and families, often requiring prolonged treatment and time away from work or school. By preventing TB disease in the first place, she said, vaccines can reduce the number of people requiring treatment and help limit opportunities for drug resistance to develop or spread.

Kobayashi said that is why vaccination is increasingly recognised as an important part of the broader response to AMR alongside diagnosis, treatment and infection control. Vaccines can help reduce reliance on antibiotics and contribute to long-term efforts to combat AMR.

Making sure access is equitable

The risk with any new vaccine is that it reaches wealthier or lower-risk populations first. Gavi said its focus is on the countries with the highest TB burden, most of which are low- and middle-income.

Drawing on more than two decades of experience supporting vaccine introductions and shaping vaccine markets, she said the goal is "to help ensure that public health need drives access." If a new vaccine becomes available, she added, the countries hardest hit "should be among the first to benefit."

Why now?

Kobayashi said the urgency of preparing for new TB vaccines was underscored by the continuing toll of the disease, which claims around 1.2 million lives globally each year. Africa bears a disproportionate share of the burden, with the region continuing to face high rates of TB cases and deaths despite progress in prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

At the same time, she said, the world was closer than it had been in decades to developing a new vaccine that could protect the communities most affected by TB and responsible for much of its transmission.

"This combination of urgent need and scientific progress makes now the moment to start preparing," said Kobayashi.

She warned that the decisions made before the vaccines become available, including forecasting demand, planning delivery strategies and ensuring adequate supply, would help determine how rapidly people will benefit from these vaccines and how much impact they can ultimately have on reducing the global burden of TB.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 15, 2026
World.content:
Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case Linked to First Patient

Kenya has confirmed a second Ebola case, 10 days after a 40-year-old man died from the virus following travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) through Uganda. The new patient, a 39-year-old close relative of the first victim, was already in quarantine when he developed symptoms. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Health officials said that both cases are linked, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Authorities have traced 128 contacts of the first patient, 113 of whom are in quarantine. Efforts to find the remaining contacts continue. Kenya has maintained that travel, trade and public gatherings remain unrestricted. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year.



Mauritius Imposes Curfew After Violent Protests

Mauritius has imposed an overnight curfew following violent protests over water shortages and the rising cost of living, marking the island's worst unrest in decades. Demonstrations escalated after a woman was shot and injured by police at a roadblock. The circumstances of the shooting were not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody. Protesters burned tyres, blocked roads and vandalised police stations and public infrastructure, prompting school and public transport closures. Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam warned that those responsible would face consequences. Police reported some overnight incidents and arrests. Analysts warn that unrest could return if water shortages persist until the rainy season in December.

Sudan's War Deepens Humanitarian and Food Crisis

Fighting between Sudan's Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season. The conflict, which began in April 2023, has displaced more than 12.4 million people and left an estimated 24.6 million facing acute food insecurity. Aid organisations warn that hundreds of thousands of young children are suffering severe malnutrition. Drought, flooding, fuel shortages and declining fertiliser supplies are worsening food production and prices. The UN's 2026 humanitarian response plan, requiring US$2.9 billion, is only 41% funded. Observers also warn that continued arms supplies and drone attacks are prolonging the conflict and increasing civilian casualties.

Amnesty Warns of Continued Abuses in Mali Despite Wagner's Replacement

Amnesty International has warned that serious human rights abuses against civilians in Mali continue despite the Russian-backed Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group in supporting Malian military operations. The organisation documented seven incidents between 2023 and 2025 in which 34 civilians were allegedly deliberately killed, alongside torture, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, looting and destruction of property. Members of Fulani, Tuareg and Arab communities along the Mauritanian border were among those most affected. Amnesty also cited allegations of abuses by Africa Corps members, including a July 2026 raid in Bombori in which six people were reportedly shot dead and three others executed. It called for independent investigations to hold accountable those suspected of war crimes and for greater protection for civilians.

DR Congo Cholera Cases Surge Amid Ebola Outbreak

The World Health Organisation has said that from January 2025 to the end of September 2026, there were more than 125,000 suspected cases of cholera and 3,644 suspected deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 2026, there were more than 51,400 suspected cases and 1,487 deaths in 21 provinces. Most of the cases were in South Kivu, North Kivu, and Haut-Katanga, which together made up almost 60% of the cases. Response efforts are being hampered by a lack of clean water and toilets, as well as by safety concerns and problems getting to remote communities. Health authorities are expanding water chlorination, household disinfection and vaccination preparations, including a planned cross-border campaign with the Republic of Congo. The crisis comes as the DR Congo continues to battle Ebola, with neighbouring Kenya recently confirming a second case linked to the outbreak.

Close 

Foot-and-Mouth Restrictions Push Up Meat Prices in Namibia

Foot-and-mouth disease restrictions in Namibia are causing meat shortages and price increases at butcheries and restaurants as limits on livestock sales and slaughtering disrupt supplies. Butchers report rising costs for meat trimmings and cheaper cuts traditionally used to make mince and sausages, forcing some businesses to switch to more expensive cuts and raise prices. Restaurants have also increased prices for selected dishes, including rump, sirloin and T-bone steaks. Others are absorbing higher supplier costs to avoid passing them on to customers. Some small businesses say they cannot obtain livestock at all, threatening their ability to operate. The disease has spread to 17 farms in the ||Kharas region. Positive cases have also been reported in the Zambezi region.

World.title: Mauritius: Mauritius Imposes Curfew After Violent Protests
World.content:
Mauritius has imposed an overnight curfew following violent protests over water shortages and the rising cost of living, marking the island's worst unrest in decades.

Demonstrations escalated after a woman was shot and injured by police at a roadblock. The circumstances of the shooting were not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.

Protesters burned tyres, blocked roads and vandalised police stations and public infrastructure, prompting school and public transport closures.

The British embassy in Mauritius cautioned its citizens about the possibility of further demonstrations, advising them to steer clear of protests and large gatherings. The French embassy also urged French nationals in the country to remain vigilant.

Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam warned that those responsible would face consequences.

Analysts warn that unrest could return if water shortages persist until the rainy season in December.

World.title: South Africa: Katlehong Shooting Suspect in Court - South African News Briefs - October 15, 2026

press review

Katlehong Memorial Shooting Suspect in Court

A suspect linked to the deadly shooting of four men at a gathering of mourners in Katlehong, on the East Rand, is set to appear in the Palm Ridge Magistrates Court, reports EWN. The victims were attending a memorial service for ANC branch chairperson Jeanette Magugu, who was killed outside her home. Two children were also injured in the shooting. The Gauteng Political Killings Task Team is investigating whether the attack was politically motivated and linked to the upcoming elections.

Mkhwanazi, Co-Accused Back in Court Over Gem Theft



Former Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Police Department deputy chief Julius Mkhwanazi and three co-accused are set to return to the Johannesburg Magistrates' Court, reports SABC News. The four, Mkhwanazi, Witness K (from the Madlanga Commission), Adrian Mackenzie and Keisha Leigh Stols, face allegations linked to the theft of precious stones worth approximately R14.9 million during an alleged bogus police raid in Killarney, Johannesburg. The case was previously postponed to allow the defence more time to study a lengthy docket. The State maintains it is ready for trial. The allegations also featured at the Madlanga Commission, where Witness K testified about the alleged planning of the raid with Mkhwanazi, who denies the allegations.

Calls for Action Against Disinformation and Incitement

Campaign for Free Expression executive director Nicole Fritz has warned that disinformation surrounding a Constitutional Court ruling on asylum seekers, which fuelled unrest in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng, threatens South Africa’s constitutional democracy, reports EWN. Fritz said freedom of expression does not protect incitement to imminent violence or hate speech intended to cause harm. World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Children Left Behind in Ebola Outbreak Response
World.content:
Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). While children face a higher risk of death from Ebola than adults, they also represent a significant proportion of those affected by the current outbreak. According to Epicentre, MSF’s epidemiological research centre, nearly one in four confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu is a child. Médecins sans Frontières (MSF) is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact of the disease on children and calls for more attention to their specific vulnerabilities in both the medical and research response.

While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. In North Kivu, children have been particularly affected by the current outbreak: 24% of confirmed cases are among children under five years of age, compared with 13% in Ituri, while infants under one year old account for 13% of cases, compared with 6% in Ituri. At the Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have observed that the case fatality rate among children was particularly high. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children—most of whom under the age of five—died from the Bundibugyo virus in this ETC alone. The rapid progression of the disease in communities and limited access to specialised care at the health facility level are contributing to such alarmingly high fatality rates.

“Primary health facilities often lack the specialized expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside healthcare facilities.” Strengthening infection prevention and control (IPC) measures in health facilities, ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE), and reinforcing the training of healthcare workers in non-Ebola health centres across at-risk areas are critical to maintaining essential services while preventing healthcare-associated transmission.



While efforts have been made to reduce the emotional toll of isolation on children in ETCs, including the creation of visibility areas where parents can see and communicate with their hospitalised children, being admitted to an Ebola Treatment Centre remains a deeply distressing experience for young patients. Children may be too young to understand their situation or meet their own basic needs. To help address this situation, MSF has recruited and trained caregivers who provide daily support and comfort to children inside several MSF-supported ETCs while wearing full personal protective equipment (PPE). These caregivers come from diverse backgrounds, including but not limited to Ebola survivors. Today, 13 caregivers are supporting children at Kitatumba Ebola Treatment Centre in Butembo. While far from a perfect solution, this initiative provides essential human contact and emotional support for children facing the outbreak.

"On top of enormous challenges caring for young patients, medical facilities are dealing with a lack of paediatric dosing guidance, and limited availability of child-friendly formulations of investigational medicines. A child-centred approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts", said Dr. Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF.

Children have been disproportionately affected by the current outbreak, yet they are left behind when it comes to access to innovative medical tools. Historically, children are often excluded from clinical research or included only after significant delays, creating dangerous gaps in evidence and access to potentially life-saving interventions.

"Treatments, vaccines, and other preventive tools should be evaluated for use in children from the outset of research efforts and made available to them without delay. Yet in the current outbreak, children are still being left behind, with very limited access to vaccination trials and campaigns, as well as the latest therapeutic innovations despite bearing a significant burden of disease. Children cannot continue to wait for data generated in adults before benefiting from advances in Ebola care and prevention," added Dr. Guyguy Manangama.

Close 

MSF urges national authorities, research institutions, pharmaceutical developers, and international funders to prioritise the inclusion of children in all ongoing and future Bundibugyo virus studies. Ensuring equitable access to research and new medical tools, including vaccines, is essential to reducing preventable deaths and improving outcomes for one of the most vulnerable groups.

The impact of the outbreak on children extends beyond Ebola infection itself. Disruptions to essential health services can rapidly increase risks from vaccine-preventable diseases, malnutrition, and other common childhood illnesses. Preserving routine immunization, nutrition programmes, and access to primary healthcare must therefore be considered a core component of the outbreak response, not an afterthought.

World.title: Africa: WHO Urges Faster Action to End Lead Exposure Which Kills 3.5 Million Annually
World.content:
Countries must accelerate efforts to prevent lead exposure, which is estimated to cause more than 3.5 million deaths globally each year and affects hundreds of millions of children, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Thursday.

The UN agency issued the call ahead of International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week, which runs from 18-26 October.

Although exposure is entirely preventable, fewer than half of countries had confirmed legally binding controls on paint containing lead, according to the agency's latest global assessment.



'Stealing children's potential'

The risks to children are particularly dangerous because their developing brains and nervous systems are highly vulnerable to the toxic effects of lead.

"Lead poisoning should not be stealing children's potential in 2026," said Bruce Gordon, interim director of WHO's Department of Environment, Climate Change, One Health and Migration.

"We know where many exposures come from and we know how to prevent them. Countries now need to move upstream, removing lead from products and environments before it reaches a child's bloodstream."

Irreversible harm, lifelong consequences

Lead contamination can occur through paint, cookware, cosmetics, spices, informal recycling and industrial sources. There is no known safe level of contact, and even relatively low exposure can cause irreversible harm.

Lead poisoning affects multiple organs and contributes to health problems such as cardiovascular and kidney disease in adults and irreversible damage to the brain, health and development of children.

Lifelong consequences include learning difficulties, behavioural issues and poor health. As symptoms may not be immediately visible, many cases go unnoticed until significant damage has already occurred.

Action plan and guidance

WHO Member States have recognized lead exposure as a pressing public health concern and mandated the agency to develop a Global Action Plan on Lead Mitigation that will be presented to the World Health Assembly (N-dash) - WHO's governing body (N-dash) - next year.

The agency will also launch the PREVENT Technical Package on Lead Poisoning Prevention in 2027, to provide countries with practical guidance to identify priority sources of exposure, determine which interventions can have the greatest impact, strengthen and enforce regulations and monitor progress.

Close 

Last year, WHO joined partners in the Lead Poisoning Prevention Initiative to build and improve laboratory capacity to test blood lead levels, thus enabling early detection of lead exposure.

Capacity building and technical support will be implemented in locations in Brazil, India, Nepal and in six countries in sub-Saharan Africa: Ethiopia, Ghana, Malawi, Rwanda, South Africa and Tanzania.

World.title: Chad: New Cameroonian Army Camps Alone Won't Secure Lake Chad
World.content:
analysis

Much-needed military reinforcements against Boko Haram must be matched by sustained territorial control and well-coordinated operations.

Cameroon's Defence Minister Joseph Beti Assomo last month announced the formation of a Rapid Intervention Battalion (BIR) Lake Chad military unit in response to increasing jihadist violence in the Lake Chad region. Recent assaults in Darak, Bargaram and Hilé-Alifa have seen over 11 300 residents flee their homes.

While the new force may enhance immediate protection for civilians, its effectiveness hinges on achieving genuine territorial control and collaboration with neighbouring countries' defence and security forces.

BIR Lake Chad's establishment marks a significant development in a region where remote and under-resourced military outposts have long been a weak point in counter-terrorism efforts.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Military bases at Bargaram and Hilé-Alifa were inaugurated last month to house the new force. Hilé-Alifa features the second-largest barracks for rapid intervention battalions, complete with dormitories, a battalion command post, a company command post, kitchens, fuel tank, garage, police station, gymnasium and medical centre. Bargaram has newly constructed dormitory blocks, a company command post and an infirmary.

During the inauguration of the Hilé-Alifa base, BIR General Coordinator Brigadier-General François Pelene said the new unit would be enhanced by establishing companies in Darak and Blangoua.

BIR Lake Chad's primary goal is to disrupt armed groups' logistical networks and prevent Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) from extending its north-east Nigerian stronghold into northern Cameroon. The new force also aims to establish a permanent presence in areas where jihadists have taxed locals, creating economic and logistical hubs for terrorist activity.

The intensification of operations against Boko Haram's ISWAP and Jama'tu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'awati wal-Jihad (JAS) factions is also intended to bring military forces closer to communities that have fled due to ongoing attacks. Bargaram has become a hotspot for military clashes and civilian assaults. Over three days in February, 668 households comprising 4 223 people left Bargaram and Darak to seek shelter in safer areas such as Blangoua and Hilé-Alifa.

The establishment of new bases and the BIR Lake Chad command post at Hilé-Alifa will streamline decision making and shorten the response time between alerts and interventions. This is important because armed groups often quickly retreat across the border to their bases in northeast Nigeria.

Deploying a force known for its rapid response capabilities in asymmetric combat, adaptability and significant firepower is a crucial response to terrorism. Guided by commanders familiar with the terrain, the militants use reconnaissance and kamikaze drones, and improvised explosive devices. BIR Lake Chad signals a shift from defence to rapid reaction against incursions.

But this transition also requires suitable naval resources to counter groups that have harnessed covert approaches, using papyrus tei-tei rafts combined with audacity, surprise and brutal attacks.

BIR Lake Chad's 1 000 personnel bolster the nearly 500 troops stationed in Makary and Blangoua. The latter are part of the Multinational Joint Task Force's (MNJTF) First Sector, headquartered in Mora, Cameroon. The MNJTF plans to reopen a post in Soueram, where its First Sector's joint battle group - formerly stationed in Wulgo, Nigeria - will be deployed. This group comprises amphibious, field artillery and airborne battalion troops.

With the addition of BIR Lake Chad, Cameroon now has four distinct military units engaged against Boko Haram: the 4th Joint Military Region, BIR Alpha Force, BIR Lake Chad and the Special Forces. Numerous other Cameroonian units operate under the MNJTF First Sector's command.

Alongside these military forces, efforts by the Directorate General for External Research, Cameroon's primary intelligence agency, as well as the police and gendarmerie, should be considered. Introducing the new force could further complicate the 'cacophony on the battlefield' - a term the media used to describe the lack of coordinated action by Cameroonian forces against Boko Haram.

So, beyond the challenges posed by the terrain - including flood zones, swamps, islands and informal waterways - a significant hurdle is coordinating efforts among the various actors involved in countering terrorism. The lack of a unified military command structure makes it hard to concentrate efforts and economise on forces, hampering a coherent response.

Tactical alignment with commanders on the ground is needed to prevent misunderstandings and avoid friendly fire incidents. At the operational level, the 4th Joint Military Region commander's role should be enhanced, with clearly defined responsibilities to prevent overlapping commands. Also, cooperation is needed between personnel under the armed forces' general staff and those supervised by Israeli contractors who report to the president.

Lastly, engaging with the armed forces of Nigeria, Niger and Chad deployed around Lake Chad is essential to addressing this regional challenge.

Close 

During the inauguration of BIR Lake Chad's headquarters, the strategic alignment displayed by the 4th Joint Military Region, 4th Gendarmerie Region and MNJTF First Sector commanders, alongside government officials and local leaders, sends a strong message that coordination is vital.

Above all, the newly established force must be equipped with capabilities that extend its reach beyond its bases. This should ensure that the expansion of barracks and other military infrastructure does not result in some areas being poorly monitored.

In conjunction with ongoing civil-military initiatives, increased land and maritime patrols can provide a security presence in local communities, markets, waterways and lakes, and border areas. Such measures will prevent armed groups from retreating into Nigeria and rearming, and will also help restore the confidence and security needed for displaced civilians to return home.

Raoul Sumo Tayo, Senior Researcher, Central Africa Observatory, ISS

World.title: Franklin Graham shares toll of Billy Graham’s time away evangelizing, recalls not recognizing own father
World.content:

The Rev. Franklin Graham is opening up about the toll his father Billy Graham's worldwide ministry took on their family, recalling a heartbreaking moment when he failed to recognize his own dad after months apart.

"Mama, who's that strange man in the bed with you?" Graham recalled asking his mother after his father returned from a six-month trip to Australia.

The evangelical leader shared the memory, which he attributed to his mother, during an interview on Sean Hannity's podcast, "Hang Out with Sean Hannity," describing how his father's extended travels sometimes kept him away from home for months at a time.

Graham explained that the trip took place before jet aircraft became commonplace, when reaching Australia required multiple stops which drew out the experience along the way, including lengthy layovers in Hawaii and Fiji.

EXCLUSIVE: FRANKLIN GRAHAM VISITS EMERGENCY HOSPITAL TREATING VENEZUELA EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS

"You would fly to Hawaii, then you'd stay a couple of days, then you'd fly to Fiji and stay a couple days, and then you're going down to Sydney or Melbourne or wherever you're going," he recalled.

"But my father spent all that time in Australia, and so when he came home ... we [his children] just didn't recognize him," he added.

Graham said the incident "hurt" his father, whose evangelistic endeavors remained a cornerstone of his life's work. The world-renowned reverend, who spent decades traveling the globe to preach the Gospel, became one of the most influential figures of the 20th century, reaching millions through his evangelistic crusades, television broadcasts and other outreach efforts.

SEAN HANNITY, RILEY GAINES SHOWS AMONG PODCASTS JOINING FOX ONE'S EXPANDED STREAMING PORTFOLIO

Today, Franklin Graham follows in his late father's footsteps, teaching the message of God's word around the world as president and CEO of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and serving as a prominent voice on matters of the Christian faith.

World.title: Trump's intervention in Folarin Balogun red card prompts FIFA to revisit suspension rules: reports
World.content:
It has been four months since Folarin Balogun's suspension from a red card was lifted in controversial fashion, and its effects remain ongoing.

In the United States Men's National Team's Round of 32 World Cup match against Bosnia and Herzegovina, Balogun, the USMNT's best player in the tournament at that point, was given a questionable red card, automatically suspending him for the next game against Belgium.

The day before the match, though, Balogun was ruled eligible to play in the game. Ultimately, it didn't matter, as the U.S. lost, 4-1.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

President Donald Trump admitted to calling FIFA president Gianni Infantino to ask for a review of the red card. Infantino and Trump have grown a relationship, which critics say is a conflict of interest.

Well, reports say that FIFA is set to amend the rules that prohibit red-card suspensions during a large meeting on Thursday.

Infantino, eight vice presidents and 28 other members will meet for the first time since the World Cup, and that's hardly the only controversy surrounding Infantino and FIFA.

PSG’S LUIS ENRIQUE HOPES MAN CITY AVOIDS SANCTIONS AFTER FINANCIAL RULES VERDICT

Nine days after the World Cup final, FIFA proposed details of a company called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would allow private investors to buy shares in the World Cup, a secret plan that was widely criticized and rejected, and then quickly scrapped.

Balogun admitted to CBS he "could almost see within my teammates a bit of nerves" as the controversy brewed further.

"All I did was I asked for a review because I didn’t think it was a foul," Trump said. "And, again, I’m good at this stuff. I didn’t think it was a foul. I thought it was two great athletes who crashed into each other and got entangled. That was not a guy punching somebody in the face or anything, that would be different.

"I think it’s a terrible … if they wouldn’t allow a top player, maybe the best, maybe among the best on the team, to play, I think it would have had a big stain. I relayed it. I didn’t tell him what to do. I don’t believe he made the decision. I think it was a committee that made the decision, and they made the right decision because, No. 1, it wasn’t a foul, and you want to see a game with your best players."



The president was awarded the first FIFA Peace Prize at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., during the World Cup final draw in December. The prize will also be reviewed at Thursday's meeting.

Fox News' Ryan Gaydos, Paulina Dedaj and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Hillary Clinton concedes infamous 9/11 near-fainting episode in 2016 was a 'mistake' on her part
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton revisited the video showing her appearing to stagger and nearly faint after a 9/11 commemoration ceremony in 2016, conceding on Wednesday that campaigning while having pneumonia was a "mistake."

The former secretary of state spoke to Kara Swisher on their new joint podcast about Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico's nine-day absence from the campaign trail after he said he contracted the flu.

His absence from public appearances led to a viral online rumor wrongly alleging that he had secretly been admitted to an Ohio mental health facility, which Clinton and Swisher said was "easily disproven."

HILLARY CLINTON INCLUDES 2016 LOSS IN 'HARD TIMES' LIST FOR DEM VOTERS, INCLUDING 9/11, 2008 FINANCIAL CRISIS

Clinton compared Talarico's experience to her own after the 2016 video went viral as she ran for president, arguing that critics portrayed her as being "on death's door." Swisher said that President Donald Trump was "quantumly sicker" than Clinton had been, though "they hide it," and asked Clinton to respond.

"They tested me and they said, 'Oh, you've got pneumonia. You need to take like five or six days off.' I said, 'I can't do that.' And my doctor said, 'Well, that's what you should do.' And I thought, 'Well, yeah, that's what I should do.' But I'm campaigning and I have to show up on 9/11 because it means a lot to me since, as you know, I was a senator [during the attacks]. So, I kept going, which was a mistake," Clinton recalled.

'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS CHALLENGE JOY BEHAR AFTER SHE SAYS TRUMP'S HEALTH GETS LESS MEDIA SCRUTINY THAN BIDEN'S

She added, "They did have the video of me struggling to get to the car to be able to, you know, take some breaths and recover myself. From my perspective, it worked because it was just papering social media, papering traditional media. 'I was dying. I was lying about my health.' This is from a guy who has never given us an honest medical report ever. Ever."

Fox News Digital reached out to Clinton's team for comment.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said Clinton should think about moving on from the 2016 election.

"President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration, when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people," Ingle told Fox News Digital. "President Trump is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises, and he remains in excellent health. Meanwhile, Crooked Hillary Clinton is still whining about her spectacular 2016 election defeat. It’s time for Hillary to move on."

According to a law enforcement source at the time, Clinton was described as "clearly having some type of medical episode" as she appeared to fall on her way to a van and required help from security. Clinton's campaign later released a statement confirming that she was fighting pneumonia and "felt overheated" at the time.

FIRST ON FOX: A new White House economic report warns that immigration policies backed by the Democratic Socialists of America could cost American taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars over the next decade, as the Trump administration sounds the alarm over the potential financial consequences of mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits.

As President Donald Trump touts 16 consecutive months without illegal immigrant releases at the southern border, a Council of Economic Advisers report estimates that mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits under Democratic Socialists of America-backed immigration policies could cost taxpayers between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade.

Socialist-aligned candidates have gained ground in 2026, winning key Democratic primaries and expanding their influence within the party.

"President Trump … supercharged ICE to remove criminal illegal aliens from our communities, including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members and terrorists," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS

"Meanwhile, radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies and grant amnesty to the illegal aliens they released into our communities. Not only will these radical policies make America less safe, but they will cost the American taxpayer billions of dollars."

With the midterms approaching and Democrats campaigning heavily on affordability, the White House is casting the DSA's immigration agenda as a potential financial and public safety threat — warning that its policies could compound the very cost-of-living pressures Democrats have used to hammer Republicans.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

The council's findings go beyond the cost of mass amnesty, examining the potential impact of expanded federal benefits and reduced immigration enforcement, policies the White House warns could impose a significant financial burden on American families.

The council estimates that the average illegal immigrant carries a lifetime net fiscal cost of $166,716, with the current illegal immigrant population projected to account for between $1.4 trillion and $1.9 trillion in taxpayer costs under its model — figures the administration is highlighting as the "true costs of extreme open borders [and] mass-amnesty socialist policies."

CALIFORNIA FACES UNLIKELY TAX REVOLT AMID BILLIONS IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT HEALTHCARE COSTS

The CEA's estimated $166,716 lifetime taxpayer cost per illegal immigrant exceeds the roughly $124,000 it would cost to put a student through four years at an average in-state public university, including tuition, housing, food and other expenses, according to College Board's 2025–26 figures — putting the figure in perspective as American families also grapple with college affordability.

The Council added that while illegal immigrants are generally prohibited from federal benefit programs, some on the left want to reverse that standard and provide subsidized healthcare and programs like food stamps to those in the country unlawfully.

SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

Beyond expanded federal benefits, the council estimates that ending Trump-backed immigration enforcement measures would wipe out between $227 billion and $287 billion in projected taxpayer savings, producing a net estimated cost of $79 billion to $139 billion over the next decade after accounting for reduced enforcement spending.

An interactive White House webpage released alongside the report allows Americans to explore the projected costs of "socialism" across several policy areas, with the council estimating that the Democratic Socialists of America's broader agenda could cost $49 trillion over ten years — roughly $355,000 per American household. That sweeping projection extends far beyond immigration, which the council separately estimates could cost between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade.

DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS

If the immigration policies examined in the report were implemented, the White House estimates that expanded eligibility for SNAP, federal housing assistance and Medicaid would add between $361 billion and $475 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

The report estimated that expanding federal benefits under the proposed immigration policies would add $3.6 billion to $4.7 billion in annual food stamp costs, another $2.3 billion to $3 billion in federal housing assistance, and as much as $40 billion a year in additional Medicaid spending.

US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

Along with the report, the White House highlighted a 73% uptick in drug interdictions through August 2026 compared with the same period in fiscal year 2024, while separately pointing to declining fentanyl-related deaths as evidence of its broader border enforcement strategy.

The administration also highlighted another key aspect of the immigration-cost paradigm that it changed — remarking that Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for certain foreign-national groups "returned … to its original purpose: temporary."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SLASHES TIME REFUGEES HAVE TO CHALLENGE LOSS OF LEGAL STATUS

The administration's efforts to terminate TPS designations for certain countries have faced legal challenges, underscoring the ongoing dispute over the scope of federal immigration authority.

World.title: Maryland's lone Republican House member calls woman 'rude' for laughing during debate

Maryland's only Republican House member was heard telling a woman "you are rude" after she started laughing while he was speaking during a debate.

The clash between Rep. Andy Harris and the audience member unfolded Tuesday in Cambridge as the Republican was talking about rising diesel prices during the U.S.-Iran war.

"Let's get the facts straight, the facts are that diesel is, the facts are that diesel prices have gone up, there is no question about it. Why has it gone up? Because the Democrats have environmental regulations..." Harris said before he was interrupted by a woman laughing in the audience.

"Ma'am, I gotta tell you. This is the problem, you all say you believe there is a First Amendment, but only if you agree with you," Harris told the crowd. "You should let me finish the sentence, ma'am. You are rude. You're rude, OK?"

AMERICA'S TRUCKERS ISSUE DIRE WARNING AS SOARING DIESEL COSTS THREATEN 'DOMINO EFFECT'

Harris then turned to the debate moderator and said, "I'm sorry," adding that if she wasn't going tell the audience they were rude, he had to do it himself.

"Let me finish the sentence why there is a shortage of diesel in the world and in the country," Harris continued, before another audience member started talking.

"You are rude too. So do you believe in the First Amendment? Do you believe in my First Amendment right to express myself? It's my turn to express myself, not yours," Harris said.

PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEMOCRAT GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION

Harris, who has represented Maryland's 1st Congressional District since 2010, is running for re-election against Democrat challenger Dan Schwartz.

The debate moderator then asked both candidates to speak to their supporters and ask them to be "polite and respectful" during the debate.

"That is very important that you guys are able to hear from both of us tonight, so please if you don't mind, let's keep all reactions for later when you get home and let's let the congressman speak," Schwartz said.

World.title: Apple wants to move into your home. Should you let it?
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Your kitchen counter probably has enough gadgets already. Apple would like to put one more there, and this one recognizes your face. At its "Welcome Home" event on Oct. 13, Apple introduced a $299 smart display called HomeView that promises to make running your home as easy as having a conversation.

And Apple has bigger plans for Siri. The company also unveiled a new HomePod mini, an upgraded Apple TV 4K and a collection of smart home accessories. Together, they could change how you interact with everything from your front door to your television. But there's a catch. Some of the most interesting AI features require compatible Apple devices, and buying into Apple's connected home could get expensive.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

IOS 27 IS HERE: 10 IPHONE FEATURES YOU’LL WANT TO TRY NOW

Apple's $299 HomeView recognizes who's standing in front of it

The biggest announcement from Apple's "Welcome Home" event is HomeView, a new 7-inch touchscreen that doubles as a smart home control center. It sits on a rounded speaker base and comes in four colors. Apple also offers a wall-mounted version for people who would rather keep their countertops clear. Here's where things get interesting. HomeView can recognize up to six household members by their faces. Walk up to the screen, and it can switch to your personalized home screen with your calendar and reminders. Another family member can approach and see their own information instead. Initial setup and support for multiple household members require a compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software, although general Siri AI conversations don't require that device to support Apple Intelligence.

Apple says personal information stays protected through facial recognition and checks involving a paired iPhone or iPad. To display sensitive content, the system requires the recognized person's paired device to be nearby and recently unlocked. That adds an important layer of security, especially in homes where several people share the same screen. Beyond the personalized experience, HomeView handles FaceTime video calls with Center Stage, which keeps you in the frame as you move around. It can display recipes while you're cooking or help locate a missing iPhone using Find My. You can also control compatible smart home equipment without opening another app.

One feature caught my attention. HomeView can display up to nine live security camera feeds simultaneously. You could check a package delivery or see what's happening in the backyard without pulling out your phone. Both HomeView models cost $299. Preorders opened Oct. 13, with availability beginning Nov. 13. However, the wall-mounted version requires a separate mounting accessory, starting at $59.95.

Siri AI wants to become the assistant you've been waiting for

For years, Siri has been useful for simple requests, but longer conversations haven't always gone smoothly. Apple's new Siri AI is designed to change that. It can handle more natural conversations, understand what's displayed on a screen and answer broader questions using information from the web. For example, you could ask Siri to find a recipe someone emailed you or locate a song a friend recommended in a message. With the right device connected, Siri can search relevant personal information and help complete those requests. Apple also says conversations started on HomeView can continue in the Siri app on other compatible Apple devices.

However, there's an important compatibility requirement. HomeView can provide general Siri AI conversations without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. More personalized features require a paired, compatible device running current software with Siri AI enabled. Siri AI on HomeView is also launching in beta. In addition, Apple says certain AI features that use server-based models will have daily usage limits. The company plans to offer expanded access for a fee in the future.

HomePod mini 2 gets better sound, but Siri AI comes later

Apple's HomePod mini 2 is getting its first major refresh. The compact speaker now costs $149 and comes in five colors, including pink and green. Inside, Apple added an S10 chip that processes audio in real time to improve sound performance. There's also a new feature called Sound Glow. The speaker's illuminated top responds to music, changing colors and pulsing along with what you're playing.

The bigger story is what happens when Siri AI arrives. Apple says the speaker will eventually support more natural conversations and personalized requests when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone. It can also recognize different household members by their voices. However, Siri AI won't be available when HomePod mini 2 first ships. Apple says it will arrive through a future software update. That's a pretty important detail if the smarter assistant is your main reason for upgrading. HomePod mini 2 is available for preorder now and goes on sale October 30.

ASKED SIRI TO CALL YOUR BANK? A SCAM COULD COST THOUSANDS

Apple TV 4K finally lets you talk without grabbing the remote

Apple also introduced a new Apple TV 4K, and one of its most useful features has nothing to do with picture quality. The fourth-generation streaming box includes three microphones that can hear Siri requests from across the room. That means you can search for a show or ask a question about what you're watching without reaching for the remote. Siri AI can also handle follow-up questions, such as asking where a program was filmed.

The new Apple TV 4K runs on Apple's A19 chip, which the company says delivers up to 50% faster CPU performance than the previous generation. It also supports a four-speaker surround sound setup using compatible HomePod speakers arranged in matching front and rear pairs. And there's one improvement I think plenty of people will appreciate. The newest Siri Remote can play a sound to help you locate it. It also supports Precision Finding with certain compatible iPhones. That's helpful when the remote disappears somewhere in the couch.

The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and arrives November 13. However, you may not need to buy one to try Siri AI. Apple says the assistant is also available in beta on second-generation Apple TV 4K models and later. To use it, you or the person managing your Apple Home will need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software with Siri AI turned on.

Apple's new smart home collection could make life easier

Apple is also making a bigger push into the connected home with Apple Home Collection. The company worked with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to develop cameras, smart locks and thermostats that connect directly through Apple's Home app. The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock is particularly interesting. It uses Ultra Wideband technology to recognize when someone approaches with a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch carrying a home key. The door can then unlock automatically without requiring a tap. You can also use a PIN or backup key. The lock starts at $349.95.

Apple also introduced an LG video doorbell with two cameras. One captures visitors while the other helps monitor packages left near the doorstep. It starts at $249.95. Meanwhile, an indoor camera starting at $199.95 can automatically tilt down to stop monitoring when a household member returns home. For temperature control, LG and Schneider Electric are offering smart thermostats starting at $199.95. Using Apple's Home app, supported systems can adjust heating and cooling based on whether someone is home. In eligible locations, they can also respond to electricity rates to help manage energy costs. One convenience I like is that these accessories work directly through Apple's Home app. You don't need to create separate manufacturer accounts or download additional apps to manage them. Apple says the collection will start arriving in December, with certain products following in early 2027.

What happens to your privacy when Siri moves into your house?

This is the part of Apple's announcement that deserves a closer look. A screen that recognizes your face can be convenient, especially when several people share a home. But what happens when that same system connects to your security cameras and personal information? Apple says HomeView uses protected processing environments called Secure Exclaves to isolate camera and microphone data from the rest of the system. Separately, HomeView checks that it recognizes the user's face and that their paired iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked before displaying personal information. Siri requests can run directly on the device or use Apple's Private Cloud Compute technology. Apple says data processed through Private Cloud Compute is neither stored nor accessible to the company.

For compatible security cameras, Apple also supports end-to-end encrypted HomeKit Secure Video storage. Certain AI video summaries and recording features require an eligible iCloud+ subscription. Those safeguards are encouraging. Still, I would want to understand exactly which household members can access the system before setting everything up. I'd also review camera placement and sharing permissions, particularly for devices inside the home. For additional privacy guidance, see our CyberGuy article, Are Apple devices spying?

APPLE'S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: HOW TO CLAIM UP TO $95

What this means to you

Apple's latest announcements could make managing a connected home easier, especially for households that already rely on iPhones. HomeView gives you a shared control center, while the upgraded Siri could make everyday requests feel more natural. However, the cost adds up quickly. HomeView starts at $299, and the new Apple TV 4K costs another $299. Add compatible cameras or a smart lock, and you're spending considerably more. Some camera features also require an iCloud+ subscription.

There's also the question of how much of this technology you actually need. If you already have a smart speaker that controls your lights and a television that streams your favorite shows, Apple's latest hardware may offer more convenience than you need. I'd start by checking which Apple devices you already own and whether they'll support the new Siri features. Then think about which upgrades would actually make your day easier. After all, spending hundreds of dollars to save a few taps on your phone deserves a little consideration.

Kurt's key takeaways

Apple wants a bigger role in our homes, and I can see the appeal. I like the idea of asking Siri a question without having to repeat myself or reaching for my phone every time I want to control something. And for families juggling different schedules, a smart display that recognizes who's using it could be genuinely helpful. But I'm still not convinced everyone needs another screen in the house. Will Siri AI finally be as smart and helpful as Apple promises? And how comfortable should we feel giving an AI assistant access to our personal information and home security cameras? Apple has outlined some strong privacy protections, but I'd want to know exactly what information these devices collect and who can access it. For now, I'd be selective. If your current devices work well, there's no reason to rush out and replace them. HomeView has some interesting possibilities, but at $299, I'd want it to make my day easier in a meaningful way. The real test will be how well all these products work together once they're in our homes.

Would you feel comfortable having an AI-powered screen that recognizes your face and connects to your home's security cameras? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Suspicious white powder sent to election offices in 3 states
World.content:
Secretaries of state’s offices in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma were sent packages this week with mysterious powders, just weeks before the offices are set to oversee the midterm elections.

Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it.

The national groups representing secretaries of state and state election directors expressed concern about the suspicious letters in a letter Wednesday.

“As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties,” the National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement.

“Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities,” the statement added.

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday echoed the sentiment that election officials should “never have to fear for their personal safety while performing their duties,” adding that his office was working with state and federal law enforcement following the mailing targeting it.

“Fortunately, delivery of the letter was preempted by investigators at the U.S. Postal Service, who are dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states,” LaRose said, while thanking the Postal Service.

Ohio is one of a few states facing tight elections in just a few weeks.

The election bodies of Oklahoma and Louisiana, facing fewer contested elections, were threatened Tuesday, when each state announced it had received packages with suspicious powders.

“We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today’s incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections,” Oklahoma State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said in a statement.

Louisiana Secretary of State spokesperson Trey Williams said in an email Wednesday that an employee in the office’s Election Division opened a package containing a white powder and was taken uninjured to the emergency room “as a precaution.” Williams added that law enforcement did not find evidence of “harmful substances.”

“Tuesday’s event did not impact any election operations in preparation for the upcoming election,” Williams said.

Louisiana State Police said in a statement that it responded to reports of a white powdery substance found in a package at the secretary of state’s office.

“LSP is working with the FBI to identify the substance, which was successfully recovered and submitted for testing at the FBI’s crime lab. No employees have reported injuries or adverse health effects related to the incident,” state police spokesperson Jacob Pucheu said in an emailed statement.

NBC affiliate KTAL of Shreveport reported Tuesday that the Baton Rouge building was evacuated.

The FBI declined in an email to confirm specific instances or locations. The agency said in a statement that it and the Postal Service were “investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.”

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the FBI’s national press office said.

It is not the first time that states’ election officials have faced threats near an election. In 2024, at least 20 states were targeted with letters containing suspicious powders. In one instance in Utah, a mailing with a suspicious powder was intercepted, with a letter signed by a so-called United States Traitor Elimination Army.

The mailings prompted several agencies, including the Justice Department, to release guidance about protecting personnel against hazardous materials.

World.title: DOJ threatens legal action against California over alleged noncitizen voters
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department is threatening legal action against California unless state and local officials review a list of potential noncitizen individuals on their voter rolls.

Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter on Tuesday sent letters to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan with a list of names of possible noncitizens identified by the federal government. The letters demand they review the list by noon on Thursday.

“Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” McCotter wrote in the letters, which was obtained by NBC News.

McCotter wrote that the DOJ provided a password-protected thumb drive with a list of individuals the federal government “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the 2026 election. He asked that county election officials “segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots” until their citizenship status was determined.

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections,” a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement. “It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”

Reuters first reported on the letters.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said the federal government has no authority supporting its demands.

“They can send the letter,” he said. “California doesn’t have to do anything about it.”

Federal law prohibits systemic list maintenance within 90 days of a federal election. At this point, less than three weeks out from Election Day, the only changes to the voter rolls can come from individualized information, like notification from the Social Security Administration that someone has died.

A DOJ spokesperson said the department is asking California to sequester ballots, not change their voter list.

In a statement Wednesday, Logan said his office had not accessed the thumb drive the DOJ provided “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” He added, “We do not consider the device a secure medium.”

“Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office,” Logan said in the statement. “Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”

Weber said in a statement Wednesday that the DOJ did not provide a list of purported noncitizens to her office and that the administration lacked the legal authority for its request.

“The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said in the statement. “California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election.”

All registered voters in California receive mail-in ballots, which started going out on Oct. 5.

The legal threats came amid a broader campaign by the Trump administration to zero in on what voting experts say is a relatively rare phenomenon of voting by noncitizen individuals. Trump has long made unfounded claims that voting is marred by widespread fraud.

Election officials in several states — including Georgia, Connecticut, Nevada and Washington state — say they have received federal subpoenas in recent months for election records.

Some officials said they fear these actions were designed to set up possible legal challenges after the midterm elections.

“What we have seen is some groundwork laid out for postelection challenges,” said Stuart Holmes, the director of elections in Washington state. “Whether that’s the seizure of voting equipment, ballots themselves, tabulation equipment ... we’re preparing for any and all eventualities in that case.”

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said officials in his state are also preparing for potential challenges to this November’s results. He added that he viewed the administration’s moves as “an effort to dissuade people from participating in the elections.”

“You have a president who’s trying to choose the voter base rather than the voters choosing the elected, and that’s not how our democracy works,” he said in an interview. “It’s the people control our elections, and when you try to take that control out, you do it through intimidation, you do it through threats, and you do it by trying to dissuade people from participating.”

Levitt agreed with the election officials’ conclusions.

“Are they laying the groundwork to say that voting was fraudulent? Of course they are, 100% they are,” he said, referring to the Trump administration. “Is the boy who cried wolf going to cry wolf? Yes, that’s what the boy who cried wolf does.”

Since Trump took office, his administration has brought over 100 cases involving allegations of voting by noncitizens. More than 154 million people voted in the 2024 election, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.

During the second Trump administration, the DOJ has sought voter registration data from every state in the country. It has filed lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing.

World.title: Inflation hit businesses even harder than consumers last month
World.content:
Businesses were hit by inflation last month at levels not seen since late 2022.

The latest U.S. wholesale inflation report showed that the prices businesses paid to produce goods in September jumped sharply, to 6.3% on an annual basis.

From August, prices overall rose 0.6%, the producer price index report showed.

The PPI report is typically seen as a sign of what’s to come for consumer prices, and this one followed a consumer price index report Wednesday that also reflected a jump in prices.

Both reports indicate that inflation is back on the rise. But unlike high inflation earlier this year, the current effects of rising prices are distributed broadly across the entire economy — beyond merely those sectors exposed to soaring gas, diesel and jet fuel prices.

The consumer and producer price indexes are also the last major inflation readings before voters across the country head to the polls in the midterm elections. At many locations, early voting is already underway.

Oil and gas prices have soared ever since the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.

“Half of the September increase” in producer prices was from the rising cost of gas, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Thursday.

Likewise, prices for “diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose.”

Economists say that the most troubling recent price hikes have been those for diesel.

Diesel fuel is critical to powering the farming, transportation and shipping sectors. When diesel prices go up, the knock-on effects of those higher costs can show up in just about every sector of consumer goods.

Months of efforts by the Trump administration to bring down prices have failed to make a meaningful dent in rising costs.

All of the key numbers in Thursday’s PPI report were far more than had been expected by economists and analysts.

The so-called “core” PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, jumped 0.7% from August. From this time one year ago, it rose 5%.

The report reinforced some market expectations that the Federal Reserve could hike interest rates sooner than expected, during its Oct. 27-28 meeting.

A rate hike would add more pressure on consumers, who are already facing high borrowing costs due to rising bond yields. The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage Thursday was 7.45%.

Bond yields fell sharply Thursday in early trading, although this was primarily because investors were seen as moving money out of interest rate-sensitive tech stocks and into bonds.

Tech stocks have become highly sensitive to interest rates in recent years because the top players are spending hundreds of billions of dollars — much of it borrowed with interest — to build data centers around the world.

World.title: Lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy mistrial says he has felt harassed
World.content:
The lone holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s high-profile murder trial said he had been harassed since the trial ended in September, and doubled down on his stance that he did not have reasonable doubt during deliberations.

The juror, Michael P. Desronvil, was the sole holdout who wanted to convict Clancy in the strangulation deaths of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — in January 2023, other jurors have said since the judge declared a mistrial in the case last month.

“It was like night and day,” Desronvil said of his life before and after becoming the holdout juror.

He spoke with Kayleigh McEnany on “Fox & Friends” on Thursday — his first media appearance since serving on the jury.

Other jurors have described a man they claimed was unwilling to negotiate and hostile in the deliberation room. They said that Desronvil was insistent on convicting Clancy of the murders, but that he was not following the standard of reasonable doubt and had been blocking a unanimous decision.

Through his attorney, Edward Andrew Paltzik, Desronvil has previously denied such claims, saying, “I didn’t have any doubts.”

Michael Desronvil on "Fox & Friends." Fox News

“As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented,” Desronvil said in a statement posted by Paltzik last month.

On Thursday, Desronvil said he “definitely listened” to the other jurors, but added that “some moments in that deliberation room felt like, that decisions would be swayed towards one way.”

McEnany asked Desronvil whether he had reasonable doubt. He replied: “No.” He said he had a lot of evidence to support his reasoning, but declined to share it.

He did, however, say he thought Clancy had thought out the murders, stating how “methodical” he believed she had been “in the execution of the children.”

“That was really big for me,” he added. “I thought it was logical.”

Clancy, who was accused of strangling her three young children to death using exercise bands before allegedly throwing herself out of her home’s second-story window, could have been convicted of first-degree murder, or deemed not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The jury could have also convicted Clancy of lesser charges — second-degree murder or manslaughter.

The other 11 jurors were poised to acquit Clancy by the insanity standard, they have said.

Kevin Reddington talks with Lindsay Clancy on Sept. 3. Greg Derr / USA Today via Reuters

Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings and was therefore unaware of her actions and unable to control herself.

The prosecution, however, argued that Clancy was not in psychosis when she killed her children, and that she planned the strangulations ahead of time.

The case made global headlines and women showed up in droves to support Clancy at the courthouse and online.

For those inside the courtroom, one piece of evidence in particular, from her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, made an impression, Desronvil said: a recording of the 911 call he placed when he found Clancy outside their home, injured after an attempted suicide.

“It was surreal,” Desronvil said of hearing that recording. “Hearing the pain in his voice, hearing the desperation from that clip, it was surreal.”

Patrick Clancy at Plymouth Superior Court. Greg Derr / The Patriot Ledger / USA Today via Reuters

Desronvil said he realized his identity was going to be public the day after the mistrial, as the holdout juror was referred to as “he” and “him” multiple times. Desronvil was one of only three male jurors.

Since then, he said, media outlets have swarmed his home. Despite this, he acknowledged, if he was called to be a juror again, he would do so.

Reddington, when speaking with NBC News last month about the holdout juror, defended Desronvil’s right to his own opinion.

00:00 00:00 How scrutiny of Clancy holdout juror could impact future cases 04:20

“He’s got every right to do that, and I would defend that right, but not to refuse to apply the law,” Reddington said at the time.

Desronvil has since tried to shift attention away from himself and back to Clancy’s children, visiting a park dedicated to the slain kids with McEnany. He calls them “the three angels.”

“What I would like the world to know about me is that I do extremely care about people, especially children, because children are extremely innocent,” Desronvil said.

Desronvil said he had “no idea” how big of a deal this case was in the Boston suburbs and around the country. “Even during jury selection, I had no idea of this case,” he said.

Clancy’s future is still unclear. She remains in Tewksbury Hospital while it is determined whether she will be retried. She will be back in court in November for another status hearing to decide the future of the case.
