World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: West Nile virus creeps north in record year for EU cases
World.content:
Disinfestation workers spray to combat the spread of mosquitoes in the Municipality of Kordelio after the detection of West Nile virus, Thessaloniki, Greece on September 3, 2026. | Konstantinos Tsakalidis / SOOC / AFP via Getty Images

Dozens of human cases have been recorded in the Netherlands and Belgium.

The West Nile virus is spreading across the EU at record levels and is reaching new regions of the continent, health authorities said Thursday.

In a statement, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control said 1,715 cases were reported this year, with 130 people dying from the virus, which is mainly transmitted through mosquito bites.

Greece, Italy and France are the worst affected countries, but the virus is spreading further north, authorities say.

World.title: College of Europe looted and torched during Albanian student protests
World.content:
Rama said he did not believe the damage was down to the students. “Students are the future, they are the ones who look ahead, who want to go further and faster,” he said.

Instead he accused his political opponents of being behind the destruction, claiming that those responsible were attempting to undermine Albania’s progress. The opposition parties deny any wrongdoing.

The College of Europe did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Protests in Albania have been ongoing since late May against the proposed development of a luxury resort linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and alleged government corruption. But the situation escalated on Tuesday and Wednesday as students from around the country clashed with police, set fire to government buildings and businesses linked to powerful businessmen, and damaged traffic lights, bus stops, and the city’s roads.

Alice Taylor/POLITICO

The Delegation of the European Union to Albania released a statement Thursday morning, condemning the destruction of private and public property and asking protestors to exercise restraint. “Violence has no place in democracies,” they wrote.`

Large swathes of the city were damaged during over 14 hours of protests Wednesday. The Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Education and Ministry of Finance, as well as a number of government institutions, banks, and private businesses, were broken into and set on fire. In centrally located Skanderbeg Square, protesters torched a large under-construction tower block, with flames reaching several floors.

World.title: ‘We give back’: Zelenskyy replies to Le Pen’s pledge to cut aid
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is pictured on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

The Ukrainian president argues that France and Europe are benefiting from Ukraine’s battlefield experience.

PARIS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replied to French far-right presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's pledge to cut financial aid with a message: Europe is benefitting from Ukraine.

"Ukraine will give back security. It's security and experience, the price is not so high as people's lives, that's why I think that Madame Le Pen is not deeply [acquainted] with some details," he told the Financial Times. "We give back and this is very important."

Le Pen has repeatedly said, including to POLITICO, that she would stop financial aid to Ukraine if she's elected as French president next year — but suggested France could keep training Ukraine's military and provide non-financial assistance. Le Pen, the National Rally candidate, is currently leading the polls.

World.title: Russian security service detains Swedish citizen for espionage
World.content:
The Federal Security Service published videos of the Swedish citizen, in which he confirms his identity and says he is 35 years old. | Oleg Klimov/Getty Images

Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained a Swedish citizen in the Pskov region near the Estonian border on Thursday.

The man is accused of crossing the border illegally, according to a press release published by the FSB. The accused also faces allegations of “organizing activities of a terrorist organization” and “mercenarism”.

The FSB also published videos of the Swedish citizen, in which he confirms his identity and says he is 35 years old. He also states that he signed a contract with the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s Aidar Battalion in order to carry out acts of sabotage in Russia.

World.title: NATO allies to meet over Black Sea drone attacks on shipping
World.content:
The NATO flag is seen above the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Sept. 12, 2025. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

The North Atlantic Council will discuss the crisis after series of attacks on cargo ships in the region, Romanian President Nicușor Dan tells POLITICO.

BRUSSELS — NATO allies will hold a crisis meeting to discuss how to respond to a series of drone strikes on cargo shipping in the Black Sea, Romania’s President Nicușor Dan said.

Two chemical tankers were hit by air drones in the past 24 hours in or near Romania’s territorial waters, but it is “too early” to say for sure whether Russia was behind the attacks, Dan said.

Dan was speaking on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, where he spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

“The secretary general expressed the solidarity of the alliance and there will be a NAC [North Atlantic Council] meeting at which the whole situation with the Black Sea will be discussed,” Dan told POLITICO. “Of course the conclusion is that all the hybrid attacks are trying to decrease our support for Ukraine. We will continue to support,” he said.

World.title: Ex-DUP chief in Northern Ireland given 15-year prison term for sexually abusing girls
World.content:
Ramsey, addressing a packed Newry Crown Court, read from the two victims’ statements, which described abuse that began when they were 7 or 8 years old. One of the victims described recurring nightmares: “I wonder what it is like not to be afraid at night.”

The judge noted how Donaldson, who is appealing the conviction, had “doubled down on his denials” over what he called the veteran politician’s “catastrophic descent into disgrace.”

Donaldson’s former party, which denounced him immediately after his 2024 arrest and scrubbed him from the DUP website, said in a statement Thursday that Donaldson “deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve” for what it described as “vile and disgusting crimes.”

“Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims who, having suffered such evil, were retraumatized through giving evidence at the trial. They deserve our compassion, support and respect,” the DUP statement said.

Donaldson was an MP representing Lagan Valley from 1997 to 2024, first for the moderate Ulster Unionist Party and then — after belatedly breaking with the party over its support for the Good Friday peace accord of 1998 — as a member of the hard-line DUP.

Donaldson became DUP leader in 2021, when he oversaw the collapse of Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government in a bitter dispute over the region’s peculiar post-Brexit trade rules. Just weeks before his arrest, he again played a key role in reviving the coalition, the cornerstone of the Good Friday peace deal he had once rejected.

World.title: Seven missing after tanker catches fire off Romanian coast
World.content:
A cargo ship is pictured in the Black Sea in Krapets, on October 14, 2026. | Nikolay Doychinov/AFP via Getty Images

The incident came after a drone was spotted in the area by Romanian authorities.

Seven crew members are missing after a tanker caught fire close to Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea Thursday morning, Romanian authorities said.

The San Marino-flagged chemical tanker sent a distress call at 7 a.m. local time about 13 nautical miles from Sulina, a port on Romania’s eastern coast, close to the Ukrainian border. Romanian border police, along with aviation units, arrived to assist the crew, the Romanian Naval Authority said.

Five people have been rescued so far, the naval authority told local media. Another tanker was affected by a fire late on Wednesday close to Sulina, with authorities confirming the crew were safe.

World.title: Millions of phones exposed to Israeli spyware operation through online ads, researchers say
World.content:
Researchers discovered critical details of the hacking tools by analyzing devices belonging to journalists and staff at the Al Jazeera media network, finding that 45 devices of journalists and staff were targeted and some infected with Israeli-made spyware known as Candiru.

At the heart of the hacking campaign is the Israeli company Discover-Tech that describes itself as an advertising business. Citizen Lab researchers said the company facilitated surveillance for commercial spyware operators. Its platform, called Controlium, allegedly allowed spyware makers like Candiru — which in 2025 was acquired by Integrity Labs — to identify, track and target devices by loading s on websites and apps.

Discover-Tech and Integrity Labs did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The scale is striking: An analysis of four billion advertising records found that Discover-Tech's ads appeared across nearly 200,000 websites and mobile apps in dozens of countries over four months. Among the websites that featured the ads were institutional sites of NATO, the United Nations, the European Parliament, European Commission and Council of the EU.

The technique exploits real-time bidding — the automated system used by platforms such as Google to sell advertising space and target users. Rather than persuading victims to click a malicious link, attackers can exploit s to identify and potentially infect devices without any interaction from the user — a technique known as "zero-click" infections.

Discover-Tech's s directed millions of devices to servers associated with Candiru, potentially enabling large-scale surveillance and reconnaissance, researchers said. That does not mean all those devices were infected.

World.title: West Nile virus: Europe records its worst season ever as cases spread north
World.content:
Europe has experienced the most intense West Nile virus season to date as the virus spreads to new parts of the continent, transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said on Thursday.

 

European Union countries have reported 1,715 locally acquired human cases of West Nile virus infection — the highest ever reported — and 130 deaths, according to figures as of 7 October. Some of the cases came from previously unaffected regions.

“Recent detections in people and animals in Belgium and the Netherlands show that the virus is now circulating further north, a trend that is expected to continue in the coming years,” the ECDC warned.

The Netherlands has reported 59 human cases so far this year. Belgium has reported 15 cases, the first locally acquired human infections ever recorded in the country.

Italy remains the most affected country, with 748 cases reported, while Greece and France recorded 445 and 144 cases respectively, their highest numbers of human cases of the virus infection ever.

“West Nile virus is a clear example of why a cross-sector approach is essential,” Céline Gossner, senior expert at ECDC, said in a statement.

“The virus circulates between mosquitoes and birds and can cause disease in people and horses, so no single sector can address the risk alone,” she added.

While cases are rising across the continent, severity is not. The number of people who died, needed hospitalisation or developed neurological symptoms is the same as in the previous decade, the ECDC noted.

Related How to avoid West Nile virus as cases start to rise in Europe

Need to be prepared for future seasons

As the virus spreads across Europe and more people are at risk, the ECDC calls for better preparedness.

“The occurrence of West Nile virus varies considerably from year to year and is difficult to predict, but what we can do is ensure we’re prepared,” said Ole Heuer, Head of Unit at ECDC.

“Earlier detection, greater awareness and effective mosquito control can help us reduce the impact of the virus as it spreads to new areas.”

There is no licensed vaccine for humans, and treatment is limited to managing symptoms and providing supportive care in hospital for severe cases.

Mosquito repellent, loose-fitting long clothing and window screens, mosquito nets, or air conditioning can reduce the risk for people living in the affected areas.

Protection is particularly important for older adults and those with weak immune systems, who are at greater risk of developing severe symptoms.

World.title: Indonesia's skies turn apocalyptic orange as smoke blankets Singapore
World.content:
Thick smoke from wildfires in Indonesia turned the skies over Palangkaraya a striking yellow and orange on Thursday 15 October, reducing visibility to just a few dozen metres. Aerial footage shows the capital of Central Kalimantan province almost disappearing beneath the haze, with the Talawang roundabout and a nearby statue barely visible.

 

Hundreds of kilometres away, Singapore was also blanketed in smoke, leaving its iconic Marina Bay Sands complex almost indistinguishable against the skyline. Roads, bridges and passing vehicles were shrouded in the dense haze. The pollution comes from fires that have been burning across Indonesia for months, sending vast clouds of smoke beyond the country's borders.

The haze has also spread to Malaysia, the Philippines and East Timor, raising concerns about air quality across Southeast Asia. In East Timor, authorities have ordered schools to close for three days because of the smoke. The scenes in Palangkaraya and Singapore illustrate the scale of a regional pollution crisis that continues to affect daily life far beyond the areas directly threatened by the fires.

World.title: Nvidia to open Stockholm AI hub for start-ups tackling health and climate challenges
World.content:
Nvidia is opening an AI hub in Stockholm, Sweden, to help start-ups tackle health and climate challenges.

 

The US chipmaker is partnering with Norrsken, a Swedish non-profit foundation established by Niklas Adalberth, co-founder of Swedish payments company Klarna. The foundation supports start-ups working on social and environmental problems.

Called Stockholm AI Lab, the hub is due to open in central Stockholm in 2027, according to Norrsken’s announcement.

It will bring selected start-ups and Nvidia staff under the same roof, alongside a biotechnology demonstration lab.

Nvidia will contribute computing infrastructure, software tools and connections to its international start-up network. The partners have not disclosed the size of the investment in the project.

What will happen inside?

The hub in central Stockholm will provide private offices and host events connecting founders with investors, researchers, industry representatives and policymakers.

“What these founders need now is what every great movement needs: a place. Somewhere to find each other, their investors, their first customers, and the conviction that they are not building alone,” Adalberth said in the announcement.

The demonstration lab will be run by Nvidia and Stockholm-based Root Bio, a start-up using AI to design molecules for biological applications, including reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

The partners say it will show how AI can help automate biological discovery. They also plan to select further demonstration partners working in robotics, climate, health and manufacturing.

Nvidia’s software tools will support work in robotics, simulation and life sciences

However, the announcement does not specify which equipment will be installed, how much computing capacity members will receive or what they will pay to use it.

Part of Nvidia’s wider European push

Nvidia has announced similar efforts elsewhere in Europe to help businesses and researchers use AI, although the projects take different forms.

In the United Kingdom (UK), the company announced a robotics research and development hub with technology trade association techUK in September 2025, working with training company QA to develop AI and robotics skills.

In June 2025, Nvidia also announced new or expanded AI technology centres in Germany, Italy, Spain, Finland, Sweden and the UK, supporting research, training and access to AI computing infrastructure.

World.title: UK: Frieze London blurs the lines between art, gaming and reality
World.content:
At the fair, Benjamin Lallier's Mother Needham invites visitors to toss coins and make a wish, while Yuli Serfaty's Who's A Good Girl explores the relationship between gender and technology. Greek artist Theo Triantafyllidis presents Feral Metaverse (Spider), a giant climbable sculpture that doubles as a multiplayer game. Up to six visitors can enter a shared virtual world, where they must work together to create shapes such as human towers and wheels.

 

But behind the playful installations, Frieze remains a major commercial event. Art critic Tabish Khan says a struggling market is prompting galleries to favour more conventional displays, with paintings taking priority over elaborate installations.

Other highlights include Swiss artist Miriam Cahn's self-portraits exploring ageing, presented by Galerie Jocelyn Wolff, and a selection of contemporary Indian art from the Fitzwilliam Museum. Together, the works reflect a fair balancing artistic experimentation with the pressures of a challenging art market.

World.title: Albanian PM condemns 'chaos' as violent protests enter third day
World.content:
Protesters and police clashed in Albania's capital Tirana on Thursday for the third consecutive day, as Prime Minister Edi Rama condemned the "chaos" following violent protests that damaged government buildings.

 

“We will all get through these difficult hours together because Albania will continue to climb, because Albania will continue on its path to Europe,” Rama said in a video message, referring to Albania's EU accession bid, which the European Commission aims to conclude by 2027.

“No one can grab Albania by the throat. Anyone who thinks the law does not apply to them is mistaken.”

Students demanding education reforms have joined wider anti-government protests calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation over corruption allegations.

On Thursday, high school students joined thousands of protesters on marches through the centre of the capital, chanting “Rama Resign!” as they brought the city to a standstill.

The latest clashes followed Wednesday's riots, when protesters attacked government buildings, banks and businesses, leaving 89 people injured, including 61 police officers, according to the Health Ministry.

“We will be in the square every day,” Mateo Yskollari, a prominent protest organizer, wrote in an online post. “Our response to any attempt to silence us will be to expand the protest, civil mobilization, and disobedience.”

A hooded protester raises his middle fingers as fire engulfs the Justice Ministry during a violent escalation of anti-government unrest in Tirana, Albania, Wednesday, 14 Oct. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

For more than four months, thousands have protested against a luxury tourism project linked to Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has become a symbol of alleged corruption and inequality in Albania.

Political reactions

The opposition Democratic Party backed the student protests and called on Rama to form a caretaker government ahead of early elections.

“This movement is not simply a protest against the government,” the party said. “It's a revolt against a model of government created by Edi Rama that has stolen hope from young people, violated citizens’ trust and is increasingly distancing Albania from its European future.”

Rama's Socialist Party won a fourth consecutive election victory last year, with the next parliamentary elections not scheduled until 2029.

Meanwhile, a European Union delegation in Albania called late Wednesday for a proportionate response from authorities, expressing concern at “the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana.”

"We call on protesters to exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence. Violence has no place in democracies," it said in a statement.

World.title: Iconic New York hotel The Plaza set to close for four years for restoration works
World.content:
The Plaza Hotel has been a landmark on New York City’s Fifth Avenue for more than a century, instantly recognisable thanks to its iconic façade.

 

Now that façade is getting a facelift, with works set to take at least four years to complete. The hotel will close its doors in January 2027.

In a statement, The Plaza Hotel management said: “The undertaking reflects the complexity of maintaining a property of such architectural and historical significance, with careful consideration given to preservation requirements and the building’s long-term care, as well as the safety of our guests, employees, and the wider community.

“The scope and complexity of the façade works require detailed planning and coordination with relevant stakeholders, alongside adherence to applicable historic preservation requirements.”

The Plaza Hotel has been recognised as one of the Historic Hotels of America, one of just 288 properties selected by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

The history of The Plaza Hotel

The Plaza Hotel, which is styled after a French Renaissance chateau, first opened in 1907 and quickly became an icon – it even featured in The Great Gatsby and was the setting for the Eloise series of books.

Outside of the world of books, The Plaza Hotel has been shown on the silver screen numerous times, with films shot here including Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (which has a cameo from Donald Trump, who owned the hotel at the time), Crocodile Dundee and Sleepless in Seattle.

Since the beginning, The Plaza Hotel has been a hub for celebrities, with famous past guests including The Beatles, Liza Minnelli and Frank Lloyd Wright.

Afternoon tea at The Palm Court is a must for many New York City tourists, so if you’ve been putting off a trip, you might just want to book your flight ASAP or you’ll miss your chance for nearly half a decade.

World.title: Kenya records second Ebola case as outbreak in Congo keeps growing
World.content:
Kenya has recorded its second case of Ebola, the health ministry said on Wednesday, adding there was "no evidence" of any large-scale transmission of the virus.

 

The country reported its first-ever Ebola death last week after a man who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) died after returning to Kenya. The second patient is a close relative of the deceased, the ministry confirmed.

The epicentre of the outbreak is Congo’s Ituri Province, but Uganda and Kenya have also reported cases.

"The Ministry of Health confirms a second case of Ebola," it said in a statement, adding the 39-year-old man was a close family member of the first victim and already in quarantine and being monitored when the virus was detected. These are the first two cases of Ebola ever reported in the country, including all the previous outbreaks.

The patient was isolated "as soon as he developed fever, fatigue and joint pains", the ministry said, before being tested and found positive for the virus.

It emphasised that such early detection "limits the chance of passing the virus to others", and that "there is no evidence of spread in the wider community".

The ministry said it had traced 113 of the 128 people the patient identified as close contacts.

Kenya's first victim was a national, who fell ill around a month ago and had been treated in the DRC, before travelling overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, and flying into Nairobi on 3 October.

He was hospitalised in Nairobi, but later died on 5 October, according to Health Minister Aden Duale.

Related First Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine to start human trials in the UK

Cases grow further in Congo

More than 4,000 people have died in Congo since the country declared the outbreak in May.

Public health authorities have confirmed over 9,000 cases and 899 patients are hospitalised in isolation as of 13 October.

The most affected province is Ituri, where 6,734 cases, including 3,177 deaths, have been reported.

As cases in Congo continue to rise, the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warns that the outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern and the response is particularly challenging in remote and hard-to-reach areas.

The WHO also noted that contact follow-up is “a major operational pressure” and has fallen below the targets in recent weeks.

The current outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which no licensed vaccines or specific treatments are currently available.

Frontline workers in Congo are being vaccinated with Ervebo — the only licensed Ebola vaccine targeting other strains.

The vaccine was “highly effective” against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide “meaningful protection” against Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DRC, the United Nations said in a press release.

The risk of importation into Europe from the outbreak areas remains very low, according to the ECDC.

“While sporadic importations cannot be excluded, the probability of multiple independent importations is very low, even in a pessimistic scenario whereby incidence continues to rise in the affected regions,” the agency wrote on its website.

World.title: Not just cyber – Europe's businesses face more security threats than ever before
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

As Euronews reported this week, the extent of cyber threats impacting Europe's businesses are manifold.

 

According to a survey carried out for the European Commission to mark the EU's Cybersecurity Month, three in four employees are encountering suspicious emails, messages or links whilst at work, with 39% saying they have received phishing messages or been directed to fake websites designed to steal data or gain unauthorised access.

A further 18% report attempts to steal personal data, 17% said they had experienced malware attacks, while 16% reported attempts to obtain passwords.

Threats from organised groups or rogue states

But while the risk of cybercrime continues to attract most of the attention in terms of what companies should be concerned about in the way of threats, it is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the range of corporate security issues that Europe's businesses – and their leaders – face today.

Companies, their senior executives and employees are potentially more vulnerable on a wider number of fronts than ever before.

This includes threats from organised groups or rogue states, with the risks including not just cyberattacks but, for example, the danger of staff being kidnapped or abducted while on business. Bad state actors and large organisations are not the only sources of risk either: companies now potentially face an increasing number of threats from lone individuals or smaller groups, which can be much harder to identify.

Insider threats from disgruntled current or former employees

This includes the likes of insider threats from disgruntled current or former employees. According to a report last year by Ponemon Institute, the average total cost of insider threat incidents increased by around 135% between 2018 and 2025. And while companies in North America continue to suffer the highest financial impact from insider incidents, with the average annual cost of insider-related activities in this region costing $24.0 million in 2025, globally Europe ranks second with average annual costs of $18.6 million.

Another concern is an increase in violent threats to CEOs and senior executives and even their families. While the tragic shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in the US in 2024 is perhaps the case most people remember. Europe is not immune to such threats with last year's attempted kidnap of the daughter of Pierre Noizat, the French cryptocurrency chief, as a recent example.

Executives and their families face threats of physical violence

The growing risk on this front is also borne out by a survey from the International Security Management Association (ISMA), a global body representing the senior security executives of major corporations. More than half of the chief security officers surveyed reported that their organisation’s senior executives, or their families, received up to nine online, telephone, written or other direct threats of harm each year.

In today's increasingly digital world, the risks have become greater because even if a CEO does not leave a digital footprint, a family member posting on social media can unwittingly leave a trail that can be exploited by someone posing a threat. Public records and AI-enabled research have also made it easier to obtain information about employees, executives and their families, with one study of executive vulnerability assessments finding publicly discoverable home addresses in 94% of cases.

Today, risks are increasingly hard to map

Such threats to business leaders are getting more difficult to foresee. When I was a police officer, the escalation to violence was usually a path you could track as it came from fairly predictable sources.

Today, risks are increasingly hard to map. Who would have predicted the threat to the UnitedHealthcare CEO would come from an Ivy League graduate who was top of his class?

Why are the threats from hard-to-predict sources increasing?

One theory is that economic pain and politics are fusing for many people, and business can represent the nearest visible and accessible symbol. Indeed, a report earlier this year by Allied Universal surveying more than 2,300 security chiefs in 31 countries found 44% were expecting economic instability to be the top security hazard in the year ahead.

Political polarisation fuels instability, increasing business risks

The increasingly polarised nature of politics today also creates a febrile environment, heightening the risks to business.

A 2024 report for Littler, an employment and labour law practice, found 86% of European employers face at least some difficulty managing divisive political beliefs at work, up from 75% a year earlier. The upcoming Spanish general election, for instance, is taking place against a backdrop of deep political polarisation, intense civic unrest and heightened social tensions.

Highly-charged political rhetoric may mean people transfer emotions onto businesses, or their leaders, that they feel are complicit.

How should businesses address such challenges? Good practice is detailed mapping of potential "trigger points". Company announcements or external events can stir up emotions that could potentially be a catalyst for a threat or attack on a company. This could include, for instance, a company’s profit announcement or a decision not to fund research into a new drug. In a similar way, a CEO seen to be engaging in a political issue may ignite strong emotions in a potential attacker.

AI can play a major role in identifying risks and enhancing security

Because of the difficulty and time commitment required in terms of mapping the breath of risks today, AI can also play a huge role. It can be widely used in areas such as CCTV object recognition, facial recognition, social media monitoring, weapon detection and predictive analysis in terms of detecting patterns and emerging threats.

So, as Europe marks cybersecurity month, we should not forget that while cyber risks are increasing, so too are the broader threats. Europe's businesses, their executives and their employees face the most significantly elevated risk environment ever. Security concerns need to be at the top of the corporate agenda.

ISMA is a global membership organisation comprising top senior chief security officers (CSOs) who represent multinational organisations across a range of industries. Founded in 1983, its members – around 375 in total – comprise 25 companies in the FTSE 100, DAX and CAC 40, together with a majority of the Fortune 100 and 25% of the Fortune 500. It includes representatives from global brands such as MetLife, S&P Global, Sky, Four Seasons, Unilever and Novo Nordisk.

World.title: Russia arrests Swedish national, claims he's Ukraine fighter
World.content:
Russian intelligence agents have arrested a Swedish man they say led a Ukrainian drone unit. He was detained at Russia's western border and is accused of planning acts of terrorism and sabotage.

Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) on Thursday announced the arrest and detention of a Swedish national that authorities say fights for Ukraine.

What do we know so far?

The 35-year-old Swede, detained near Pskov on Russia's western border, has been charged with illegally entering the country and may face additional terrorism charges, said FSB representatives.

Russia claims to have secured documents proving that the man led a Ukrainian drone unit.

They are now investigating whether he could be charged with organizing terror attacks on behalf of Ukraine or other Western intelligence services.

According to the FSB, the man "entered the Russian Federation under the pretext of joining the ranks of the Russian armed forces with the aim of carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorist attacks on military installations."

The FSB also released a video that it claimed showed the man confessing that he had entered Russia to commit "terrorist attacks" and sabotage.

Putin on a war footing: escalation on all fronts? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

During the video the man spoke in English, saying that he was from Stockholm, had signed a contract with Ukraine's Defense Ministry and had received drone training. Russian state TV showed images of what it said was the man's contract with Ukraine.

The Pskov region borders Belarus, Estonia and Latvia — the latter two being EU and NATO member states — FSB officials did not specify where exactly the man had arrived from.

Sweden aware of incident, with no comment yet from Ukraine

The Swedish Foreign Ministry has said that it is aware of the situation but not involved.

Ukraine has not commented on the arrest.

On Tuesday, Russia arrested a Japanese journalist that Moscow accused of spying, a claim that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi rejected.

Russia itself has been accused of hiring and deploying numerous individuals to commit acts of sabotage abroad or to recruit locals willing to do so — this, beyond the country's legions of malign cyber actors.

None of the claims made by Russia and the FSB on Thursday can be substantiated.

World.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Ukraine is resuming attacks on Russian energy sites. It came after Moscow summarily ignored a claim by US President Donald Trump that an "energy ceasefire" had been agreed.

Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.

Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out. We're done."

The announcement came after Russia reported Ukrainian attacks on oil processing plants in Ryazan, where fire broke out, and Saratov.

Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Trump's 'ceasefire' on energy sites: 'We're done' Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

Kyiv blasts dangerous lack of US intel

Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.

The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."

Ukraine: Russian strikes continue as ceasefire questions remain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.

"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.

Zelenskyy: Starlink throttling a question of US 'will'

Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."

SpaceX owner Elon Musk said the US owns and operates the Starshield military version of Starlink used by Ukraine, adding that he and his company had nothing to do with the issue.

Ukraine presses allies on intelligence sharing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The FT interview comes in the wake of Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil as well as his promise to buy "millions of barrels" of Russian diesel fuel amid high fuel prices caused by the US war with Iran.

The deal, just weeks from the US midterm elections, is unlikely to bring down oil prices. But it does extend a lifeline to Russian President Putin, allowing him to continue his illegal invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy and went so far as to call for him to be replaced this weekend.

Trump's sanctions actions fly in the face of nearly five years of allied political efforts to pressure Moscow to end its invasion.

Trump's actions have enraged NATO allies and European leaders, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, for one, calling the US agreement to purchase Russian diesel "a very risky decision."

Meloni pointed out that the spike in oil prices was clearly precipitated by Trump's war in Iran and that his dealings with Putin would result in the Russian leader continuing his invasion of Ukraine rather than ending it.

World.title: Raila Odinga's legacy: Can Kenya preserve the democratic space he helped create?
World.content:
One year after Raila Odinga's death, Kenyans are reflecting on his contribution to democratic reforms and national reconciliation. However, the so-called 'handshakes', with his political rivals remain debatable.

One year after Raila Odinga's death, the former Kenyan prime minister remains a towering figure in the country's political life. For many, he symbolizes the struggle for multiparty democracyand constitutional reforms in Kenya. For others, his later political alliances raise questions about compromise, opposition politics and the direction of the movement he built.

As Kenya marks the first anniversary of his death on October 15, 2026, the question is not only how the country remembers Odinga, but whether the principles he championed can survive beyond him. "I want his legacy to live beyond the party," says 20-year-old, Beatrice Chebet, a Nairobi resident, reflecting on the values she believes should define his legacy.

She points to the Kenya Odinga wanted: a country grounded in peace, democracy, constitutionalism and the rule of law. Chebet says younger generations must carry those aspirations forward.

Raila Odinga was fondly referred to as 'Baba' or father by his supporters Image: Halima Gongo/DW

"Some of us were Gen Zs. We did not know any form of multipartism without reading Raila,” she told DW, describing how his political journey became part of the country's history and the experience of younger Kenyans.

A legacy forged in struggle

Odinga's political influence was shaped by decades of opposition politics, detentions, and campaigns for democratic change. His role in the disputed 2007 presidential election placed him at the center of one of Kenya's most consequential political crises. The post-election violence killed more than 1,100 people and displaced hundreds of thousands.

A power-sharing agreement brokered with international mediation led by the former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan, made Odinga prime minister in a coalition government with President Mwai Kibaki. The settlement also established a reform agenda, including constitutional change. Kenya adopted a new constitution in 2010, introducing a devolved system of government.

For security expert Byron Adera, Odinga's impact extended beyond electoral politics. "Raila was an institution that rocked institutions, bringing about lasting and very impactful institutional reforms for the betterment of Kenya," Adera told DW. He identifies constitutional reform and efforts to bring competing political interests together as important parts of Odinga's legacy.

A look at the life of Kenya's Raila Odinga To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet reconciliation also became one of the most contested aspects of his career. His so-called 'handshakes' of reconciliation with Kibaki (2008), President Uhuru Kenyatta (2018), followed by later cooperation with President William Ruto (2024), illustrated his willingness to pursue political agreements with former rivals.

Whereas supporters saw dialogue as a way to reduce tensions and advance national interests; critics questioned what such arrangements meant for an independent opposition. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has strongly criticized the political rapprochement between President William Ruto and the late Raila Odinga.

In May 2026, he described the handshake process as "nonsense" and argued that it had eroded Kenya's democracy by weakening the opposition's ability to hold the government accountable. His position offers a contrasting view of the alliances that shaped Odinga's later political years.

What happens to Odinga's ODM party?

The debate over Odinga's legacy is especially pressing within the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), the party he helped found and led for years.

Edwin Sifuna, a potential presidential candidate in the 2027 election, who describes Odinga as both his leader and friend, says the party's identity and direction have changed fundamentally. "We run the risk of losing our core support, people who believed in the ideals of ODM, because we were always the party of the people," Sifuna told DW.

He adds that Odinga's influence on national politics and public debate is greatly missed. His remarks point to a central challenge for ODM: whether it can preserve its identity and connection with ordinary Kenyans while navigating a changing political landscape. However, in a bid to keep the Odinga name in politics, Winnie Odinga, daughter of Raila Odinga, declared that she will run for Senator of Nairobi County in the 2027 election.

For Chebet, Odinga's legacy will be measured by whether future generations continue to defend the principles associated with his political journey. Adera, meanwhile, emphasizes the lasting importance of institutional reform and building bridges.

Their perspectives highlight the tension at the heart of Odinga's legacy: a leader remembered for expanding democratic possibilities, but whose political compromises remain debatable. A year after his death, his influence is still visible in Kenya's political arguments, party divisions and public calls for democratic accountability.

The lasting test will be whether Kenya's institutions, political parties and younger generation can carry those principles forward and whether the democratic space Odinga helped shape can endure beyond the man himself.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

World.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
World.content:
EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major elections next year.

European Union leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.

The summit is sure to include some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.

On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.

Here are the main topics on the agenda:

Chinese competition in focus

The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.

The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.

Merz and Macron wrote a joint appeal for a tougher line on Chna in the run-up to the summit Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/picture alliance

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.

The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.

Divisive EU budget

The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.

Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.

"We are in very, very difficult negotiations regarding the future finances of the European Union," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has been leading the appeals for a leaner budget, said on arrival in Brussels.

"We must significantly reduce the common budget compared with the commission’s proposals. No member state of the European Union can afford this," said Merz.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also said the proposals currently on the table were "simply not acceptable."

Talks could theoretically run late into the night Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

Italy's Giorgia Meloni is among the most vocal defenders of maintaining the traditional funds like cohesion payments, she told parliament on Wednesday that she saw "no contradiction between old policies and new priorities."

The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.

Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.

Ukraine support

The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.

"All of us in Europe want this war to end," Zelenskyy wrote after arriving. "And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine."

He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

Macron only has a few more EU summits ahead of him as term limit and presidential elections beckon in France Image: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.

Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.

Edited by: Natalie Muller and Wesley Dockery

World.title: Romania: 2 ships on fire in Black Sea, 7 crew missing
World.content:
Two chemical tankers have caught fire in Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea. The blazes occurred after Russian drones were sighted in Romanian airspace.

Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.

Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.

The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.

However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan met with NATO chief Mark Rutte to address the situation.

"This is unacceptable and it has to stop. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake," Dan wrote on X after a meeting with NATO chief Mark Rutte to discuss a recent spate of such attacks.

"NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities," Rutte said regarding the incident.

He said the military alliance would "continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed."

What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?

Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading ‌to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.

Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert ‌from ​the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.

Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.

"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.

"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.

The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.

Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.

Growing attacks in the Black Sea

Romania, which shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has ⁠reported ​repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over ​the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.

Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.

This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks ​⁠in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Thursday that the EU, of which both his country and Romania are members, will discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea at its ongoing summit in Brussels.

Bulgaria summoned the Russian ambassador over the sinking of a ship off the country's coast on Tuesday following a drone attack.

World.title: Trump says execution of Fort Hood shooter will not be livestreamed
World.content:
Trump said the execution of the Fort Hood shooter can be viewed in person by families of the victims if they wish. The decision comes after bipartisan backlash regarding the Pentagon's plans to livestream the execution.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will not be livestreamed.

The announcement comes after the Trump administration faced criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, as well as rights groups and many in the international community. Vice President JD Vance also said he would not watch such a livestream.

Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."

But the president added that "any very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."

Trump said he "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."He noted that the execution can be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose."

Hasan's execution is scheduled for Deccember 3 at the US military prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

A slew of criticism

The public execution idea drew wide condemnation from lawmakers of both main US parties, Republicans and Democrats, including top House Republican Mike Johnson, who said it could be a "recruiting tool for future terrorists."

Dozens of retired US military officers also published an open letter warning against broadcasting the execution, saying it "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it."

The letter added that such a move woud "ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers," said the officers, including more than 40 generals and admirals.

Even Vice-President JD Vance was reticent about the plan.

When asked about the public execution and whether it was acceptable in his Christian faith, Vance said he didn't know that it would actually happen.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it."

Hegseth had sought to make execution 'public'

The plan to livestream Hasan's execution was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."

Hasan was an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major when he carried out the shooting in a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009.

Soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment at the time of the shooting. Hasan shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — as he opened fire on his fellow soldiers

He was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement. He now uses a wheelchair.

During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.

The last time the US military carried out a servicemember execution was in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.

World.title: Resignation of Bärbel Bas shines light on harsh era of German politics
World.content:
German Labor Minister Bärbel Bas has stepped down, citing her need to grieve a loved one and leave behind the harsh realities of government. So how did German politics get so heated?

For a brief moment, a sense of quiet sympathy could be felt in Berlin's often unforgiving political arena: On Monday morning, Bärbel Bas, Germany's labor minister and the co-leader of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) announced her resignation from all government and party positions. The 58-year-old politician cited a personal tragedy as the reason for her decision: "Following the death of my stepdaughter, I have come to realize that I need time to work through my grief," Bas wrote in a statement.

Bas also wrote that sustained criticism from the conservative governing parties, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU), had contributed to her decision to step down. In her statement, she wrote that she had been forced to "conclude that public attacks on me, unfortunately also from within the ranks of our coalition partner, continued to intensify during this personally difficult time."

The labor minister had recently been responsible for implementing complex changes to Germany's public pension system — including increasing the retirement age — and had been urged by some conservative politicians, in rather harsh terms, not to delay the project any further.

According to a report in the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, one remark in particular appears to have weighed heavily on her: During an off-the-record briefing with journalists, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, of the CDU, reportedly criticized the pace of her efforts despite knowing that she was working through a personal tragedy.

Did Bas feel so overwhelmed by pressures both personal and political that she chose to step down rather than continue to endure them?

Mirco Liefke, a researcher with the Institute for Media and Communication Studies in the Department of Political and Social Sciences at the Freie Universität Berlin, told DW that unfairness and harshness have always been part of politics. However, he added: "What I do think is new is the potential for escalation and the speed that social media have brought to public debate. Along with that has come an incentive for individual actors to adopt ever more radical positions."

Bas (right) was asked to implement increases to the retirement age Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

Politics and media

There are few public spaces left in which politicians can speak with the expectation that their remarks will not be reported. Merz is said to have made critical remarks of Bas during an off-the-record briefing whose contents were not intended for publication.

Though he was fully aware of her personal circumstances, Merz reportedly said Bas was barely visible in public and failing to put forward proposals of her own.

"It has effectively become a business model to leak information that is meant to remain confidential and thereby generate attention," Liefke said.

A spokesperson for Merz declined to confirm or deny the report.

Politics and misogyny

Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of Germany's center-left Greens, has known Bas fior years, with both hailing from Duisburg, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, albeit born a couple of decades apart.

"Toughness and ruthlessness are nothing new in politics," Banaszak told DW. "But we still need to find a different way of doing things if we do not want to keep wearing people down."

Banaszak said the SPD was partially responsible for the treatment of Bas. "The fact that Bärbel Bas encountered so little understanding for her personal situation from within the ranks of the coalition partner, and that apparently no one in the SPD was willing to step forward, defend her, and take her out of the line of fire, is simply not a good sign," he said.

"It would be naive to pretend that the attacks on a man would have unfolded in a similar way," he added.

Liefke offered a similar view: "Women politicians are subjected to an extraordinary degree of misogynistic and sexualized abuse — and they face a level of public exposure that is entirely new."

CDU pushes back

The debate over how Bas and her grief should have been treated soon took on some of the same characteristics as the attacks that had preceded her resignation. Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, described the attacks by the CDU/CSU as "inhuman," drawing sharp criticism from many conservative politicians. Merz publicly expressed his regret over the labor minister's resignation and wished her all the best.

Liefke said this was another tremnd in German politics. Once a politician decides to step down, he argues, public expressions of concern are often far more intense than they used to be and come from all sides: "This is a facade of concern," he said. "There is something ritualistic, almost reflexive, about it. People react this way because they are following another major trend: Emotionalization."

Kühnert cited far-right threats in his resignation as SPD general secretary Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

The case of Kevin Kühnert

The attacks on Bas are just one example of the increasingly harsh tone of political debate. Formal reprimands in the Bundestag have risen sharply, particularly since the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) entered parliament in 2017. High-profile resignations have also made headlines, including that of Kevin Kühnert, the SPD's former secretary-general.

Kühnert stepped down in 2024, citing health reasons. In April 2025, however, he told Die Zeit newspaper that he had felt constantly threatened by far-right extremists. Political debate, he said, is showing "an increasing lack of respect for the views of those who think differently."

Helmut Schmidt managed to maintain his private life throughout his chancellorship Image: picture alliance / ASSOCIATED PRESS

Former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt: A public figure, yet still private

Liefke points out that politicians once managed to maintain two distinct modes of communication: One public and one private. "When you think of earlier generations of politicians, what comes to mind is the distance they maintained, the relative lack of emotional display. Take Helmut Schmidt, for example. He did not openly grieve over things that came crashing down on him. At least, he did not show it publicly." Helmut Schmidt, of the SPD, served as chancellor from 1974 to 1982.

Liefke argues: "Today, politicians such as Bärbel Bas benefit from drawing on their own life stories when they say, 'I come from a working-class background and worked my way up.' That can work to their advantage, but it also makes them far more visible, and far more vulnerable, as individuals."

Bas, who served as president of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025, intends to retain her parliamentary seat. Life is likely to become quieter for her now, while others move into the spotlight, both in public and, perhaps, in private as well.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Hamburg court jails 2 men over plot to attack Jewish leaders on behalf of Iran
World.content:
The pair was found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. The court says they planned to attack the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and president of the German-Israeli society.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced two men accused of plotting to target Jewish leaders in Germany on behalf of Iran'ssecret service to multiple years in prison.

Both were found guilty of espionage and attempted murder. One defendant was given a four-and-a-half year sentence, while the other received an eight-and-a-half year sentence as the mastermind of the planned attacks.

Prosecutors said that one defendant, a 54-year-old Dane with Afghan roots, had received his orders directly from Iran's al-Quds Brigades, the foreign arm of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

The man was said to have recruited his accomplice, a 43-year-old Afghan man living in Denmark, to carry out one of the attacks, or find someone who could.

The 43-year-old was also tasked with finding a weapon with which to carry out one of the attacks.

Beyond targeting two high-profile individuals, the 54-year-old had reportedly made preparations for an arson attack on a kosher deli in Berlin.

The defendants were arrested by Danish authorities in the city of Aarhus last year and extradited to Germany.

How Europe, the US can better protect Jewish communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who were convicted defendants planning to attack?

Among the figures the pair planned to attack was Josef Schuster, the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, the court found.

Another prospective target was Green Party politician Volker Beck, president of the German-Israeli society.

Beck called on Berlin to expel Iran's ambassador and consular officials after charges against the men were made public.

"Jewish life and a commitment to the Jewish and democratic state are repeatedly threatened with murder and attacked by the regime of the Islamic Republic of Iran on German soil," he said.

Germany's Foreign Office summoned Iran's ambassador after Danish authorities made the arrests, prompting the Iranian embassy in Berlin to release a statement rejecting what it called "unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran's enemies."
