World.title: Strasbourg court rules against Orbán: His government unlawfully restricted Hungarian teachers’ right to strike
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Hungary’s former government unlawfully restricted teachers’ right to strike, with Education and Child Affairs Minister Judit Lannert welcoming the decision and pointing to reforms introduced by the new government.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled on Wednesday that the government led by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán unlawfully restricted Hungarian teachers’ right to strike. The court found that the restrictions imposed on teachers and their trade unions were disproportionate and were not necessary in a democratic society.

The case was brought by the Teachers’ Trade Union (PSZ) and the Democratic Trade Union of Teachers (PDSZ), which turned to the Strasbourg court in 2022. The Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ) represented them in the proceedings, which were subsequently joined with cases brought by two affected teachers.

The judgment is not yet final. The Hungarian government has until 6 January to request that the case be referred to the court’s Grand Chamber for reconsideration.

Why did the court rule against the Orbán government?

The dispute dates back to February 2022, when the Orbán government introduced a decree restricting teachers’ right to strike, citing the pandemic situation. The rules established minimum services that schools and kindergartens had to maintain during strikes. These included providing childcare and holding certain lessons even when teachers were taking industrial action.

The measures came shortly after teachers’ unions organised a nationwide strike in late January 2022. More than 20,000 teachers took part in the two-hour protest. The unions challenged the restrictions before Hungary’s Constitutional Court, but their complaint was rejected on procedural grounds. They subsequently took their case to Strasbourg in September 2022.

In its latest judgment, the ECHR found that the restrictions placed a disproportionate burden on both teachers and their trade unions. The state had exceeded its margin of appreciation, the court concluded, and the limitations on the right to strike were not necessary in a democratic society.

Education minister welcomes the judgment

Education and Child Affairs Minister Judit Lannert welcomed the ruling on Thursday, saying it vindicated the new ministry’s approach to teachers’ rights.

“I firmly believe that teachers should be valued, not humiliated, and that their professional opinion should carry weight,” Lannert wrote on Facebook. “One of my first decisions as minister was to change this practice.”

She criticised the previous Fidesz-Christian Democrat government for reducing schools’ autonomy, restricting teachers’ right to strike and dismissing several teachers who had taken part in protests.

Lannert also pointed to amendments to the public education law adopted in August, which she said had restored schools’ autonomy, expanded headteachers’ powers and reinstated teaching staffs’ decision-making and consultation rights. The changes also strengthened employee representation and clarified the conditions under which teachers can exercise their right to strike.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What changes for teachers?

The ruling concerns the legality of restrictions imposed under the previous government, while the new government has already introduced changes to the legal framework governing public education and industrial action. Lannert said teachers’ opinions and criticism would be important in renewing Hungarian education.

World.title: New direct Railjet train to connect Munich and Miskolc!
World.content:
Miskolc is set to gain a direct rail connection to Munich this winter, with Austrian Federal Railways (ÖBB) planning to introduce daily Railjet services between the two cities from 13 December 2026. The new route will also serve Vienna and Budapest.

According to information published by ÖBB on Wednesday, the new connection is part of the railway operator’s timetable change for December. As reported by the Facebook page PTF – Public Transport Fan, the direct service has already appeared in the timetable search, although the final schedule could still change before its launch.

The new service will give passengers in north-eastern Hungary a direct train connection to the Bavarian capital without needing to change trains along the way.

When will the trains depart?

The timetable currently lists the following departure times for the service, although these are subject to change.

Munich to Miskolc: Railjet service RJX 67 is scheduled to leave Munich Central Station at 1.28 PM and arrive at Miskolc-Tiszai railway station at 10.51 PM.

Railjet service RJX 67 is scheduled to leave Munich Central Station at 1.28 PM and arrive at Miskolc-Tiszai railway station at 10.51 PM. Miskolc to Munich: The first train in the opposite direction is scheduled to depart Miskolc at 7.03 AM on 14 December, arriving in Munich at 4.34 PM.

The new service is expected to operate daily in both directions, adding a further international rail option for travellers between Hungary, Austria and Germany.

If you missed it: Ryanair announces 29 new summer 2027 routes, including Budapest connection to UK

Where will the train stop in Hungary?

The train will call at several major stations across Hungary, including:

Hegyeshalom

Mosonmagyaróvár

Győr

Tatabánya

Budapest-Kelenföld

Budapest-Keleti

Hatvan

Füzesabony

Beyond Hungary, the route will serve Freilassing, Salzburg, Linz, St. Pölten, Vienna Meidling and Vienna Central Station.

The precise stops differ slightly depending on the direction of travel. According to the currently published timetable, the train heading towards Munich will stop at Hegyeshalom but will not call at Freilassing.

ÖBB RailJet at Keleti Railway Station in Budapest, Hungary. Photo: Daily News Hungary

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A new international rail option for Miskolc

The connection would provide Miskolc, one of Hungary’s largest cities, with a direct Railjet link to Munich, potentially making international travel more convenient for residents, students and visitors.

Railjet trains are ÖBB’s long-distance services connecting major cities in Austria and neighbouring countries. The new route would extend the network further into north-eastern Hungary.

However, passengers should check the official timetable before planning their journeys, as departure times and stops may change before the new service launches on 13 December 2026.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán: Hungarian students to regain access to Erasmus+
World.content:
Hungarian university students will once again be able to apply for Erasmus programmes from the 2026/27 academic year, while Hungarian researchers and universities will regain access to Horizon Europe opportunities, the Minister of Foreign Affairs announced on Facebook on Wednesday.

Hungarian students now can apply for Erasmus+ again

In her post, Anita Orbán recalled that on Tuesday the Council of the European Union had adopted the European Commission’s proposal, bringing the rule-of-law conditionality procedure to a close and restoring full access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes for Hungarian students and researchers.

“When we reached an agreement in May on the path towards securing the return of EU funding, it was particularly important to me that Hungarian young people and researchers should no longer have to bear the consequences of previous disputes,” the minister said.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The European Commission decided

At the end of September, the European Commission announced that, in its assessment, the reforms introduced by Hungary’s new government had delivered results: “Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the EU’s financial interests.”

At the time, the Commission recommended that the Council of the European Union enable the release of EUR 4.2 billion in cohesion funding for Hungary and restore access to the Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe programmes for Hungarian students and researchers.

Read also: Hungary’s Semmelweis University breaks into world’s top 250 after major leap in global rankings

World.title: Croatia Rejects Serbian Accusation of Election Interference
World.content:
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic in Brussels, 15 October 2026. Photo: EPA/OLIVIER MATTHYS.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic on Thursday dismissed a diplomatic protest note from Belgrade alleging interference in the Serbian parliamentary election as “complete nonsense.”

“It is absolute nonsense to suggest that Croatia, presumably acting as both an external and an internal enemy, is interfering in the political process and the election race in Serbia,” Plenkovic said.

Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s outgoing president and the lead candidate on the “United Serbia” list, said that no country had ever interfered in another country’s elections as extensively as Croatia had done in Serbia’s upcoming parliamentary elections, Serbian news agency Tanjug reported on Thursday.

Vucic welcomed the Serbian Foreign Ministry’s decision to send Croatia a protest note, adding that it should have been done “perhaps a thousand times by now.

“It is important to leave a record that we were aware that Croatia was interfering in our electoral process in the most overt way. Therefore, we have issued a protest note,” Vucic said.

Serbian public broadcaster Radio-Television Serbia said the note stated that attempts to influence Serbia’s electoral processes were unacceptable, as were various aspects of Croatian media coverage of Serbia’s political situation.

“This narrative has been pushed for quite some time. As for the protests regarding coverage by Croatian media, I don’t know what more there is to add. As far as I recall, our media are free – people write what they want,” Plenkovic responded.

“Croatia does not interfere in such matters, nor is this an issue that concerns us. However, there are fundamental values on which Serbia needs to make progress rather than sending us ridiculous notes,” Plenkovic added.

“Unfortunately, we remember Aleksandar Vucic’s role in the [1990s military] aggression against Croatia, and 35 years later, we are witnessing the same rhetoric. This shows there has been no progress towards normalising relations in Serbia,” said Tomo Medved, Croatia’s Minister for Veterans and a member of the ruling Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, on Thursday.

Josko Klisovic, of the opposition Social Democratic Party, described the note as “completely groundless and diplomatically misguided.

“Croatia does not interfere in Serbia’s election campaign. However, it seems that Aleksandar Vucic wants to drag Croatia into it,” Klisovic said, adding that the goal was clear: “Vucic wants to mobilise his electorate to turn out in the largest possible numbers and grant him another term.

“I hope the citizens of Serbia will recognise this manipulation by Vucic and head to the polls with the reality of their current lives, and the lives they wish to lead in the future, in mind,” Klisovic said.

Marijana Puljak, an MP from the Center Party, said the dispute showed Vucic’s nervousness and that the opposition student movement in Serbia was putting him under pressure, prompting him to look for culprits everywhere.

Parliamentary elections in Serbia are scheduled for October 25 with the Student List seen as the main opponent for Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party.

World.title: ‘Family Values’ Row Returns as Kosovo Govt Revives Changes to Civil Code
World.content:
Kosovo MPs during a parliamentary session on September 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN

Kosovo’s Prime Minister, Albin Kurti, clashed with opposition MP Eman Rrahmani of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, in parliament on Thursday over stalled reforms to the Civil Code and proposed laws on medically assisted reproduction, with disagreements focusing on same-sex unions, reproductive rights and “family values”.

Three bills on these issues are included in the government’s legislative agenda from mid-November until the end of the year.

During Thursday’s session, Rrahmani accused the government of “disregarding traditional family values”.

“Why are you continuing with this agenda? Don’t you think you are offending the citizens who voted for you and disregarding the values of the traditional family?” Rrahmani asked.

Kurti responded that Kosovo needed “comprehensive reform of civil law” to provide greater legal certainty in areas including property, family relations and inheritance.

“These are the areas through which citizens live as individuals and families, and develop and prosper,” Kurti said, adding that legal ambiguities “could leave people uncertain about their rights to use, inherit or sell property”.

Kurti urged Rrahmani to consider the proposed legislation as a whole and not focus on individual provisions.

“The Civil Code contains 997 pages and 1,630 articles,” Kurti said, advising Rrahmani to examine the document in its entirety. “Focusing on just one or two articles risks becoming an obsession and does not help,” Kurti said, causing laughter in parliament.

He added that MPs did not have to agree with every provision but “should consider the broader purpose of the legislation”. He noted that a working group at the Ministry of Justice would meet next week to discuss the matter.

Rrahmani said his opposition concerned two paragraphs of the Civil Code that he believes undermine the family.

“These will not be voted through in this parliament. We will send back those provisions that undermine the family,” he said.

The proposed Civil Code has been stalled since 2022 due to disagreements over provisions that would allow for the adoption of separate legislation regulating civil unions between people of the same sex.

Rrahmani, who in 2022 was a Vetevendosje MP but later switched to the PDK, criticised provisions he said could permit marriages between men, as well as allowing women to become mothers without a father.

Kosovo law currently does not allow same-sex marriages. The constitution, on the other hand, recognises that “on the basis of free consent, everyone enjoys the right to marry and the right to create a family in accordance with the law”.

The government has often declared that it intends to bring the Civil Code before parliament, but the legislation has yet to secure final approval.

The proposed Law on Reproductive Health and Medically Assisted Fertilisation has also faced delays. The government submitted the bill in January 2023 and parliament approved it at first reading in October Attempts to pass it at second reading in 2024 then failed.

Under the draft legislation, women would be eligible for in vitro fertilisation, IVF, regardless of their marital status or whether they were in a same-sex or heterosexual relationship.

Kurti said the desire to become a parent “should be treated with understanding and respect by the state”.

“The desire to become a parent is one of the deepest expressions of human desire,” he said, adding that difficulties associated with parenthood deserved a careful response from public institutions.

The proposed law foresees IVF services and a public bank for reproductive cells. Currently, women seeking these procedures have to turn to private healthcare clinics or somewhere abroad.

World.title: US Convicts Bosnian of Attempting to Buy Arms from North Korea
World.content:
Russian SA-18 and SA-16 Igla missiles with components. Photo: US Government/Wikidata.

The US Department of Justice said on Wednesday that Sasa Micev, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been convicted of collaborating with a co-conspirator from the US and others to violate and evade restrictions on arms sales by trying to buy shoulder-launched missiles from North Korea.

Micev, 43, was described in court documents as “an international arms dealer”. He was sentenced to five years in prison by a court in New Mexico.

A Department of Justice statement said Micev attempted to broker the purchase of SA-18 Igla portable surface-to-air missiles from North Korea without the required licence or approvals from the US Treasury Department Office of Foreign Assets Control.

It stated that on multiple occasions in 2020, Micev and a co-conspirator discussed unlawfully acquiring the Igla missiles. Micev “provided pricing information, participated in efforts to obtain the items through falsified documentation, and worked to procure the weapons from North Korea despite knowing that such transactions were prohibited under US and international laws”, it said.

In late 2020, Micev and the co-conspirator traveled to Ankara in Turkey to complete the purchase of the Igla missiles. However, according to the Department of Justice, the deal fell through after a price dispute with the North Koreans.

Micev pleaded guilty to violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the North Korean Sanctions Regulations.

“Those who knowingly attempt to circumvent US export controls and international sanctions to facilitate the illicit trafficking of military weapons pose a serious threat to our national security and global stability,” said acting special agent in charge Ryan G. McRae of Homeland Security Investigations El Paso in New Mexico.

“Their willingness to profit from prohibited weapons transactions demonstrates blatant disregard for the law,” McRae added.

According to company registries in Bosnia, Sasa Micev was a co-owner of the Banja Luka-based company BSTG (Balkan Security Tech Group), which is currently in bankruptcy proceedings. The company’s website indicates that it offered services in the security sector.

BIRN attempted to obtain a comment, but the contact phone number was unreachable.

NOTE: This article was amended on October 15, 2026 to correct the surname of Sasa Micev in several instances.

World.title: Croatia Sets Eight Conditions for Backing Montenegro’s EU Accession
World.content:
The 100-year-old training ship ‘Jadran’, one of the subjects of dispute. Photo: Ministry of Defence of Montenegro.

Croatia has listed eight demands for supporting Montenegro’s EU accession, all of which are “clearly defined and achievable,” according to a document Zagreb sent to EU member states and the European Commission and European Council.

The document explains Croatia’s position on Montenegro’s accession process in detail. “Croatia seeks to facilitate, not obstruct, Montenegro’s accession,” the text states.

It notes that several issues stemming from Montenegro’s participation in military aggression against Croatia during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s must be resolved. “Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of our shared history and to build a future-oriented relationship with Montenegro,” it says.

Six of the eight demands relate to Chapter 23 in the EU acquis of legislation Montenegro needs to adopt in order to join the bloc, under the heading Judiciary and Fundamental Rights. The remaining two concern Chapter 31, Foreign, Security and Defence Policy.

The first concerns compensation for more than 300 Croatian citizens held at the Morinj camp between October 1991 and August 1992. The second concerns the preservation and permanent visibility of the memorial plaque installed at the former camp. A large metal frame has been erected around the plaque, allowing a movable panel to be placed over it.

“Such concealment would undermine this shared act of remembrance and reconciliation,” the document states.

Croatia also calls for the municipal swimming pool in Kotor, named after Zoran Gopcevic, a former international water polo player who was a guard at the camp, to be renamed. Because of the current name, Croatian clubs refuse to play at the facility.

Fourth, Croatia seeks full cooperation from Montenegro to determine the fate of 14 Croatian citizens who went missing during the aggression against Croatia in the early 1990s.

The fifth demand calls on Montenegro to prosecute those responsible for war crimes committed during the same war, including people who may bear criminal liability under the doctrine of command responsibility.

The sixth demand concerns property disputes dating back to the early 1990s, involving Croatian families who were unlawfully deprived of their property. The document notes that property has been returned to some former owners, mostly members of the Albanian minority, raising concerns about unequal treatment.

The seventh demand concerns the return of the training ship Jadran (Adriatic), which was based in Split before the breakup of Yugoslavia but was in Montenegro for repairs when war broke out in 1991.

According to the document, the Jadran dispute is part of the broader question of the division of the former Yugoslavia’s military assets. It asserts that military equipment belonging to the former Yugoslav federation, which Montenegro continues to hold and which Croatia claims was seized from its territory, has an estimated value of 2.7 billion US dollars.

In its eighth demand, Croatia calls for continued dialogue on the demarcation of the border between the two countries.

Podgorica must confirm the former border between the two former Yugoslav republics, as established by the Arbitration Commission of the Conference on Yugoslavia, commonly known as the Badinter Commission.

According to the document, experts say deviations between the former administrative border and the current situation are minor and do not exceed 220 metres.

Montenegro is currently seen as a frontrunner among Balkan states to secure EU membership and hopes to join the bloc in 2028. But Croatia has repeatedly warned that it requires any ‘bilateral disputes’ to be settled first.

World.title: Albanian PM Blames Opposition After Another Night of Violent Clashes
World.content:
Albanian students protesting on October 14, 2026. Photo: LSA.

Prime Minister Edi Rama on Thursday accused the opposition of organising student protests that have seen violence erupt on the streets of Tirana for two consecutive days.

Visiting the office of the College of Europe postgraduate institute, which was damaged by fire in the violence on Wednesday, Rama said: “Students are always welcome, and we are always ready to sit down with them to talk, discuss and find solutions to matters that require resolution.

“These, however, are different hands,” he continued. “These are the hands that seek to pull Albania down whenever it tries to rise.”

On Wednesday, the first floor of the Education Ministry was set on fire, while the Prime Minister’s office, the parliament, the Constitutional Court, the Finance and Interior ministries, the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.

Clashes continued until midnight as protesters, some of them masked and throwing stones and petrol bombs, faced off against police who deployed tear gas and water cannons. Police cars and a police station also came under attack.

The Ministry of Health announced on Thursday that 79 people received medical treatment at Tirana’s Trauma Hospital, including 61 were police officers and 18 protesters. Ten other people were receiving treatment at Mother Teresa Hospital.

The clashes led to the cancellation of a parliamentary session scheduled for Thursday. On Thursday morning, students marched towards parliament as the protests looked set to continue.

Interior Minister Ervin Dema on Wednesday accused the opposition and “foreign actors” of inciting the violent clashes, claiming that student discontent had been exploited to destabilise the country.

“Today, all of Albania saw that, in the name of the students, the oldest political element in this country … spoke the language of destruction, flames, and the ransacking of public and private property,” Dema said.

The student demonstrations began outside the Ministry of Education on Tuesday, calling for the government’s resignation, better university conditions and highlighted the high cost of living.

The students were initially called to the streets by the so-called “Flamingo Revolution” protesters. Their daily protests started in June as environmental demonstrations but evolved into an anti-government movement.

World.title: Central Europe Struggles to Square the Circle over Foreign Workers
World.content:
Politics vs economics

That has been a familiar theme across the four countries, where the economic case for foreign labour has not translated into a political consensus for such an influx. Governments and employers might recognise the need for workers, but concerns about wages, competition for jobs and immigration have made recruitment politically contentious.

While having to accommodate the “Czech first” stance of its coalition partner, the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) movement, the ruling ANO party of Prime Minister Andrej Babis has vowed to “look for nurses in Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan” and – more generally speaking – bring in 100,000 qualified foreigners by 2030.

“The current 942,000 foreign workers in the Czech Republic are still far below market potential,” ANO stated, with the ruling party planning to reduce the administrative burden, simplify the recognition of foreign diploma and certificates, digitise the entire process, and shorten permit deliveries to 30 days for highly qualified employees and 60 days for medium and low-skilled workers.

And while Czech employers and business associations have overall welcomed such plans, they have also warned of the risks to focus solely on high-skilled labour.

“Speed and predictability are crucial because Czech companies are competing for skilled workers with companies in Germany, Poland and other European countries,” Sotona of the Czech Chamber of Commerce tells BIRN.

“This is not a choice between making better use of domestic labour and labour migration. The Czech Republic needs to do both,” he says. “The objective is not uncontrolled migration, but the opposite: a legal, transparent and predictable system that enables companies to recruit workers whom they objectively cannot find on the domestic labour market.”

Across the border, “foreigners today are not just a supplement, but an essential part of the [Slovak] labour market,” according to Jakub Zagora, an analyst at the Kosice IT Valley in eastern Slovakia. “At the same time, however, we see that the demand for workers still significantly exceeds the supply.”

Obstacles to hiring foreign workers are many, ranging from uncertainty and bureaucratic hurdles to integrating them over the long term, to laborious permits procedures and enduring anti-foreigner sentiment among the population.

About two-thirds of Slovak employees see foreigners as a potential threat to their own jobs, and three-quarters worry their employment hinders overall wage growth, according to a JobsIndex survey. “Employers still see more problems and obstacles than benefits in importing workers from abroad,” assessed Martin Szabo, a labour market expert at Alma Career Slovakia.

Hungary’s restrictions have brought the tension between politics and economic needs sharply into focus. Since the government stopped issuing residence permits to people arriving under guest-worker contracts, employers have warned of difficulties filling vacancies and delays to investment. The door remains open to those applying for a so-called “residence permit for the purpose of employment”, but this is a more complicated and lengthy process, often taking nine to 12 months.

“Companies are already feeling the consequences and complaining about the lack of workers from third countries,” says Kalmar of BusinessHungary.

The organisation has been negotiating with the government to find a solution. Some urgently needed investments are already being delayed as companies are unsure whether they will be able to find enough suitably qualified workers.

The debate intensified during the summer when the owner of Master Good, one of Hungary’s largest agrifood companies, threatened not to proceed with a 120-billion-forint investment, worth about 330 million euros, in a new meat-processing plant if guest workers were not allowed into the country.

Critics accused the company of seeking to keep wages down, arguing that foreign workers, who are often willing to work longer hours than Hungarians, drive down pay. Yet Master Good’s owner, Laszlo Barany, countered that there were jobs for which the company simply could not find Hungarian workers. “There are shifts starting at 02:00 in the night, and the temperature in the processing plant is under 10 degrees Celsius all day,” he told Telex.hu. The company has employed guest workers from the Philippines for years to fill those positions.

Kalmar argues that Hungarian and guest workers are often not alternatives to one another. “In many cases, employing guest workers for certain jobs serves the interests of Hungarian workers,” he says. If there are no food couriers, he explains, a cook’s job could be at risk; if there are no workers at the end of an assembly line, an engineer might also lose their job.

The claims that foreign workers earn more than Hungarians are dismissed by Kalmar and, he says, is legally impossible. He acknowledges, however, that in some cases where a company has had to lay off workers, those dismissed were mostly Hungarian, while workers from third countries were retained. “They simply performed better,” he says.

A survey conducted by HR company WHC found that 70 per cent of medium-sized and large Hungarian companies could not imagine operating without foreign workers. The same survey found scepticism about the government’s plans to bring 300,000-400,000 so-called inactive Hungarians back into the labour market.

The problem with this proposed reserve is that people who are unemployed or economically inactive do not necessarily have the right skills, live in the right places or want the jobs on offer. “The problem is that this reserve usually does not match companies’ needs, either geographically or in terms of skills or motivation,” Kalmar explains.

Poland’s experience illustrates a related difficulty: even when migrants are available, employers cannot assume they will remain in the jobs that are hardest to fill. In research involving employers in agriculture and hospitality, Kaczmarczyk’s team found that businesses had stopped advertising some jobs in Polish altogether because nobody responded.

In agriculture, peak season can mean six or seven days a week and 10- or 12-hour shifts – conditions few Polish workers are willing to accept. Foreign labour has filled much of that gap, but workers who settle and integrate may eventually move into more attractive employment.

World.title: Black Sea Drone Attacks Expose Holes in Bulgarian Security Strategy
World.content:
For Bulgarians, the war in Ukraine this month came closer to home than ever before.

Two drone attacks on commercial ships in the country’s Black Sea zone, on October 6 and October 13, raised difficult questions about Bulgaria’s preparedness for further escalation, and its government’s tendency to avoid direct criticism of Russia.

Each attack sank a ship and damaged another. The exact death toll has yet to be confirmed.

“We don’t have solid evidence to blame either side but logic suggests the strikes have been of benefit to the Russian Federation,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev, himself a former air force commander, said in the wake of the second attack.

He summoned Russian ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who claimed that “a third side” may have been responsible.

Whatever the truth, former deputy defence minister Velizar Shalamanov says Bulgaria’s inaction is dangerous.

World.title: Rising Violence is a Sign that Serbia’s Ruling Party is Panicking
World.content:
During a recent protest against Aleksandar Vucic's visit to the town of Uzice, ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, supporters assaulted and beat several citizens, while police stood by without intervening.

In Belgrade, a group of men attacked and injured an official observer from Serbia’s Anti-Corruption Agency, an independent state institution, while he was documenting campaign activities at a stand operated by the ruling party.

In Novi Sad, SNS supporters led by one of the party’s parliamentary candidates confronted activists and candidates of the opposition student-led electoral list and attempted to seize their banner.

In another incident, Belgrade’s Mayor Aleksandar Sapic was reported to have physically assaulted a female opposition councillor in the street, although he denied this. A week later, an N1 television journalist was attacked and threatened by a prominent SNS supporter while investigating potential electoral fraud. In the city of Nis, a journalist from an independent website was assaulted and injured while filming SNS campaign activities, with police reportedly refusing to intervene.

This week also saw revelations from SNS hired hand Momcilo Marjanovic, who told BIRN that he spent a decade providing ‘security’ for the ruling party, a role that involved buying votes and beating protesters.

These are not episodes scattered across years of political turmoil. They have all been reported in the space of a few weeks, as Serbia gets closer to parliamentary elections on October 25.

World.title: Will Croatia Prevent Montenegro EU Accession?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Croatia has multiple conditions for entry into the bloc, but could it go as far as to block the Montenegro EU accession?

Croatia has very clearly warned neighbouring Montenegro that a series of unresolved bilateral issues could slow its planned entry into the European Union by 2028. Among the open topics are war crimes, property restitution and the definition of the border, Index reports.

This week, Zagreb sent a document to the other EU Member States listing eight demands that Montenegro must fulfil before the conclusion of accession negotiations. Montenegro is otherwise widely regarded as the front-runner among the candidate countries and hopes to become the 28th member of the Union by 2028. Nevertheless, long-standing disputes with Croatia, which mostly date from the time of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, represent an obstacle to those plans.

blockade progress

“Croatia sincerely wishes to close this painful chapter of our shared history and to build a future-oriented relationship with Montenegro. However, mutual trust and genuine and lasting reconciliation cannot be achieved without resolving these issues,” the Croatian document states. On Monday, Montenegro advanced in its negotiations with the EU after closing the chapters on statistics, economic policy and employment. This brought the total number of closed chapters to 21 out of 33.

Croatia, however, is blocking progress in four other areas: transport, external relations, fundamental rights and internal affairs. Every member state has the right of veto over the enlargement process, which gives Zagreb significant influence over Montenegro’s path to membership. The document elaborates in detail the objections that the Croatian Ministry of Foreign Affairs already put forward back in July, which largely stem from the wars of the 1990s.

a list of croatia’s open issues

One of the most sensitive demands concerns compensation for around three hundred Croatian citizens who were detained and abused in the Morinj concentration camp in Montenegro from October 1991 to August 1992. During the conflict, Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly taken to that camp. Croatia also demands that the memorial plaque at the site of the former camp remain permanently visible. The plaque was enclosed in a metal structure after protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups. Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people who are still listed as missing from the Homeland War.

Zagreb is therefore asking Montenegro for help in locating their remains and describes this as an important humanitarian issue that has not yet been resolved. Croatia also demands that in the cases of already convicted war criminals for crimes against civilians in Morinj, command responsibility be taken into account.

long-standing disputes from the 1990s

Zagreb also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes from the early 1990s concerning Croatian families whose property was confiscated without adequate compensation. The document notes that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region with a predominantly Albanian minority, which “raises concerns about unequal treatment in similar cases.”

Zagreb also seeks the return of the “Jadran” vessel which has been under Montenegrin control since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1991. Finally, Croatia demands the resolution of territorial disputes over the land and maritime border in accordance with the decisions of the Arbitration Commission on Yugoslavia. Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although that did not prevent it from joining the European Union back in 2013.

“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve the open bilateral issues and at the same time has actively supported its entry into the EU. Despite Croatia’s constant efforts and constructive approach, none of the open issues has yet been resolved,” the document concludes.

World.title: How Will Croatia Actually Benefit From the €50 billion Data Centre?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – In what way will Croatia actually concretely benefit from the giant €50 billion data centre in Topusko that has many deeply concerned about the environment and water?

The previously announced construction of the huge and very controversial Pantheon data centre in Topusko, whose value is estimated at as much as €50 billion, raises a series of questions about the real benefits Croatia could gain from such an investment. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this gigantic project recently took another step towards realisation. Sisak-Moslavina County has initiated amendments to the spatial plan in order to create the conditions for the construction of the centre and the accompanying infrastructure.

Although a series of procedures and the obtaining of the necessary permits still lie ahead before construction can begin, below we provide answers to some of the key questions about the project, its possible benefits and costs. For the purposes of this text we also received an expert comment from Tomislav Vazdar, an expert in cybersecurity and artificial intelligence.

intended for large tech companies with little care for anyone else

According to Ryan Rich, executive partner of Pantheon AI, who wrote about the project for the Wall Street Journal, the centre is intended for large technology companies that need enormous computing capacity for continuous operation and the development of artificial intelligence. Rich also stated that the infrastructure would be available to European defence, intelligence and commercial users.

Pantheon representatives were asked about who specifically will use the future data centre and whether there are already agreed tenants, but we had not received a reply by the time this text was published. Project manager Mario Gudelj explained to Večernji list in July that the final value of the investment will depend on the requirements of future users, whom he described as large technology companies developing artificial intelligence. According to the announcements at the time, the first users should start using the centre’s capacities at the beginning of 2029.

Vazdar explained to us who the most common users of such data centres are. “The largest users are global cloud service providers, companies developing large artificial intelligence models, and increasingly the defence and security sector. In a centre of this scale, AI models would primarily be trained and run. Money is earned by renting out capacity, most often through long-term contracts with a few large clients,” Vazdar commented for Index.

is there any benefit to anyone outside of big tech?

Part of the investment will relate to construction works and infrastructure, and a significant part to the purchase of computer and other technological equipment. The value of the campus construction is estimated at up to €12 billion, while the total investment, including IT equipment, should exceed €50 billion. One of the possible long-term benefits is the construction of electricity infrastructure. In addition to the construction of a 500-megawatt solar power plant, for which cooperation with the international energy group Greenvolt has been announced, according to project representatives’ announcements, the construction of approximately 280 kilometres of power lines and a new substation is planned, and the investment would be financed by the investor.

The built infrastructure should then pass into the ownership of the Croatian Transmission System Operator. “The benefits won’t come by themselves; all of that has to be contracted in advance. So, a share of capacity for domestic companies, universities and the public sector, engagement of domestic contractors and investment in the network that remains with the state. Equally important is control over the data. If data is processed in Croatia but control over it remains outside the European legal framework, the state bears the risk and does not gain digital sovereignty,” Vazdar said.

are there any benefits for croatian companies?

One of the concrete opportunities for Croatian companies is linked precisely to the construction of the mentioned electricity infrastructure. At the end of April, Končar signed a non-binding letter of intent on cooperation on the Pantheon project, which envisages the participation of several companies from its group, including Dalekovod. One of the investors, entrepreneur Jako Andabak, claimed on HRT back in April that the majority of the works during the construction and equipping of the centre should be carried out by Croatian companies, using domestic knowledge and workforce.

what about new employment opportunities?

As announced at the project presentation, more than 3,000 workers should be engaged during construction, around 1,500 people employed after the centre starts operating, while the project could indirectly contribute to the creation of a further 6,000 jobs. Andabak stated that approximately half of the 1,500 permanently employed should have higher education qualifications. That would mean around 750 highly qualified jobs, primarily linked to the operation and maintenance of complex technological infrastructure.

It is not yet known how many of the employees will be from Croatia, and especially how many jobs could go to residents of Topusko and the surrounding area. “The most jobs are created during construction, and once the centre is up and running there are few permanent employees, although these are highly qualified positions. Realistic expectations should be based on signed commitments, not on announcements,” Vazdar said.

how will pantheon help croatia’s own tech sector?

One of the potentially greatest long-term benefits of the project could be the development of Croatia’s technology sector, especially companies dealing with artificial intelligence. Large computing capacities are needed for the development and training of advanced artificial intelligence models, and access to such infrastructure could open new opportunities for domestic companies, universities and research institutions.

Project manager Mario Gudelj spoke to N1 in May about the ambition for Pantheon to bring the industry of the future to Croatia and position it among the leading countries in digital transformation. Vazdar said more about the importance of Pantheon for the development of artificial intelligence and the domestic technology sector. “The significance is potentially great, but only with clear access conditions for domestic companies and scientists. Without that, the centre can operate at full capacity for foreign clients, while the domestic sector gets almost nothing from it,” he added.

how much will the state and the local community benefit financially?

In addition to employment and the engagement of domestic companies, one of the more important potential benefits of the Pantheon project relates to tax and other public revenues. The Municipality of Topusko has particularly high expectations. Its mayor Ivica Kuzmić stated on HRT in May that the realisation of the project could increase the municipality’s revenues three to four times. He emphasised that the additional funds would primarily be used to improve communal infrastructure.

However, a detailed financial projection showing how much the state and the Municipality of Topusko would earn annually from the centre’s operations has not yet been publicly presented. The amount of tax revenues will depend, among other things, on the centre’s business results, the number and salaries of employees, and the way in which the business of the companies involved in the project is organised.

will electricity prices shoot up?

One of the more important questions relates to the high consumption of electricity and water and the possible consequences for the general public, for whom a giant data centre represents little but a deep worry. As Gudelj announced, Pantheon in full operation would consume around five terawatt-hours of electricity per year, 1.5 times more than Zagreb and a little more than a quarter of Croatia’s consumption.

However, he stated that electricity would not become more expensive for citizens because of the centre. According to his announcements, the centre would primarily be supplied from renewable sources, and the investor would also finance the necessary electricity infrastructure. “A data centre of this scale consumes as much electricity as a large city, and continuously. That means great pressure on the electricity system and a risk that the cost of adapting the network will spill over onto all users if the rules are not set in advance,” Vazdar adds.

“Cooling data centres down also requires significant amounts of water, so it is necessary to transparently determine how that will affect local sources. All of this must be publicly and independently assessed before any decision,” Vazdar says.

data centres and their devastating environmental impact

The impact of Pantheon on the environment is a separate and extremely important topic that deserves an analysis of its own. We have already written about this in detail on Index, and here we will only recall that part of the public is mainly concerned about the high water consumption, noise, waste heat, interventions in the space and potential consequences for the local ecosystem.

Vazdar warns for Index that cooling a data centre requires significant amounts of water, which is why it is necessary to transparently determine the possible impact on local sources and to assess everything publicly and independently before any decision is made. Gudelj says that the final solution has not yet been chosen. Pantheon, as he emphasised, will not connect to the public water supply or use water from rivers and streams, and hydrogeological research is being carried out. Earlier, the investors claimed to Index that the impact on the environment would be negligible or non-existent. In any case, the strategic environmental impact assessment and the assessment of acceptability for the ecological network are only part of the procedures that must precede construction. Therefore it still remains to be determined what consequences the project could have for the environment and what protection measures will be necessary.

World.title: Split High on Quality of Life in Relation to Costs Ranking – But Should It Be?
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Split has occupied a high position in terms of quality of life in relation to costs of living, being above Stockholm and and Copenhagen, but should it rank this highly?

Two of Croatia’s largest cities also made it into the aforementioned quality of life ranking. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that according to this research, Zagreb and Split are cities with above-average, even high, quality of life, but at the same time they are extremely expensive relative to the median salary.

does split really offer a better life than 94% of other european cities?

The analysis shows that Split offers a better life than 94 percent of other European cities, including Copenhagen, Prague, Stockholm and Madrid, but in order to enjoy its benefits and advantages one needs to earn 29 percent more than the net median salary, which in Croatia back in July amounted to 1,346 euros. The median salary means that half of employees received a net salary lower than 1,346 euros, and half received at least that much or more.

Zagreb fared somewhat worse, or better, depending on which parameter on the chart you look at. In the capital, the chart says, the quality of life is significantly lower than in Split: Zagreb is better than 64 percent of other European cities (for example Graz, Rome, Berlin and Milan). On the other hand, the mentioned standard is also significantly more accessible and one needs to earn only three percent more than the net median salary.

the worst quality of life is in belgrade

The best and most affordable life, according to the research, is lived in Vienna, Helsinki and the Dutch cities of The Hague and Eindhoven. And the worst and most expensive in Skopje, Belgrade, Sofia and Bucharest. That is at least how it was calculated by Alessandro Palombo, an Italian entrepreneur and doctor of legal sciences, who published the research in the form of several charts on social networks and his website.

Of course, what immediately catches the eye on the chart is the paradox that Skopje is more expensive than Paris and London, and that Oslo and Geneva are cheaper than Zagreb. However, Palombo did not take into account absolute living costs, according to which the largest European cities are certainly expensive, but the ratio of costs to the median salary in those cities. The contradiction is nevertheless only apparent: a city can be very expensive, but the local median salary can be sufficient for an excellent standard of living. Likewise, a city with relatively low prices can be difficult to afford for local residents with low salaries.

numbeo deemed “an unreliable data source”

The fundamental problem that largely calls into question the validity of the research is the source of the data. As usual when it comes to such analyses, Palombo uses data from Numbeo, an online database that, based on user inputs, collects and compares information on living costs, prices, salaries, safety, quality of life and other indicators in cities and countries around the world.

Numbeo is often quite unreliable as a source because anyone can enter data in a certain category. Although there are automatic filters for suspicious values, its data and analyses should generally be taken with a large dose of caution. For this reason, Palombo himself does not present his comparisons as infallible. In a discussion on X he admitted that he considers the quality of such data limited and that some components of quality of life are inevitably subjective.

Specifically, according to the October data on prices on Numbeo, for Split in the previous 12 months data was submitted by 37 different participants, and for Zagreb by 156. Dozens of voluntary participants are not a representative sample for a display on a map with seemingly precise coordinates. Numbeo’s standard quality-of-life index includes eight factors: purchasing power, safety, healthcare, property prices relative to income, cost of living, commute time, pollution and climate.

Palombo states that he calculated quality of life without Numbeo’s price-related indicators. What remains are the criteria of safety, healthcare, traffic, pollution and climate, which at Numbeo to a large extent rest on the perception of the website’s users rather than on official statistics. Financial affordability is shown separately by Palombo on the horizontal axis.

croatia’s housing structure makes a major difference

However, quality of life in this research does not take into account other important criteria at all, such as the quality of education, employment opportunities, availability of kindergartens, cultural offer, social protection and the real possibility of finding long-term housing.

It should also be borne in mind that the research is based on a single person who earns the median salary and lives in a rented one-bedroom apartment outside the city centre. That in no way corresponds to the financial status of the majority of the population. For Croatia specifically, this difference is particularly important. According to Eurostat data, in 2024 91 percent of Croatia’s inhabitants lived in their own property. A person living in their own paid-off apartment, a young tenant, a married couple with two salaries, a four-member family and a pensioner have completely different relationships between income and living costs. This clearly shows how much the author’s model differs from reality.

It is also not explained by what criterion these particular 79 cities were selected. It is not entirely clear whether the author of the research took into account the median net salary in the entire country, the region or only in the specific city.

osijek finds itself (surprisingly) on the list

Interestingly, Palombo also offers another interactive map that, according to the same criteria, compares 322 world cities. Among Croatian cities, Osijek is the biggest surprise. It is at approximately the 99.7th percentile of quality of life, which places it among the highest-rated cities, even slightly ahead of Vienna, Helsinki, Split and Rijeka. The only problem is that the basic (and entirely bizarre) assumption is an annual gross income of 86,000 US dollars, which is deeply unrealistically high for Croatian standards. Only a few thousand employees in Croatia receive such a salary.

World.title: Massive Changes for Private Landlords in Croatia Coming in 2027
World.content:
October the 15th, 2026 – Major changes for private landlords in Croatia are coming in 2027, with new categorisation every 10 years and mandatory registration numbers just part of it.

By the end of the year, the Croatian Government intends to pass a new Hospitality Activity Act that will introduce a series of changes for private landlords, hotels, campsites, hospitality operators and short-term rental platforms. Poslovni reports that one of the most important novelties starts in 2027: rooms, apartments, studio apartments and holiday homes advertised via online short-term rental platforms will have to have a unique registration number.

Without it, the property will not be allowed to be advertised on such platforms. It’s important to note that this obligation is not yet in force. The Ministry of Tourism and Sport has explicitly warned landlords that during 2026 there is still no obligation to obtain a registration number. The exact start date of application will be published after the new Hospitality Activity Act is adopted.

the number will be free of charge and issued by the relevant ministry

The registration number will have to be obtained by owners (both natural and legal persons) who offer rooms, apartments, studio apartments or holiday homes via short-term rental platforms. The procedure is expected to be completely free and digitalised, and the number will be issued by the Ministry of Tourism and Sport upon request. The landlord will then have to display it with the listing on the platform.

The goal is to link all of the national data held with the online platforms so that it can be verified whether the property being advertised is genuinely registered for the provision of accommodation services. This should make it significantly more difficult to advertise apartments, rooms and holiday homes that are rented out without the required permit.

greater responsibility must come from the platforms themselves

The new rules will not apply only to accommodation owners. Online short-term rental platforms will have to cooperate with the state system, exchange prescribed data and check whether listings have the required registration number. The draft law also provides for high fines for platforms that fail to meet these obligations. The registration system stems from the European Regulation on the collection and exchange of data on short-term rentals, and Croatia is regulating the manner of its implementation with the new law.

re-categorisation for landlords

The registration number is not the only change looming in 2027, as the new law will introduce for the first time mandatory periodic re-categorisation for private landlords as well. According to the proposal that has passed the first reading in Parliament, rooms, apartments, studio apartments and holiday homes will have to undergo re-categorisation every ten years, after alignment with the new rulebook (pravilnik). The aim is that the number of stars and the category of the property do not remain permanently linked to the condition the accommodation was in at the time of the first decision, but that they correspond to its actual condition.

For hotels and campsites the current four-year re-categorisation deadline would be extended to five years. For certain other accommodation facilities, such as hostels, overnight stays, and mountain and hunting lodges, a re-check every five years is introduced.

a shakeup for residential premises…

Another important change concerns legal persons and craftsmen. According to the current draft law, in future they would no longer be issued new decisions for rooms, apartments and studio apartments in premises that have a residential purpose. The possibility would remain for holiday homes. The government justifies this measure by protecting the basic function of housing and reducing the pressure of short-term rentals on the availability of apartments for long-term housing. This concerns new decisions; the law will ultimately determine the transitional regime for existing facilities.

big brother will be watching illegal rentals

The circle of bodies that can participate in the supervision of unregistered provision of hospitality services is also being expanded. In addition to the State Inspectorate, the Customs Administration and municipal wardens would also be involved in supervision, and in certain cases nature wardens as well. An additional reason for revoking a decision from a hospitality operator or landlord could also be established non-payment of the tourist tax. At the same time, administrative procedures in tourism should almost entirely move to the digital eTurizam system, from submitting applications and categorisation to communication with competent authorities and issuing decisions.

The Croatian Government sent the draft of the new Hospitality Activity Act to Parliament at the end of June, and MPs accepted it in the first reading on the 3rd of July. 78 MPs voted in favour, 14 against and 37 abstained. Now, after remarks from the parliamentary debate, the final draft of the law is being prepared, which must again pass the Government and Parliament. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković announced on Tuesday that the adoption of the law is expected by the end of 2026.

Only the final text will show whether some of the rules from the first draft have been further amended. For private landlords the most important thing is that they do not yet need to request a registration number during 2026. After the law is adopted, the Ministry will publish the exact date from which, during 2027, those who advertise their accommodation units via online platforms must have it.

World.title: New Dinosaur Species Discovered in Croatia
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – An apparently brand new, previously unknown and uncategorised dinosaur species has been has been discovered in Croatia.

An incredible underwater dinosaur bone site has just been discovered in Croatia. An international team of scientists is currently extracting remains from the sea that are about 130 million years old, and according to the paleontologists’ initial assessments, the bones belong to a previously totally unknown species, HRT reports.

Poslovni reports that the fascinating remains found belong to a large, long-necked herbivorous dinosaur. Paleontologist Frano Vidaković compared it to a scene from the film Jurassic Park. “Do you remember that dinosaur from the beginning of Jurassic Park, when the paleontologists get out of the jeep in disbelief? Well, one like that – a long-necked dinosaur, large, with pillar-like legs, a long tail and neck, that fed on vegetation from the tops of trees,” Vidaković said.

American paleontologist Matthew Lamanna confirmed that this is an exceptionally important site. “The dinosaur we are excavating is without doubt a new species,” he emphasised. Scientists have so far found parts of the cervical spine, lumbar bones and ribs, and Lamanna explained how a fossilised bone differs from stone.

“To many this would look like a stone, but one detail tells us that this is a dinosaur bone. These are these small pores called trabeculae. They tell us that this is much more than a stone, that this is a dinosaur bone 130 million years old,” he explained.

croatia is home to a truly unique site

This is the only site in the world where dinosaur bones have been found in the sea, at depths of one and a half to six metres. Paleontologist and geologist Aleksandar Mezga highlights the uniqueness of the location. “This is the first such case in the world. People who have visited all the sites say they have never seen anything like this anywhere,” Mezga emphasised.

The site is located within the Datule-Barbariga paleontological reserve. 130 million years ago, the land that today forms Istria was part of a completely different landscape and was located roughly in the area of present-day North Africa. The first dinosaur bones in this area were discovered back in 1993, and completely by chance. Andrea Deklić from Natura Histrica recounted how it happened. “Mr Boscariolli was extracting date mussels here and breaking rocks to get to the shells. By chance, he came across a bone in the rock. Fortunately, his acquaintance was Fabio della Vecchia, a well-known Italian paleontologist,” Deklić said.

That is how Istria got its first dinosaur, named Histriosaurus Boscariollia. The newly discovered remains belong to a related but definitely different species. Scientists believe that the seabed near Bale hides more remains of Istrian dinosaurs that are still waiting to be discovered.

World.title: Huge Croatian Tourism Projects Are Springing Up, But There’s a Big Problem…
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – Some huge Croatian tourism projects are springing up, but with that come some major problems that don’t point quite towards sustainable tourism…

Thousands of new beds are planned across southern Croatia. Although those in power like to say that the country is moving towards sustainable tourism, what is happening on the ground paints a different picture. Paula Klaic Saulacic reports for Dnevnik that from the Dubrovnik littoral all the way down to Konavle – over a road distance of 60 kilometres, around 5,000 new beds are planned. They’re all connected by one single road, the Adriatic Highway, which during the summer months is bursting at the seams – and all roads ultimately lead to Dubrovnik. That city is still teeming with tourists even in October, and precisely by those visitors who come at that time because they want to avoid the summer crowds.

ecological, technological and workforce issues…

“One road, yes, we drove for a long time. It’s nice here, but any more would be too much,” commented Toby from Australia. Thousands of new beds from the Dubrovnik littoral to Konavle are not only a problem when it comes to crowds and the number of guests; the problem is with infrastructure, the workforce, and also with ecology. Some experts believe that even drinking water is under threat. Civil engineer Tomislav Paviša, in an open letter to local leaders as well as the Government, warns that projects such as Tri Sestrice, the Resort in Cavtat, Kupari and others are endangering the water supply.

“We’re witnessing that dry periods are getting longer and longer and that, consequently, there will be less and less water at the springs for a regular water supply. In order for the Dubrovnik region to approach the realisation of these projects ready, it is necessary to form a competent institution composed of hydrogeologists, hydrologists and hydraulic engineers that would deal with this vitally important problem, as well as with protection against water pollution due to accelerated urbanisation in the neighbouring country,” he said.

the water supply

Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković was not available for comment today, while the mayors of Konavle and Dubrovačko primorje earlier said that for Cavtat and Doli they see no concern for the water supply.

“There were three important conditions that had to be met, which the Municipality requested from the investor. The first is to enable the western entrance to Cavtat, the second to secure a water reservoir that will be sufficient for the next 30 or so years so that Cavtat and all the hotels have a secure water supply. The third is that all ecological standards be respected to the utmost,” said Božo Lasić, Mayor of the Municipality of Konavle (HDZ), at the end of September. “As for water, water comes from three directions: one is Doli itself with its wells, from Ston via the Oko spring, and the third from Slano via Banići, so water should not be a problem either,” said Nikola Knežić, Mayor of the Municipality of Dubrovačko primorje (HDZ), a few days later.

When asked whether, given the dry summer, golf courses and new capacities, he thinks this can be infrastructurally sustained in the future, he replied: “It can.”

The Mayor of Župa dubrovačka says that restrictions are necessary. In a municipality that is home to 8,000 inhabitants and the same number of beds, tourism has reached its peak. “These are all real and objective questions and we have to seek answers from the profession; in spatial plans all tourist zones need to be revised,” said Marko Miloslavić, Mayor of Župa dubrovačka (ŽUPKA). There are many questions, and the answers are urgent because all these projects, at least according to the investors, are proceeding according to plan – some are even of national interest. Nevertheless – water, the environment, space and the quality of life of the local community should be the only real national interest.

World.title: Natural Disaster Declared for Municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – A natural disaster has officially been declared for the municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća on the island of Brač after the recent fire.

Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban has issued a Decision on the declaration of a natural disaster caused by fire for the area of the municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća. Morski reports that all affected people and legal entities are invited to report any and all damage to their properties as soon as possible, and no later than the 20th of October.

The Prefect issued the Decision on the declaration of a natural disaster caused by fire for the area of the Municipality of Milna and the Municipality of Nerežišća on Monday the 12th of October, according to a statement from Split-Dalmatia County.

By the Prefect’s decision, the municipal commissions for assessing damages in the affected municipalities are tasked with urgently carrying out all actions prescribed by law, processing the reports and entering the data into the national Register of Damages.

The fire that struck the wider Milna area caused extensive damage and directly threatened human and animal lives, homes, cars and other property, not to mention hotels and resorts who were forced to evacuate their tourists. It marked a summer in which the Croatian coast burned in a way that was deeply concerning.

Despite wildfires being the unfortunate norm in the tinder dry, scorching hot Dalmatian landscape in summer, the situation both on the island of Brač and across the channel on the mainland in Omiš stood out in all the wrong ways. Fires up in Zadar which were deliberately caused also threw a new angle onto an already tragic summertime reality.

World.title: Total Renovation Coming for Zagreb Railway Station
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – A total renovation is on the cards for the iconic Zagreb Railway Station, with new facilities and much needed modernisation coming as part of it.

Zagreb Main Railway Station is one of the most recognisable places in Zagreb. It was opened back in 1892, at a time of strong development of railway traffic and modernisation of the city, according to a design by the Hungarian architect Ferenc Pfaff. Poslovni reports that while the beautiful station has served as a backdrop for many series and films, passengers frequently complain about the lack of facilities, as well as the fact that the space should be renovated. That is precisely what is about to happen.

“HŽ Infrastructure, together with the consortium of bidders Intekonzalting d.o.o. and PlanAxis d.o.o., has signed a contract for the preparation of technical documentation for the complete renovation of the Zagreb Main Railway Station building. The preparation of the conceptual and main design, including the obtaining of all necessary permits, is currently underway. The preparation of the technical documentation is proceeding according to the planned dynamics, and its completion is scheduled by the end of 2027,” they say at HŽ.

protected cultural property

They note that the project envisages a complete structural, energy and architectural renovation of the Zagreb Main Railway Station building.

“A comprehensive rehabilitation and strengthening of the load-bearing structure will be carried out, and the selected methods will be minimally invasive in order to preserve the structural system, original materials and design elements. The architectural and construction renovation covers the façades, roof structure and interiors under conservation supervision in order to preserve the cultural and historical value of the building, which has the status of a protected cultural property. Special emphasis is on the energy renovation, which includes the replacement of existing windows and doors and the installation of heat pumps with the possibility of using renewable sources,” they explain at HŽ Infrastructure.

a brand new underpass? maybe…

The start of construction works on the Zagreb Main Railway Station building is planned after the completion of the project documentation and the implementation of the procurement procedure for the execution of the works. The planned duration of the construction works is around three years, and completion of the works is expected in 2031.

“During the renovation of the Main Railway Station building it will be necessary to close certain parts of the building, and depending on the organisation and phases of the works it is also possible to close the entire building. The organisation of passenger movement, train traffic and everyday use of the station zone will be adapted to the needs and dynamics of the renovation, taking into account passenger safety and the uninterrupted flow of railway traffic. As part of the project, the possibility has been left open for the construction of a new direct underpass beneath the Main Railway Station building, i.e. beneath the vestibule, which would directly connect the building with Tomislav Square. Further elaboration and possible realisation of the underpass are within the competence of the City of Zagreb,” our interlocutors say.

World.title: Elisa to shut down 2G network in 2028, competitors hold back for now
World.content:
Phone operator Elisa is to shut down its 2G mobile network in 2028, Sakala reported .

The service will be phased out region by region, and the closure will leave older phones and devices that rely only on 2G or 3G without a connection, as Estonia's 3G network has already shut down.

Elisa spokesperson Toomas Polli said the technology dates from a time when a phone's main job was calling and sending messages, and that the role of networks has changed beyond recognition.

Competitors Telia and Tele2 said they will be closing down their 2G networks too, but not before 2029-2030 – Tele2 spokesperson Tanel Sarri said security devices and gate systems still depend on 2G.

Elisa network services development director Kristo Kork said the 2G closure will happen in phases by region, but the exact timetable and order of regions is still being drawn up and with customers noted in good time - Elisa would not say how many devices on its network are 2G-only, but said most already support 4G and 5G.

The original Sakala piece is here.

Elisa stated on its own website it shut down 3G at the end of 2024, and while most calls and data already run on newer networks, some devices in Estonia still rely on 2G.

Alongside older phones, these include security and alarm systems, electricity and water meters, payment terminals, and industrial and property automation equipment.

Polli said most people won't need to do anything, but devices with a longer lifespan than phones need attention. "Some surveillance, measurement or automation devices may have been installed ten or even more years ago and are still operating on a 2G network," he said.

2G networks, which launched in Finland in 1991, are also being phased out in other North European countries. Sweden and Norway set are to do so in 2027, while Iceland already did so last year. Further afield, G networks have already been shut down in Australia, Japan, and the U.S. Elisa recommends travellers with concerns check whether their device supports 4G and/or VoLTE.

World.title: Estonia mulls allowing dual citizenship in certain circumstances
World.content:
The coalition parties want to allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The opposition questions what problem the change is intended to solve.

On Wednesday, the Reform Party and Eesti 200 parliamentary groups in the Riigikogu jointly introduced a bill that would allow Estonian citizens by birth to hold dual citizenship. The bill would allow Estonian citizens by birth to apply to have their Estonian citizenship restored even if they had previously lost or renounced it after acquiring citizenship of another country.

Under the Constitution, Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. However, the Citizenship Act stipulates that people who are Estonian citizens by birth but also hold citizenship of another country must choose between the two when they turn 18.

Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) said at a government press conference that this was the wrong approach. "There is no reasonable justification for this whatsoever," she said. Pakosta argued that if an 18-year-old receives a letter telling them to choose between U.S. and Estonian citizenship, for example, but wants to retain both, they are fully entitled to do so.

Dual citizenship would be possible only in the case of select countries

According to Pakosta, this is precisely why the law needs to be brought into line with reality. The countries with which dual citizenship would be permitted include European Economic Area member states, as well as the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Switzerland. These countries are home to large Estonian communities.

The opposition does not understand what problem the proposal is intended to solve. Estonian citizens by birth cannot be deprived of their citizenship. Vadim Belobrovtsev, deputy chairman of the Center Party's parliamentary group, suggested that the coalition was trying to push through a proposal ahead of the elections that actually requires more extensive debate.

He said that because the bill applies only to Estonian citizens by birth, it would give some people an advantage over others.

Military service one potential stepping stone

Evelin Poolamets (EKRE) said the bill would create further confusion, particularly regarding compulsory military service. She explained that questions would arise over whether a young person should complete military service in Estonia or another country and which country's military reserve they would be assigned to.

Poolamets noted that the Citizenship Act contains various provisions affecting citizens, including matters related to social security and pensions. "Perhaps the goal is precisely to give dual citizens more opportunities," she said. However, Poolamets added that there was no guarantee a person would contribute equally to both countries.

Valdo Randpere (Reform Party) said times and circumstances have changed, with many young people living abroad and that citizenship is one way to maintain ties with Estonia. Randpere hopes the bill will secure the necessary 51 votes this time.

"I've spoken with both unaffiliated MPs and opposition representatives and I haven't received a firm no," Randpere said. He has not discussed the issue with EKRE representatives. "They would definitely say no," Randpere explained. He hopes at least one opposition party will allow its MPs a free vote.
