World.title: Estonian ex-soldier jailed in Russia after visiting his wife
World.content:
A former Estonian Defense Forces member is currently in a Russian prison, accused by the FSB of planning to fight for Ukraine — a charge his family says was forced out of him.

Artur Kirmjõe, 30, is married to a Russian national who is banned from entering Estonia, leaving him to travel to Russia to visit her. He had done so over 10 times before he was detained on April 29.

In a video published by the FSB — Russia's main internal security organ — in the Vladimir oblast in June this year, a man with his face concealed states he got in touch with Ukrainian contacts and asked to join Ukraine's armed forces.

"My attitude towards the war in Ukraine became sharply negative. On my own initiative, I contacted Ukrainian contacts and asked them to help me join Ukrainian military units to fight on their side against Russia," the man is heard to say.

Relatives confirm it is Artur, but say he was induced to say what he does in the video.

"He said what he was forced to say, but it is all lies. It is not true. He was just reading it, I don't know, from a screen or from a piece of paper," said his brother, Jüri.

Artur Kirmjõe served in the EDF'Scout's Battalion. Source: ERR

Artur's mother, Inga Allikas, points out the absurdity of the charges given how and why her son had traveled there. "If a person wants to go and fight on Ukraine's side, they don't take big suitcases and a cat and travel to Russia to their wife," she said.

The "Pealtnägija" report was the first time Jüri and Inga have spoken publicly on the episode under their own names and faces. The family had not drawn attention to the case earlier, hoping it was a misunderstanding which would resolve itself. Now they want international attention drawn to the situation: the 30-year-old Estonian citizen faces 7 to 12 years in prison based on what they call a trumped-up confession.

Artur was born in Tallinn and grew up in nearby Maardu. He is bilingual and studied in Russian for his first eight school years, and in Estonian after that. After high school he studied at the maritime academy, was conscripted, and stayed on as a regular EDF member — serving as a paramedic in the Scout's Battalion at Tapa from autumn 2018 to the end of 2020.

The chain of events leading to his current plight began shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In late March that year, a couple arrived from Russia — a married couple, aged just over 20, referred to in the report as Lina and Sergei. In early April 2022 they applied for international protection in Estonia, saying life in Russia was dangerous for them due to their anti-war views.

"Lina was persecuted because of her political views, which were clearly opposed to the Russian state," said her lawyer, Merili Laansoo.

Indrek Aru, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border guard bureau, said not all circumstances could be commented on, but that the grounds given were checked and no sufficient basis for protection was found.

Artur with his wife Liina (name changed). Source: ERR

When the PPA refused protection, Sergei and Lina appealed. Tallinn Administrative Court found they were not in real danger in Russia: no criminal cases had been opened against them, they were not on any wanted lists, and the likelihood of attracting the authorities' attention was low. The pair appealed to the Supreme Court without success. In November 2023, they were banned from entering Estonia for three years — a detail that matters much in respect of what followed.

"He was quite shocked. You could see he was very uncomfortable, because he started crying. Just uncontrollably," said their friend Lars-Eerik Väina.

While the court cases were unfolding, a romance unfolded too, between Artur and the still-married Lina. The pair were working as security guards at the Kauplus Aasia club in Tallinn. Lina divorced Sergei in summer 2023.

Since Lina had to leave Estonia a few months later, in November 2023, Artur and Lina married in Russia on June 1, 2024, at a registry office in Vladimir, 200 kilometers from Moscow. The couple said they hoped the entry ban would now be lifted, but the PPA refused again — seeing it as suspicious that the application to live in Estonia had come so soon after the marriage, which in turn had followed soon after the entry ban.

As a result, Artur shuttled between Estonia and Russia more than ten times between 2023 and 2026 to see his wife. The lawyer representing them repeatedly pointed out that traveling to Russia could be dangerous, particularly as Artur was a former serviceman, but the PPA downplayed any danger.

"A significant number of Estonian citizens live permanently in Russia. In this case, the specific person has traveled back and forth to Russia repeatedly. Yes, at certain stages our wording may not have been the best. I admit that in hindsight," Aru said. He added that the official information presented at the time was not meant to encourage Estonians to travel to Russia, and that it was an unfortunate choice of words.

"I think those decisions are made en masse; everyone gets the same reply under their application. Nobody looks through the files, nobody looks at the applicant's background, whether it is genuinely safe for them or not," Inga said.

Artur in EDF uniform with his mother, Inga Allikas. Source: ERR

Inga now lives in Helsinki and works as an accountant, but she previously spent years working as a translator for the PPA. She believes official indifference cost her son his freedom. Separation from his wife has caused Artur mental health problems, the family says, and in April this year he traveled to Russia again, after six months apart.

"I lived with him for about 20 years. And the fact that he went there means love told him that it was the only thing worth going for — love," said his brother Jüri.

At the end of April, the FSB arrested the Estonian citizen in Lina's kitchen. Then in June the video appeared on the FSB Vladimir office's Telegram channel and spread to other outlets. In it, Artur appears to confess to anti-Russian activity.

Relatives, who can only communicate with Artur by letter via Lina, believe the video statements are entirely fabricated. "Artur has never been to Ukraine, not even out of tourist interest. To comment on what the charge is based on — some correspondence that was found, maybe. I don't know," said Inga.

Aru said the family's view is now seen differently in light of the arrest and detention. "But in hindsight, would that change anything? We cannot change the past. It is, unfortunately, a tragic story," he said.

Lina says she is currently not facing persecution, but, citing her safety, declined to appear in the report and asked that her real name not be published.

Artur's family has hired a lawyer in Russia and recently appealed to the Estonian Foreign Ministry for help, so that consular officials can assist and diplomats can perhaps pull international strings. "I know Estonia should somehow contact the United States — I don't know which institution — and start negotiations to have Artur added to an exchange list, so he might get home sooner than if he serves all those years," Inga concluded.

World.title: Tartu prison director: Dissatisfaction with prison life hardly out of the ordinary
World.content:
Tartu Prison Director Merle Ulst acknowledged that renting out prison space is a new situation for all parties involved, requiring both the Estonian Prison Service and the inmates brought to Estonia to adapt.

The inmates complained that prison officials did not speak English well enough and that they had been sent to Estonia against their will. Among other things, the inmates were unhappy that the two televisions in their cells were positioned side by side, that the beds lacked guardrails and that they had no privacy when washing.

Ulst noted that the visit by the Office of the Chancellor of Justice took place nearly two months ago when the vast majority of Swedish inmates had been at Tartu Prison for just two days. Most of the issues and concerns raised at the time had already come up in the prison staff's daily work.

"Addressing these issues is part of the prison's day-to-day work. We explain the rules and procedures to inmates, listen to their feedback and make adjustments based on practical experience where reasonable and possible. When new procedures are introduced, it is only natural that some arrangements need to be refined and improved based on initial experience," Ulst said.

She emphasized that inmates cannot expect all the comforts they are accustomed to outside prison and that certain restrictions are an inevitable part of prison life.

"Our task is to ensure humane conditions, respect for inmates' rights and a safe environment for everyone in our custody. These principles also guide us when making changes. We take legitimate needs into account, but not every request warrants changing existing procedures," Ulst said.

The Tartu Prison director noted that the issues raised by Swedish and Estonian inmates regarding everyday living conditions, restrictions and prison procedures are fairly similar.

"Dissatisfaction with certain aspects of prison life is not unusual and addressing such concerns is part of the prison's daily work. Regardless of an inmate's background, we follow the same principles: We ensure their rights and humane conditions while maintaining clear boundaries necessary for the prison to function," she said.

World.title: Eesti 200 to decide Sunday on running with Greens at Riigikogu election
World.content:
Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas is to propose at Sunday's party board meeting that the party run alongside the Greens in the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.

The Greens (Rohelised) will discuss the merger at their own general assembly later in the month. Both parties are polling far below the 5 percent threshold required to win seats, at 1.2 (Eesti 200) and 0.7 percent (Greens), even though Eesti 200 is in office with Reform at the national level.

Media reports that the two parties were considering joining forces emerged late last month.

Kallas, who is also education minister, told ERR she will make the proposal at Sunday's meeting and was unwilling to comment further on the possible merger, or her own political plans before then.

Rasmus Lahtvee, one of the Green party's leaders, said the exact date for their discussions is still not set, but the merger with Eesti 200 will certainly be talked about..

"There is talk [with Eesti 200]. We have been feeling out various possibilities and what the two parties have in common. It is clear that something has to change on the Estonian political landscape," Lahtvee said.

"The merger certainly has to be decided by the general meeting, and that will stay at the end of October," he went on.

Asked whether the parties' possible decisions would be followed by more serious merger talks in November, Lahtvee said some clarity must come soon, as the president will declare the Riigikogu elections by December 6 at the latest. Polling day is set for March 7, 2027.

Eesti 200 has been struggling with very low ratings for several years now. A Norstat poll published this week put support for the party at 1.2 percent, with the Greens at 0.7 percent. The latest ERR-commissioned Emor poll in September put Eesti 200 at 1.9 percent and the Greens at 1.1 percent.

Eesti 200 was founded in 2018 and won 14 Riigikogu seats in 2023, entering government with Reform and, until spring last year, the Social Democrats (SDE). Lauri Hussar, a former Eesti 200 chair, has held the Riigikogu speaker position since April 2023, while Margus Tsahkna is its Foreign Minister.

Eesti 200's rating started to collapse soon after the 2023 election, however, after a donations to Ukraine scandal engulfed a former MP. Another MP, former Green leader Züleyxa Izmailova, who herself had replaced the disgraced MP, returned to her original party, SDE, in 2024. Then in late summer this year, high-profile MP and former Riigikogu Defense Committee chair Kalev Stoicescu quit the party, to join the non-parliamentary Parempoolsed. This left the ruling Reform-Eesti 200 coalition as a minority government.

Eesti 200 has also approached SDE and also the Free Party (Vabaerakond) about mergers, but without success. The Greens in fact have more members now — 705 to Eesti 200's 579 — but their candidates mostly cannot afford the €946 election deposit, which is part of what Eesti 200 could offer.

A party needs a minimum of 500 members to be legally registered.

World.title: Foreign minister: One must ensure one's own survival when inflicting pain on Russia
World.content:
Estonia's decision to keep a Russian supplier to Silmet off the EU sanctions list was necessary to protect European industry, Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said, but stressed that the company must end its dependence on Russian raw materials or face further sanctions.

Estonia has been a leading advocate of sanctions for years. Now it turns out that we have nevertheless been feeding the Russian war machine through Silmet. How is that possible?

Estonia has been and will continue to be one of the most active advocates of sanctions and supporters of Ukraine in Europe. And just on Monday, we imposed sanctions on 1,600 companies and individuals. But my question is rather the other way around: How is it possible that, in the fifth year of the war, Europe remains so dependent on Russia, particularly for rare earth elements, for example? And that is not a question for Estonia. Rather, the question is how actively Europe has been working to eliminate these dependencies. We know that we are buying less energy, but Europe still continues to consume Russian energy.

What we are doing now is setting out our conditions for Silmet. And now that Silmet has also received notification from the European Commission that it has been included on the list of strategic companies, this provides a basis for obtaining European funding. But that funding must come with conditions and one of those conditions must be that the company eliminates its dependence on Russia.

But Estonia has held itself up as a moral beacon in the European Union when it comes to doing business with Russia. How can we now point fingers at others who want to do business with Russia or refuse to impose sanctions?

I would not exaggerate this position of being Europe's moral beacon quite so much. We have simply been very exemplary in our actions and we have absolutely never discussed...

This particular case shows that we have not been exemplary.

Yes, but this particular request also came from the European Commission. We also have to ask the question the other way around: If Russia were to stop supplying these raw materials to Europe altogether, European technology companies, including those in the defense industry, would be in very serious trouble.

So this is not a question of our being a moral beacon. We will continue in that role. Unfortunately, there is still a great deal of lobbying going on in the corridors of the European Commission, not specifically on strategic issues where Europe is dependent, but also purely in the interests of business. This is something that Estonian viewers do not usually learn about.

But we will continue our work as advocates of sanctions and Silmet's owners have also been told very clearly that they have a certain amount of time to eliminate their dependence on these raw materials. And this particular company will be added to the sanctions list at Estonia's own initiative.

How exactly did Silmet's supplier, a Rosatom subsidiary, end up on the proposed sanctions list? Who put forward that proposal?

We do not know how this particular company ended up on the list. Estonia has also made a great many different proposals concerning both companies and individuals. And in a sense, that is the problem with the European Commission's procedure: Before a draft reaches the member states' ambassadors, quite a few names and companies disappear during the process.

That happened this time as well. In fact, of those 1,600, I estimate that more than 50 have disappeared. We do not know who made those proposals, which is not even such a big problem. But we do not know at whose request those individuals and companies were removed from the list.

Now, Estonia acted very honestly and clearly. When the draft was already complete, the Commission pointed out that this particular magnesium plant was very directly connected to Silmet's supplies and that Silmet accounts for a very large share of what Europe needs for its industry. They asked us to look into it and it turned out that Silmet was dependent on this particular plant in its supply chain.

Did Estonia ask for Silmet's supplier not to be included on the list?

On the Commission's recommendation, we said that this particular proposal should be removed from the draft until the supply problem involving Russia had been resolved.

Did that proposal come from the Estonian government or from Silmet?

No, the proposal came to us from the Commission and I, as foreign minister, acting under the existing government mandate, confirmed that this would indeed have real consequences for European industry and that, until the supply problem was resolved, this company would not be included on the sanctions list.

We have been working for several years to find some kind of solution, but Silmet is not a state-owned company. Silmet is a private company. Silmet's owner is Neo Group, which is listed on the Canadian stock exchange.

Now that we have a real means of leverage, for example through funding, we can set our conditions directly for Neo Group. And that is what we have done.

I hope this problem will be resolved next year and that this particular company in Russia will also be on the sanctions list. It is not that easy to change the mines from which these raw materials originate. The issue is not only that there is enormous global competition, but, according to Silmet, it also requires changes in technology, and that is precisely why investment is needed.

Four and a half years have passed since the start of the war. Have you previously spoken with Silmet's management about the fact that importing these materials from Russia is not a particularly sensible thing to do, given that they would inevitably be sanctioned at some point?

We have discussed this repeatedly and we have also discussed how to attract investment here so that this specialized industry can develop in Estonia. Our goal, in fact, is to bring rare earth production, magnet manufacturing and the entire research, development and innovation center to Estonia. There is enormous competition for this around the world.

Silmet and Neo are the world's largest producers of rare earth elements outside China. So, for example, we are currently negotiating with the United States to conclude a memorandum of understanding. The European Union has already done so with the United States.

And we have been working to get Silmet and Neo included on Europe's list of strategic companies, which happened last week, and to bring European Union investment here.

Incidentally, a Neo magnet plant opened in Narva last year and the European Commission has already invested in it. So there are enormous opportunities here for Estonian industry and for our own economy.

But one specific problem that remains unresolved in Europe is this dependence on Russia and it must now be addressed as quickly as possible. It certainly will not be easy, but the only thing the Estonian government can do is apply pressure. We do not actually want to lose our own industry either.

By the way, are raw materials still being shipped from Russia's Solikamsk Magnesium Plant to Estonia today?

We are in contact with Neo's representative and my understanding is that another shipment still needs to be made. They have already factored that in. This morning (Wednesday — ed.), they also issued a public press release announcing their intention to use the available opportunities to end Russian supplies and eliminate this dependence.

Four and a half years after the start of a war that everyone has long known about. Can we trust them? And what happens if they still have not found a new supplier by the end of this year or the beginning of next year? Will national sanctions be imposed or what happens then?

If Europe has taken the necessary steps to make this technological change possible and Silmet, for example, still does not make that change, then it is no longer our responsibility. In that case, this particular company must be added to the list.

We have simply provided an opportunity for this change to take place. And this is not something that began because the company appeared on a proposed sanctions list. Work on this issue had already been underway.

Let's clarify one more thing about the timeline. Did the prime minister know that Estonia did not want to impose sanctions on a Rosatom subsidiary?

This was part of the normal working process and it was handled at my level. We bring individual decisions to the government when, for example, we are going to block a sanctions list.

That is what almost happened with the sanctions against individuals when two oligarchs were removed at France's request. If we had decided, for example, to be the only country to vote against the list and the entire list of 3,000 individuals headed by Putin had ultimately been left without sanctions, decisions of that kind would go through the government.

The prime minister is certainly aware that Silmet depends on Russian raw materials or that European industry depends on Russian raw materials. But this particular process is managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

But the Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee did not know about this either?

That Europe depends on Russian raw materials? I think that...

Were they aware that Silmet imports raw materials from Russia?

I think the entire Estonian public knows that because, as far as I know, Silmet's story has been discussed for more than 10 years.

As for the working process, this is actually how it operates because there is constant work going on between the member states and the Commission on these sanctions lists, proposals and everything related to them. That is precisely the work of our diplomats.

Why was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' initial reaction that this information should not have become public?

I do not know where the idea comes from that this information should not have become public.

That initial reaction, suggesting that this was some kind of retaliation against Estonia, that we had done something and now information had become public about which company in Russia might face sanctions?

Everything that happens in the Committee of Permanent Representatives, or Coreper, is not some kind of state secret. In that sense, I cannot say what the big secret here is.

Perhaps it is even a good thing that this has become so public and that Estonian society as a whole and Europe more broadly are recognizing that we still have a very significant strategic dependence on Russia.

What is even worse is that Europe is actually dependent on China, and, to be frank, I do not see any solution whatsoever to that problem.

We will resolve this Russian problem, or rather, the company must resolve it, not the Estonian state. But I think Europe's dependence on China will remain for a very long time.

In your assessment, did the Ministry of Foreign Affairs act correctly? Was its reaction in the first few days exactly what it should have been?

I think the reaction of the Estonian public was entirely...

The ministry's reaction.

The Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs is doing its job and we have never concealed what we are working on.

If I were in the same situation I was in a few weeks ago, I would make exactly the same decision because we are talking about European industry, we are talking about Estonian industry and we are talking about the need to eliminate our strategic dependence on Russia.

So there is no need to look for any conspiracy theory here. Communication has been very open.

But perhaps we should openly acknowledge that, in certain cases, we have no other choice. This company is so important to our economy that, in some cases, exceptions have to be made and imports from Russia have to continue.

In certain cases, when supply problems have not been resolved and these are existential issues for us, then inevitably that is how things are.

But that does not mean we should in any way abandon our support for Ukraine or stop applying additional pressure on Russia, which we have no intention of doing.

In a sense, I am even pleased that Estonian society is so uncompromising that we do not accept any such deviations or alternative interpretations.

Unfortunately, that is not the case across Europe. Increasingly, we are seeing that it is becoming harder and harder to agree on new sanctions packages. In fact, when you start working on something, you often have to take several steps back.

How can Estonia demand that other countries adopt these sanctions packages when we ourselves seemingly cannot even comply with them very well?

We can comply with them very well. Estonia has called for a complete trade embargo. Just today, at my decision-making meeting, I approved new proposals and this changes absolutely nothing about our course.

This is completely normal work for other member states as well. When issues like these come up, they are raised. This is not just about Estonia's interests or anyone's business interests. It is actually a European problem.

These matters must be discussed openly and, as foreign minister, I have no problem explaining them because any reasonable person in Estonia can understand this.

This is not some kind of moral competition. We are talking about how to inflict as much pain as possible on Russia while also ensuring our own survival.

And the question should rather be asked the other way around: How is it possible that Russia holds such powerful leverage over the whole of European industry?

What do you think the answer is? Why has Europe backed itself into a corner when it comes to raw materials?

It is not just Europe. This is actually a broader global issue and it is not just about Russia. China's influence is even greater.

In this context, perhaps what is unfamiliar to Estonia is that this particular rare earth industry and magnet industry are of such enormous importance to the entire world, especially Europe.

Europe has simply been unable to respond in the way many other countries have. And if we look, for example, at what President Trump is doing in this field today, the sums of money involved are enormous and so is the political influence.

We will get to Trump, but I want to ask one final question on this subject. You met with your Ukrainian counterpart on Monday. How could you look him in the eye in light of all this?

I looked him in the eye the same way I always do.

They are facing a very difficult winter, during which they will need very substantial assistance from Europe.

By Monday, it was also already clear that Trump had once again put Ukraine under pressure.

So I think we should focus on what the truly existential issues are and how we can help Ukraine survive this winter.

Those are the issues we actually discuss with our colleagues from Ukraine and Europe.

Eesti Ekspress reported today that there are 22 kilometers of spare gas pipeline in southeastern Estonia intended for Russia. Should Estonia maintain a gas pipeline intended for Russia in working order?

If that is what you mean, then it can be kept in working order, but not open.

Keeping it in working order also costs money.

Well, that is some kind of international obligation, since it is an international gas pipeline. But the question is whether the pipeline is open. It is not open.

It has been open on certain occasions?

Exactly, and that is why I met with the prime minister this morning and our climate minister has also been given the relevant instructions.

In fact, the valves are located in Latvia and a large part of the infrastructure is in Lithuania.

This is a European Union issue, but it is certainly one of the ways, let's be frank, that we could put pressure on Russia at some point because gas and gas transit are not subject to EU sanctions.

Let's talk about Trump and Putin. As we know, the U.S. president struck a so-called diesel deal with Putin. Why has the U.S. president begun bringing Vladimir Putin out of isolation?

First of all, this is not the first time that many people who sympathize with Ukraine have suffered what you might call a nervous breakdown, gone gray or lost a few brain cells.

But I think these questions should, of course, be put first and foremost to U.S. President Trump.

I think the answers are primarily connected to the midterm elections, which are fast approaching.

What is Estonia's position on this?

We have stated very clearly that this is a step in completely the wrong direction, considering that it allows Putin to earn additional revenue.

But this has now also been accompanied by pressure that goes beyond buying diesel. What is particularly serious is the pressure on Zelenskyy to stop his attacks on oil refineries.

That is actually where Putin and his capabilities can be significantly weakened.

Ultimately, the volume involved is not decisive in terms of either the global market or U.S. consumption.

And this is largely a political game aimed at his own voters, in response to a situation of his own making in which oil and gas prices have risen very sharply.

Has Estonia communicated its position to the United States in any way?

We have stated it completely publicly and our positions are well known.

Going back to the beginning of the interview, we criticize Trump, saying that this move is wrong. Yet through Silmet, we ourselves are feeding that same Russian war machine. Isn't that hypocritical?

These are two completely different issues.

One is whether you go and offer a deal to buy diesel or propose that kind of cooperation.

The other is when you are trying to eliminate your own strategic dependence.

These are not comparable issues.

How has this company been trying to eliminate that dependence for four and a half years without succeeding and now we are hoping it will manage to do so in just a few months?

That is what they say and I think the company's representatives should come on this program and explain to you what they have done over the past four and a half years.

By the way, have you been in contact with Silmet's CEO again over the past week?

I have been in contact with him before, personally.

But not recently?

I have. I spoke with him on Friday and our people are in contact.

Perhaps as a result of this pressure, the company, as a publicly traded company, also issued a press release this morning, which I recommend reading.

Returning to Trump, is Trump now so angry that, for the Ukrainians, this means receiving less intelligence, none at all or receiving it with a delay?

Today, I met with NATO Secretary General Rutte who was visiting Estonia and this was one of the questions we discussed.

NATO is very well informed and as of today, the United States has not restricted its intelligence sharing.

I hope that remains the case.

So this appears to be primarily political pressure, but who knows? Trump is unpredictable.

So, as things stand, at least according to NATO's assessment, the Americans have not started reducing the intelligence reaching Ukraine or causing any delays in its delivery?

Yes. The information our secretary general had was that intelligence sharing has not been reduced.

Military assistance provided through the PURL mechanism has also not been reduced or suspended.

I hope that remains the case.

Finally, a little about Estonian domestic affairs. President Alar Karis criticized the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, meaning you, in his latest speech. Do you accept the criticism?

I think Alar Karis should now move on with his life, just as he appeared to be doing in the photo he posted on Facebook, sitting in a comfortable chair by the sea.

Tomorrow, I am meeting with the new president, Ülle Madise. We have also sat down together since her election by the Riigikogu and our team is working very well with her.

So I would not go down the path of commenting on the views of a president who is already leaving office.

But what will communication between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the presidency as an institution look like now? Will cooperation with Ülle Madise be better?

Just as cooperation was excellent during President Karis' term, it will also be excellent with Ülle Madise.

World.title: Estonia still importing Russian food products
World.content:
Estonia's trade with Russia has dwindled since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but imports of food products have continued alongside rare earth metals.

Tespi, a wholesale warehouse store, imports Russian and Belarusian food products that are not subject to sanctions into Estonia. Some of these products are also sold by other grocery stores. The retailers are reluctant to discuss Russian goods.

Apart from certain chemicals and rare earth metals, for which Estonia sought special permission from the European Union to supply Silmet, food products now account for most imports from Russia to Estonia. In August, for example, imports of Russian food products and animal products totaled around €1 million, although last year there were months when the figure reached €3 million. Imports have declined since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but not significantly.

"The fluctuations in food import figures are due to the size of the shipments transported by sea," said Ursula Riimaa, deputy director general for customs at the Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA).

Overall, however, little remains of Estonia's trade relations with Russia.

"Trade with Russia has changed significantly, both in terms of imports and exports. Before the war, Estonia imported approximately €2.2 billion worth of goods from Russia. In the first eight months of this year, imports totaled around €40 million. We're talking about volumes that have fallen more than tenfold," Riimaa said.

The European Union's sanctions policy has primarily targeted sectors of the Russian economy that fuel its war machine, such as exports of petroleum products and mineral resources. Product categories that generate less revenue for Russia have so far largely been excluded from the restrictions.

"Food products and medical supplies have been the two main categories of goods that have largely remained exempt from sanctions so far. However, certain food products classified as luxury goods are subject to restrictions on both imports from and exports to Russia," said Kadri Elias-Hindoalla, director general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' sanctions department.

Compared with prewar levels, EU exports to Russia have fallen by 60 percent, while imports have dropped by 90 percent. Additional restrictions are being introduced with each new sanctions package.

The most significant measure set to take effect next year is a restriction on imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG), which several European countries continue to purchase from Russia.

World.title: Company managing Narva border queue asks city for support after traffic dries up
World.content:
Cross-border vehicle traffic has come to a standstill and the city-owned company is struggling to make ends meet. City officials have not ruled out suspending the company's operations.

Transservis-N, the company that has managed the border crossing queue in Narva, has been struggling financially for two years. In better times, when thousands of vehicles crossed the border, the company paid dividends to the city of Narva. Now it is asking its owner for financial support to stay afloat — €50,000 this year and twice that amount next year. The city of Narva has yet to decide what to do with the company.

"If we shut it down, it will be very difficult to get it up and running again. The buildings will deteriorate and what would we do with the parking lot? We are still finding some use for it today. Cars from Latvia, Lithuania and Finland are parked at the Transservis-N lot, belonging to tourists who cross the border on foot. That brings in some revenue. But the number of Finnish tourists and people crossing the border here in general is steadily declining. We will start discussing this. We may indeed have to make a difficult decision," Narva Mayor Jaan Toots said.

The mayor nevertheless hopes that the border will reopen to vehicle traffic and that the company will not have to close.

Narva's opposition believes there is no point in holding out false hope as border traffic is only likely to decline further during the war, rather than increase. City officials must take this into account. Keeping the company operating solely to provide parking makes little sense.

"These are not even cars belonging to Narva residents and this is certainly not an essential service for us. I think it would make sense to temporarily shut down the company and reestablish it if the border does reopen for some reason. But that can only happen after the war ends," Narva City Council member Katri Raik said.

Narva city officials will decide the fate of Transservis-N as they prepare next year's budget. Vehicle traffic across the border in Narva was suspended in early 2024 when Russia began rebuilding the vehicle terminal at the Ivangorod border crossing. The work is reportedly scheduled to be completed this December.

World.title: BP to help Iraq produce 450,000 barrels per day from Kirkuk oilfields
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The development plan for four oilfields in northern Iraq has entered a new phase, a move aiming to support Baghdad’s efforts to increase oil production capacity to 10 million barrels per day over the coming years.

The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Thursday that operations for four major oilfields in the northern province of Kirkuk have been transferred to a joint operating body. This initiative aims to consolidate efforts to develop oil and gas assets and to enhance the efficiency of the country’s resources.

Iraqi Minister of Oil Basim Khudair oversaw the transfer of the management of the Kirkuk oilfields from the North Oil Company and the North Gas Company to a joint operating entity. The action is part of the government’s strategy to enhance the nation’s resources and optimize the performance of its production sectors.

These developments are bolstered by British Petroleum’s (BP) participation in a project to develop four oilfields in Iraq, a move that aligns with larger attempts to broaden the base of foreign partners.

The development plan intends to achieve a significant increase in oil and gas output in the next few years.

Khudair highlighted that the transition of operations to the joint operating entity represents a significant milestone in the initiative to develop the four Kirkuk oilfields.

The plan aims to reach an oil production level of 450,000 barrels per day, in addition to 500 million standard cubic feet of gas per day, according to Khudair.

The four oilfields—Kirkuk, Bai Hassan, Jambur, and Khabbaz—are key oil assets in northern Iraq and represent an important part of the government’s plans to increase production.

In 2025, BP reached a deal with Iraq’s North Oil Company to develop oil fields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk, with investments projected to reach $25 billion.

Khudair affirmed that BP is a strategic partner in the oil and gas sectors. He noted that working together as a team will support the project’s implementation and help address any obstacles that may arise during the development phases.

The development plan for the Kirkuk fields includes training Iraqi workers, transferring expertise and technology, and implementing community-focused initiatives, such as building service facilities for the local population.

World.title: Erbil to get first Mövenpick resort under Accor, KRD Holding deal
World.content:
Erbil (IraqiNews.com) – Global hospitality giant Accor has inked a deal with Erbil-based KRD Holding to build a 150-room Mövenpick resort overlooking Gomaspan Lake in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, with an opening date of 2030.

The Mövenpick Erbil Gomaspan Resort will be the brand’s first resort in the Kurdistan Region and second in Iraq, after the Mövenpick Hotel Al Zaytoon Baghdad.

The proposed building, less than 30 minutes from Erbil’s city center, would have 150 rooms and suites, restaurants, cafes, a spa, a family leisure club, and indoor and outdoor swimming pools.

The resort will also include over 1,300 square meters of meeting and event space, aimed at weddings, business meetings, conferences, and leisure travel.

KRD Holding, the local development partner, is a diversified investment company based in Erbil that operates in real estate, tourism, hospitality, healthcare, transportation, consultancy, and entertainment.

Its portfolio includes Visit Kurdistan, a tourist marketing campaign; Erbil City Bus, an urban transportation project; and companies that specialize in architecture, property management, hospitality, and infrastructure development.

Raki Phillips, Accor’s Regional President for the Premium, Midscale, and Economy divisions in the Middle East, Africa, and Turkey, said that Erbil’s growing connectivity and domestic tourist industry make the Kurdistan Region an appealing location for development.

He added that the agreement will launch a new lakeside hotel product and boost Accor’s footprint in Iraq.

Daban Hamid, Deputy CEO of KRD Holding, said that the deal highlighted the company’s efforts to recruit worldwide hotel brands and encourage investment in the Kurdistan Region’s tourist infrastructure.

Accor now runs one hotel in Iraq with about 260 rooms and has five more hotels under construction, totaling over 1,300 rooms.

The Gomaspan project will broaden the group’s Iraqi portfolio outside Baghdad and Erbil’s main city-center hotel markets.

World.title: Iraq’s IDC starts major maintenance operation on well in Zubair oilfield
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The state-owned Iraqi Drilling Company (IDC) started on Thursday a major maintenance operation on well ZB-510 in the Zubair oilfield in the southern province of Basra.

The company said in a statement that it used the IDC-47 workover rig to resume repair operations on oil well ZB-510 after a suspension that lasted four months, the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.

Workover operations are specialized technical processes designed to address the specific needs of a well. These operations focus on rehabilitating the well based on its technical condition and the approved program, aiming to restore it to operational status.

In July, Iraq’s IDC completed drilling a new deviated oil well in the Zubair oilfield as part of the Ministry of Oil’s efforts to increase output and enhance operational efficiency.

To boost the development of the Zubair oilfield, the new well was drilled to a depth of 3,846 meters with a 20-degree inclination.

The new well is part of a string of wells designed to keep production levels stable and improve the Zubair oilfield’s capabilities in the next phase.

The field has large reserves, officially estimated at over four billion barrels of recoverable crude oil. According to unofficial estimates, modern extraction technologies might increase these reserves to roughly five billion barrels.

As part of the Ministry of Oil’s attempts to prevent gas flaring and generate electricity, the oilfield has seen achievements in the recovery of associated gas, with a rate reaching 147 million cubic feet per day.

The Zubair oilfield is located onshore in Iraq and is operated by Italy’s Eni. Economic calculations indicate that production will continue until the field reaches its economic limit in 2047.

Eni and its partners are aiming to raise the oilfield’s output capacity to 700,000 barrels per day, with a long-term government objective of 850,000 barrels per day.

With a daily output capacity of around 450,000 barrels, the oilfield presently accounts for around nine percent of the country’s oil production.

World.title: Iraq discusses $250 million Kempinski hotel project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s National Investment Commission (NIC) is exploring a $250 million luxury hotel complex to be operated by worldwide hospitality giant Kempinski, after talks with a team headed by Iraqi businessman and banking investor Jawad Al-Kassab.

According to a statement released by the NIC, Chairman Adel Dakhil Mohammed al-Yasiri met with Al-Kassab and his investment partners to discuss potential in Iraq’s hospitality industry.

The preliminary concept is for the development of a hotel and residential complex on roughly 20 to 30 dunams of land, including hotel rooms, private villas, serviced residential units, and conference and event facilities.

The site has not been specified, and the project is still in the negotiation stage, with no development timeline or formal investment agreement declared.

Al-Kassab has vast expertise in international property development and hotel investment. He is the founder and chairman of Jawad Al Kassab International Holding Group, which has assets in the Middle East, Europe, and North America.

His portfolio includes the Kempinski Hotel Ishtar Dead Sea and Kempinski Hotel Aqaba in Jordan, as well as assets in Saudi Arabia, Switzerland, Canada, and the United Arab Emirates.

Within Iraq, Al-Kassab has participated in the Al-Kawthar residential development in Babil governorate, demonstrating his long-standing involvement in the country’s housing and building industries.

Aside from real estate and hospitality, Al-Kassab is also involved in Iraq’s financial industry as Chairman of the Board of Directors of Arab Bank Iraq, linking his investing operations to the growth of the country’s private banking sector.

The bank commenced operations as a private Iraqi shareholding business in 2025, following the receipt of its final banking license in 2024.

It has set up a headquarters in Baghdad’s Jadriyah area and announced intentions to grow its branch network and digital banking services.

If the Kempinski development goes forward, it will be another significant hospitality investment in Al-Kassab’s Iraq portfolio.

The NIC said that it was ready to assist and facilitate the project’s processes, as Iraq wants private investment in tourism, hotels, and supporting infrastructure.

World.title: Iraq, Qatar sign business cooperation agreement at Doha forum, plan joint business council
World.content:
Doha (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi and Qatari business executives convened in Doha on October 7 for the Qatar-Iraq Business Forum, where the chambers of commerce from both nations inked an agreement to boost trade and investment relations and form a joint business council.

The meeting, organized by Qatar Chamber, brought together members from the Federation of Iraqi Chambers of Commerce (FICC), government officials, and private-sector executives to examine investment potential in Iraq and ways to strengthen bilateral economic collaboration.

The two chambers signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to enhance institutional collaboration and facilitate commercial partnerships between Iraqi and Qatari enterprises.

The anticipated formation of the Iraq-Qatar Business Council is a key component of the agreement, with the goal of linking firms, discovering investment possibilities, and facilitating joint ventures.

The Iraqi delegation, headed by FICC President Amer Khalaf Alawi, comprised delegates from the International Chamber of Commerce in Iraq (ICC Iraq).

Chairman Mohsin Al-Hamid and Secretary General Ahmed Al-Yasiri represented the ICC Iraq delegation.

Other attendees were the Iraqi Prime Minister’s advisor on the Development Road and Railroads, the director general of the Ministry of Trade’s Private Sector Development Department, Iraqi business executives, and Iraq’s Ambassador to Qatar, Mohammed Jaafar Al-Sadr.

The forum included talks on bilateral commerce and Iraq’s Development Road project, which is a proposed transportation and logistics corridor that would link the Gulf with Turkish and European markets via Iraq.

The forum indicates a rising interest in improving Iraq-Qatar economic ties, especially as Baghdad attempts to attract Gulf investment, diversify its economy, and increase private sector activity.

The planned Iraq-Qatar Business Council might help transform conversations into long-term business partnerships.

World.title: Iraq’s SOMO begins settling outstanding oil payments to Gulf Keystone at international prices
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Gulf Keystone Petroleum announced on Thursday that Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) has begun compensating international oil companies operating in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region for outstanding oil export payments, taking a significant step toward resolving financial disputes affecting the region’s oil industry.

The London-listed business said the first cargo of extra crude oil, known as top-up barrels, was recently lifted after SOMO allocated them under the temporary tripartite export agreements comprising Baghdad, Erbil, and foreign oil companies.

Top-up barrels are extra amounts of crude oil delivered as compensation instead of direct cash payments. They enable oil corporations to recover the difference between the income previously earned for their exports and the amounts to which they are entitled under global market pricing.

In Gulf Keystone’s situation, the first allocation is designed to align oil export sales in the fourth quarter of 2025 with worldwide prices and begin to reduce the company’s outstanding receivables.

The move is a significant step toward completing payment agreements between the Iraqi Federal Government, the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), and foreign oil corporations, whose financial conflicts have hampered northern Iraq crude exports and investment plans.

Gulf Keystone CEO Jon Harris welcomed the decision, citing the commencement of the compensation process as an important milestone for both the company and Iraq’s oil sector.

“The commencement of the top-up payments is a significant positive milestone,” Harris said.

He said that obtaining the company’s entire production-sharing contract entitlement at international rates was in line with Iraq’s modified federal budget legislation and current contracts.

Harris also praised Baghdad and Erbil’s commitment, saying it improved the investment prospects for Iraq’s oil industry.

Gulf Keystone added that it will continue to pursue collection of its remaining outstanding top-up receivables, since the first allocation does not constitute complete settlement of the sums owing.

The business expects the new payment system to spur more investment in the Shaikan oilfield in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, where it hopes to develop significant oil reserves and resources.

The declaration provides an initial precedent for paying producers with more crude allocations; however, Gulf Keystone did not specify the amount of the first cargo or the entire remaining balance.

World.title: Why is Shell facing lawsuits over climate disasters in Brazil and the Philippines?
World.content:
Washington – A typhoon in the Philippines and flooding in Brazil. Twice in less than a year, British energy giant Shell has been the target of a new type of lawsuit seeking to make polluters pay part of the cost of specific extreme weather events.

“We chose Shell because it’s an emblematic company. It meets all the criteria,” Thales Miola, a lawyer for the Brazilian NGO Instituto Preservar, told AFP.

On Friday, the organization and federal prosecutors jointly filed a lawsuit against Shell’s subsidiary in South America’s largest country.

They are seeking the equivalent of $108 million in compensation for catastrophic flooding in southern Brazil in 2024. The disaster killed nearly 200 people, displaced half a million and caused widespread destruction.

Until now, the only lawsuits filed over the disaster had targeted public authorities.

Shell is not Brazil’s biggest oil company — that distinction belongs to state-owned Petrobras — but it has operated there for decades, and its contribution to global warming is well-documented and “a huge amount for a single company,” Miola said.

According to estimates by the think tank Carbon Majors cited in the lawsuit, Shell holds responsibility for 2.02 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel and cement-making.

Much of those emissions come from burning the hydrocarbons the company produces and sells. Shell’s share is more than three times that of Petrobras.

At the heart of the legal argument is an attribution study published in a journal belonging to the Nature group, which estimates that climate change intensified the extreme rainfall in 2024 by 12 percent.

The plaintiffs want Shell to pay for that additional intensity in proportion to its contribution to global emissions: two percent of the 12 percent increase.

“In Brazil, it is the first time that we use attribution science against a carbon major company,” Miola said. “Choosing Shell does not exempt the other companies from being prosecuted in the near future.”

– Super typhoon –

In the Philippines, too, the plaintiffs want Shell to pay for its history and its size.

In December 2021, Typhoon Rai, known locally as Odette, devastated several islands. More than 400 people died and hundreds of thousands lost their homes. It was one of the worst disasters in the country’s history.

Four years later, in 2025, around 100 survivors, supported by NGOs, filed a lawsuit against Shell in the United Kingdom, where the company is based.

The lawyers base their case on the company’s “historic carbon emissions” and the link between those emissions and global warming, which climate scientists have shown intensifies cyclones.

– Aggravating factor –

The plaintiffs cite an additional aggravating factor: Shell’s “history of misinformation regarding the causes and impacts of climate change,” said Greg Lascelles, a lawyer at Hausfeld, the firm handling the lawsuit in London.

“There’s a lot of evidence about Shell knowing as early as in the 1960s” that fossil fuels contributed to global warming, said Madeleine Lynch, a campaigner on the “Odette case.”

The lawsuit argues that this establishes negligence under Philippine law.

The Brazilian lawsuit also cites Shell’s past record, including an internal company report from 1986 that acknowledged fossil fuels’ role in increasing greenhouse gas emissions and global warming.

Shell has not responded to the Brazilian lawsuit. However, in December, following the Philippine lawsuit, the company said “the suggestion that Shell had unique knowledge about climate change is simply not true.”

– ‘Test cases’ –

Claims seeking compensation from major companies for specific climate-related damage — sometimes in countries where those companies are not even based — are only just beginning to emerge.

Swiss cement maker Holcim is being sued by residents of an Indonesian island being eroded by rising sea levels. Pakistani farmers are suing two companies in Germany, including a cement manufacturer.

“The cases we’re seeing in the world are test cases, to see whether it is a viable legal strategy,” said Noah Walker-Crawford, a researcher at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics.

“If these cases are successful,” he said, “We could expect to see a lot more of these cases against more companies as well.”

World.title: Iraq to continue economic, financial reforms
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Finance Minister Faleh Sari reaffirmed on Wednesday Iraq’s commitment to continuing economic and financial reforms, diversifying revenue sources, and strengthening the role of the private sector.

According to Sari, these measures aim to bolster economic stability and enhance the country’s capacity to deal with regional challenges.

The Iraqi minister’s remarks took place during his speech at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a statement released by the Finance Ministry.

Sari emphasized that the government is addressing the economic consequences of the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz by reprioritizing expenditures, increasing non-oil revenues, and maintaining the state’s essential obligations while pursuing structural reforms.

According to Sari, overcoming current challenges requires a transition toward a more diversified and sustainable economy.

“Iraq Vision 2050” represents a strategic plan for reducing dependency on oil, broadening production, empowering the private sector, and achieving inclusive and sustainable economic growth, according to Sari.

The minister noted that the reform package includes enhancing public financial management, automating customs and tax operations, boosting the business and investment climate, upgrading the banking sector, and increasing electronic payment systems.

According to Sari, the partnership with the IMF and the World Bank Group supports the economic and financial reform program.

The minister highlighted the value of leveraging the technical and institutional expertise provided by these institutions to strengthen the sustainability of public finances and facilitate the implementation of Iraq’s development priorities.

World.title: Amit Shah vows to eliminate every trace of Naxalism after five decades of tribal suffering
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Home minister

on Thursday called for eliminating every trace of Naxalism to restore vibrancy and growth after the near elimination of militancy in Bastar, Chhattisgarh.

"Every trace of Naxalism must be eliminated, and Bastar must once again become a vibrant and thriving region," said Shah, adding "significant work had already been undertaken in this direction as traditional tribal leadership in the Bastar region had made a major contribution."

Shah remarked as he virtually addressed an assistive devices distribution ceremony in Bastar for the differently -abled, including victims of Naxal violence.

Shah emphasised that five decades of Naxalism had caused immense suffering to the poor tribal communities of Bastar. He called using improvised explosive devices (IEDs) to maim innocent civilians in pursuit of political objectives the gravest violation of

.

The home minister said assistive prosthetic devices were being provided in Chhattisgarh to ease the lives of tribal persons with disabilities who had suffered as a result of Naxal violence.





The distribution programme, held in Jagdalpur from October 5 to 7, 2026, benefited more than 3,600 persons with disabilities. Of these, more than 1,570 beneficiaries were from Bastar alone.

Shah said the government had been firmly committed to eliminating Naxalism from the entire country before March 31, 2026, and that this goal had now been achieved. However, the Minister emphasised that the end of Naxalism alone would not erase five decades of suffering.

"We must heal the wounds inflicted by this suffering, help victims stand on their feet again, and ensure they can live with dignity and respect", Shah said.

The home minister added that the region where gunfire and bomb blasts once created an atmosphere of fear was now witnessing thousands of young people taking part in sports and keeping their traditions alive.

"A region where the sounds of gunfire and bomb blasts once prevailed, and fear was widespread, thousands of young people are now participating in sports and keeping their traditions alive," Shah stated as he mentioned several initiatives undertaken by the Chhattisgarh government, including the Bastar Olympics, Bastar Pandum, Niyad Nellanar and the chief minister's Samuhik Bus Yojana.

World.title: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response on plea to hold protest organisers liable for damage
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Centre,

and others on a plea seeking to hold organisers of protests personally or jointly liable for loss of life, injuries, damage to public or private property and the costs incurred by the authorities.

A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was hearing the petition, which also sought a direction that protests, dharnas, demonstrations, processions and public assemblies in the national capital should not be held without prior written permission from the competent authority.

The plea sought to make organisers, callers, leaders or convenors of protests liable for losses arising from unlawful acts or omissions, including when an assembly is held without permission or violates the conditions imposed for its approval.

The bench issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police and other parties, seeking their responses to the petition, according to news agency PTI.

Plea seeks designated protest sites in Delhi

The petition also sought directions to the authorities to identify and notify designated locations for protests, dharnas, demonstrations and public assemblies in Delhi. These sites, it said, should be situated away from densely populated, commercial and central areas.





It further proposed that every application seeking permission for a protest, demonstration, procession or public assembly should be accompanied by an affidavit from the organiser disclosing the source of funding.

The declaration should also specify whether any part of the funds had been received, or was expected to be received, from a foreign source or an unidentified source, the plea said.

According to the petition, a false or incomplete declaration should provide grounds for revoking permission, recovering compensation and costs from the organiser and those found to have financed the assembly, and initiating prosecution in accordance with the law.

Supreme Court hears multiple pleas linked to Delhi protests

The hearing came as the Supreme Court considered several petitions connected to protests in Delhi, including pleas concerning alleged assaults on journalists and lawyers, police action and restrictions on demonstrations.

In a separate matter, the bench issued notices to the Centre and the Delhi government on a plea challenging the Delhi Policeâs decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

The petitioner, advocate Swaty Malik, argued that removing the designation violated the fundamental right to protest. The plea maintained that demonstrations should be permitted at a location where protesters could make their grievances heard by the state administration.

Justice Bagchi observed that the concept of being heard should also be considered in the context of technology.

âThe word âheardâ must be used in the perspective of technology alsoâ, Justice Bagchi remarked.

The court agreed to examine the petition and sought responses from the authorities.

In other pleas linked to the protests, the Supreme Court sought responses from the authorities over allegations involving journalists and lawyers. It also directed law-enforcement agencies to preserve CCTV footage and other digital records relating to the demonstrations.

The bench further directed that the order issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) be placed on record.

The provision empowers authorised executive magistrates to issue urgent prohibitory orders to prevent public danger, disturbances or riots.

The court indicated that the Union government would file a consolidated response to the batch of petitions while relevant material relating to individual cases was preserved.

Court also takes up pleas on voter roll revision

Separately, the Supreme Court issued notices to the Election Commission and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on a petition filed by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and 12 other opposition leaders over alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

The bench also took note of submissions concerning the October 12 march to the Supreme Court by Rahul and other opposition leaders.

âNobody can browbeat us (judiciary),â CJI Surya Kant said during the hearing, adding that the court was aware of statements made both inside and outside the courtroom.

The court said it would ask one of the petitioners about his conduct at the next hearing, without naming the individual.

The petition by Rahul and the other opposition leaders sought an independent audit of deletions and modifications made during the SIR, to be conducted by a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge and assisted by technical experts and other prominent citizens.

It also sought safeguards against deleting votersâ names without notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, along with measures to allow eligible voters in Punjab and other poll-bound states to seek inclusion in electoral rolls within the time permitted by law.

World.title: J&K HC restricts motorboat operations on Dal Lake
World.content:
The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has ordered a ban on fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake.

Court stresses need to protect Dal Lake from pollution

Solar-powered boats suggested as an alternative

The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has prohibited the operation of fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake until further orders.A division bench comprising chief justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri passed the directive on Wednesday while hearing a petition filed by Mohammad Rafiq Mir.The court directed the authorities, including the lakes conservation and management authority (LCMA), the tourism department and the police, to ensure strict implementation of the ban.âIn the larger interest of justice, taking a comprehensive view of the submissions made, it is directed that the respondent authorities LCMA, tourism, and police shall ensure that no motor boat, whether it be a shikara motorboat or Jet Ski which operates by fuel, is operated in the Dal Lake until further orders,â the bench said.The court also warned that any violation of its directive would amount to contempt of court, instructing the concerned officials to strictly prohibit such operations, according to the new agency PTI.The bench observed that protecting lake ecosystems has become increasingly important, making it necessary to restrict activities that contribute to pollution.It also emphasised that the policy governing motorised boats should strike a reasonable balance between tourism-related activities, environmental protection and ensuring uniform rules for all operators.The judges suggested that solar-powered and electric boats could provide a viable alternative, allowing tourism operators to continue their activities while safeguarding the lake's ecological health.The court asked the government to examine whether conventional motorisation could be replaced with solar-powered systems or electric engines.Senior additional advocate general Mohsin Qadri was asked to explore the possibility of replacing existing motorised boats with solar-powered electric engines and present the findings before the court.The government had earlier been directed to submit a comprehensive policy on the operation of motorised boats.However, the court clarified that the prohibition would not apply to boats used for emergency services, law and order, disaster management and safety-related operations.The matter has been listed for the next hearing on October 30.

World.title: 'Stunned': Rahul urges President Murmu to put Dushyant Gautam’s appointment as Sikkim Governor on hold
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha

has written to President

, urging her to reconsider Dushyant Gautamâs appointment as Sikkim Governor amid renewed demands for justice in the 2022 Ankita Bhandari murder case.

The move comes as Ankitaâs parents warn of nationwide protests if the appointment is not revoked.

In a letter shared alongside a post on X, Gandhi said the identity of the alleged VIP mentioned in the case remained unresolved nearly four years after of 19-year-old Bhandariâs murder. He alleged that the investigation into the VIP angle was proceeding slowly and questioned Gautamâs appointment while the inquiry remained pending.

âMadam President, 19-year-old Ankita Bhandari refused to compromise her dignity for a VIP, which led to her murder. Even four years later, due to the CBI's sluggish investigation, the question remains: who was that VIP?â Gandhi wrote on X.

He added that many people, including Bhandariâs family, believed Gautam was connected to the case. These remain allegations, and Gautamâs alleged links to the crime have not been established in the information provided.





In his letter, Rahul argued that a Governorâs constitutional position could complicate any future criminal proceedings. He cited Article 74(1) of the Constitution, saying the President could ask the government to reconsider its advice.

âI request you to ask the Government to reconsider this appointment, and that Mr. Gautam not take office until the CBI has completed its investigation,â he wrote.

Rahul also referred to the familyâs continuing demand for justice, saying, âAnkita refused the repellent demand made of her and paid with her life.

Her parents, who are still fighting for justice, are now protesting this appointment and being detained by police. Please act-provide solace to Ankita's grieving parents and protect the high post of Governor.â

He also criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi over the appointment. âWhile serving as Governor, no criminal proceedings can be initiated against him. By advising the appointment of Dushyant Gautam, Prime Minister Modi has proven that he has absolutely no concern for women's safety.

I appeal to you to advise the government to reconsider this appointment and not allow Dushyant Gautam to assume office until the investigation is complete.

Do not let the hope for justice of Ankita's parents be shattered", Rahul wrote.

Ankitaâs parents issue 24-hour ultimatum

Rahulâs letter comes a day after he met Bhandariâs parents at India Gate in Delhi, where they were protesting against Gautamâs appointment. On Thursday, Delhi Police briefly detained the family and several Opposition leaders during a sit-in at Delhi's India Gate.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Bhandariâs father, Virendra Singh Bhandari, issued a 24-hour ultimatum to the government, warning of nationwide protests if the appointment was not revoked.

âWe are giving the government a 24-hour ultimatum. If it does not revoke Dushyant Gautamâs appointment, people across the country, in every state, will take to the streets to demand justice for Ankita Bhandari,â he told IANS.

Bhandari, who worked as a receptionist at the Vanantra resort near Rishikesh, was murdered on September 18, 2022. Resort owner Pulkit Arya and two employees were convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. The alleged VIP angle has remained a focus of the familyâs demands, and the CBI inquiry into it is ongoing.

Rahul's appeal now places the Presidentâs response and the governmentâs position on Gautamâs appointment under scrutiny, as the family presses for the investigation to be completed before he assumes the constitutional post.
