World.title: Tajikistan to host UN-backed peace conference in Dushanbe in May 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Tajikistan plans to hold a high-level international conference in Dushanbe in May 2027 dedicated to the International Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations, President of Tajikistan Emomali Rahmon said at the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, the press service of the President of Tajikistan announced.

"Tajikistan has put forward an initiative to declare 2027-2036 the International Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations, which was approved by the UN General Assembly. Together with the United Nations and other international partners, Tajikistan plans to hold a high-level international conference on this topic in Dushanbe in May 2027," the statement said.

Addressing the summit, Emomali Rahmon noted that Tajikistan’s initiative to declare 2027-2036 the International Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations had been approved by the UN General Assembly.

According to Emomali Rahmon, implementing the decade’s objectives will contribute to the development of interstate dialogue, the promotion of a culture of peace, and conflict prevention.

The president expressed confidence that the international conference, organized jointly with the UN and other international partners, would help ensure a successful launch of the decade and further strengthen dialogue, solidarity, and partnership at the global level.

The 7th CICA Summit is taking place in Baku under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, bringing together heads of state and government, as well as delegations from CICA member states, observer states, observer organizations, and partner entities.

The summit provides an opportunity to discuss dialogue and confidence-building among member states amid rising interstate tensions, escalating conflicts, and the emergence of new hotspots of tension, including in Asia.

One of the summit's key outcomes is the admission of Laos as a new CICA member. The summit is also expected to see the adoption of documents aimed at intensifying the organization's activities and strengthening cooperation in specific areas.

World.title: ADB, Uzbekistan sign $200M deal to upgrade power grid
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) and Uzbekistan have signed a $200 million loan agreement to modernize the country’s electricity distribution system, including upgrades to 60 substations and the introduction of digital technologies to reduce power losses and improve grid reliability, during a meeting on October 15 in Bangkok.

This was reflected in a post by Masato Kanda on his LinkedIn account. The agreement was signed by ADB President Masato Kanda and Uzbekistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok on October 12-18.

"I was pleased to meet Uzbekistan Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov today on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. I was gratified to hear his appreciation for ADB’s speed and responsiveness, in a partnership that ranges from schools to irrigation," Kanda said.

The project aims to strengthen Uzbekistan’s power distribution network as economic growth drives electricity demand and the government pursues ambitious development targets.

Under the project, 60 electricity distribution substations will be upgraded, while digital systems will be introduced to reduce technical losses, improve the reliability of electricity supplies and support the integration of more renewable energy into the grid.

Kanda said he had discussed the partnership with Kuchkarov and noted the Uzbek official’s appreciation for ADB’s responsiveness and speed in delivering support across sectors ranging from education to irrigation.

The project is ADB’s first energy investment under the Full Mutual Reliance Framework with the World Bank. The framework allows the institutions to rely on each other’s due diligence and implementation arrangements, helping reduce duplicated work and transaction costs and improve the efficiency of development financing.

The investment is expected to support the modernization of Uzbekistan’s electricity infrastructure and strengthen the network’s capacity to accommodate growing demand and renewable energy generation.

World.title: TAP achieves Gold Standard for methane emissions reporting
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP) consortium has achieved Gold Standard Reporting under the United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) Oil & Gas Methane Partnership 2.0 (OGMP 2.0), an initiative led by the International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO), TAP AG said on October 15.

To achieve the Gold Standard, companies must meet OGMP 2.0’s highest reporting requirements, which involve reconciling source-level emissions estimates with site-level measurements.

“The recognition marks an important milestone in TAP’s efforts to improve the quality, transparency and robustness of its methane emissions reporting, demonstrating the high quality of methane measurement, reporting and management of methane emissions across its operations. As we look ahead, this work will continue as part of our broader efforts to reduce methane emissions, decarbonize our operations and ensure that TAP is resilient and ready to adapt to a changing energy landscape,” the consortium said.

TAP forms the European section of the Southern Gas Corridor, transporting natural gas from Azerbaijan’s Shah Deniz field to European markets.

The 878-kilometer pipeline runs from the Greece-Türkiye border through Greece and Albania, crosses the Adriatic Sea and reaches Italy’s southern coast.

With the potential to expand its capacity, TAP plays a key role in diversifying Europe’s gas supplies and strengthening energy security by facilitating Caspian gas exports.

TAP has delivered more than 60 billion cubic meters of natural gas to Europe, including 50 billion cubic meters to Italy.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan pledges global security support during 2027–2028 UN term
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. Kyrgyzstan intends to contribute to strengthening international peace, security, and multilateral cooperation during its membership of the United Nations Security Council in 2027–2028, President Sadyr Japarov said at the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan announced.

"With the support of 142 countries, Kyrgyzstan has been elected to the UN Security Council for the first time for the 2027–2028 term. We view this as a great responsibility and intend to contribute to strengthening international peace, security, and multilateral cooperation," he said.

Addressing the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, Sadyr Japarov noted that Kyrgyzstan had secured its first-ever election to the UN Security Council with the support of 142 countries, describing the achievement as a major responsibility.

Speaking about regional security, Sadyr Japarov emphasized the importance of achieving lasting stability in Afghanistan through sustained dialogue, economic recovery, and coordinated action by the international community.

He noted that strengthening mutual trust, avoiding escalation, and respecting international law could create conditions for long-term peace and stability.

As an example, Sadyr Japarov cited the experience of Central Asian countries, which had managed to resolve a number of complex interstate issues through political will and direct dialogue.

According to Sadyr Japarov, Kyrgyzstan is ready to share this experience with partner countries and continue engaging with states across the region.

The 7th CICA Summit is taking place in Baku under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, bringing together heads of state and government, as well as delegations from CICA member states, observer states, observer organizations, and partner entities.

The summit provides an opportunity to discuss dialogue and confidence-building among member states amid rising interstate tensions, escalating conflicts, and the emergence of new hotspots of tension, including in Asia.

One of the summit's key outcomes is the admission of Laos as a new CICA member. The summit is also expected to see the adoption of documents aimed at intensifying the organization's activities and strengthening cooperation in specific areas.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s Ala-Too Resort targets 2 million annual tourists
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 15. The Ala-Too Resort year-round tourism cluster project being implemented in Kyrgyzstan is designed to accommodate up to two million tourists annually and create around 5,000 jobs, President Sadyr Japarov said at the 7th CICA Summit in Baku, the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan announced.

"Kyrgyzstan continues to implement the Ala-Too Resort year-round tourism cluster project. This infrastructure project will accommodate up to 2 million tourists annually and create around 5,000 jobs," he said.

According to Sadyr Japarov, the project is part of the country's efforts to develop its tourism infrastructure.

The Kyrgyz president noted that tourism development complements the country's efforts to expand international economic cooperation and attract investment in infrastructure projects.

Sadyr Japarov also said that Kyrgyzstan is interested in developing energy cooperation, including the creation of cross-border infrastructure and the expansion of electricity trade.

The 7th CICA Summit is taking place in Baku under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, bringing together heads of state and government, as well as delegations from CICA member states, observer states, observer organizations, and partner entities.

The summit provides an opportunity to discuss dialogue and confidence-building among member states amid rising interstate tensions, escalating conflicts, and the emergence of new hotspots of tension, including in Asia.

One of the summit's key outcomes is the admission of Laos as a new CICA member. The summit is also expected to see the adoption of documents aimed at intensifying the organization's activities and strengthening cooperation in specific areas.

World.title: Remains may be earliest evidence of ancient human speared to death
World.content:
An oddly circular hole in a Neanderthal's shoulder bone may be the oldest known evidence of an ancient human fatally wounded with a wooden spear.

That's according to research published today in Scientific Reports.

The UK and Spanish team also found evidence of burial and caregiving behaviour in the species.

First author Emma Pomeroy, an archaeologist at the University of Cambridge, says it shows Neanderthals were even more complex than previously understood.

"We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature — care and violence — juxtaposed in the same individual," Dr Pomeroy said.

"We have a tendency to romanticise hunter-gatherer or pre-agriculture lifestyles as peaceful and close to the natural world … but it's not that simple."

But other experts were not convinced by the evidence outlined in the study.

Neanderthal lived with 'painful' tooth injury

The Shanidar Cave In Iraqi Kurdistan has revealed a plethora of Neanderthal remains since it was first excavated 1953.

The new study looks at recently discovered 75,000-year-old remains of a Neanderthal man in his 40s known as Shanidar A.

"Their body was placed in a very specific spot in the cave, tucked in behind a huge rock that stood between them and the cave mouth," Dr Pomeroy said.

"Over the subsequent years or decades, the remains of at least four other Neanderthal individuals were placed directly above."

Shanidar A's remains, which include a mostly complete hand, teeth and a left shoulder blade, have multiple signs of damage.

The teeth, which the team says were quite damaged, healed partially while the man was still alive.

Seven teeth from Shanadar A were found in the cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. (Supplied: Dr Emma Pomeroy)

"They must have been hit very hard in the face, which made one of their bottom front teeth split in half," Dr Pomeroy said.

"The broken edge became covered in hardened plaque showing they continued living afterwards without that part of the tooth.

" The injury would have been incredibly painful. "

This, the researchers said, might indicate the man's family group provided care and support, at least in the short term.

"They likely needed some care and support from their group with drinking, communicating, eating," she said.

Killed with a wooden spear

While Shanidar A survived the dental issues, the team suggested an unusual, smooth-edged and circular hole in his shoulder blade indicated the likely cause of his demise.

Lack of healing on the bone, and fragments found nearby suggested the injury happened about the time of death.

The researchers suggest a spear might have pierced muscle, bones and potentially organs. (Supplied: University of Cambridge)

"It had to be something that could make a hole through a shoulder blade and all the muscle, bones and organs over the top – something like a weapon," Dr Pomeroy said.

The team hypothesised the circular hole was made with a wooden spear.

Wooden spears dating between 200,000–400,000 years old have been found in Europe.

"The diameter of the shaft near the pointed end fits well with the size of the hole in the scapula," Dr Pomeroy said.

"[But] we can never be sure because, of course, the wood has not preserved.

Conclusion 'needs more support'

Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University not involved with the discovery, said that, while some of the conclusions were "bold", the team needed more evidence to support its claims.

"I think it's a bit of a stretch with the justification they have so far," she said.

Dr Samper Carro agreed the circular damage to the shoulder blade was "weird" and not how bones usually break.

"Bones usually break in more kind of orthogonal … more linear fractures," she said.

Neanderthal remains were first found in Shanidar Cave in 1953. (Supplied: Professor Graeme Barker)

However, she said, it was "very difficult" to know the cause of death, unless the weapon was also found.

"It's unusual that you get those circular shapes, but correlating that with the cause of death? I think it's a bit too much," she said.

Despite this, Dr Samper Carro said the site still had plenty to offer.

Dr Pomeroy's team is still excavating the Shanidar Cave site, examining the transition period when modern humans began to use it.

"We are investigating what Neanderthals and humans ate based on the animal bones they left behind, how they prepared plant and animal food … and a whole host of other questions," Dr Pomeroy said.

"There is so much fascinating work still to do."

World.title: Breaking: Donald Trump calls off planned live stream of firing squad execution
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad will not be live streamed.

The decision came after intense backlash to the announcement that the execution would be shown online.

Hasan killed 13 US army soldiers and injured another 32 during a shooting at a Texas military base in 2009.

Australian politicians were among those critical of the decision, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese flagging that the federal government was exploring ways to prevent the stream being shown in Australia.

Mr Trump had previously indicated he approved of the live stream, but acknowledged on Thursday, local time, that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

In a social media post, Mr Trump said publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan".

Hasan's execution is scheduled for December 3, according to the Pentagon.

The execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan will no longer be live streamed, US President Donald Trump has said. (AFP: Bell Country Sherriff's Department)

Mr Trump said the execution could still be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims, "if they so choose".

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement earlier this month that the execution would be live streamed prompted significant blowback within the US from both Republicans and Democrats.

Concerns were raised that the images could be used to fuel radicalisation.

Among those saying they would not watch the execution was Vice-President JD Vance.

“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Mr Vance said.

PM seeking advice on US execution live stream Anthony Albanese says the government is exploring all options to prevent the potential live streaming of a US execution from being seen in Australia.

In Australia, Mr Albanese said social media platforms had a moral duty to block the stream.

"I think anybody broadcasting this will damage their own reputations as well. They have a social responsibility here to do the right thing," he told the ABC's Afternoon Briefing on Tuesday.

The eSafety Commissioner, however, said the government could not prevent platforms from showing the footage.

Politicians from the Liberal Party, the Greens and One Nation all expressed opposition to the execution being live streamed online.

World.title: Zelenskyy 'done' with US-made energy ceasefire that Moscow ignored
World.content:
Ukraine has struck a Russian oil refinery after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was "done" supporting a US-orchestrated ceasefire on energy targets which has been ignored by Russia.

US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy, with Kyiv then suspending strikes on Russian refineries.

Mr Trump blames the attacks on energy infrastructure for raising diesel prices on global markets.

But in the days that followed, Russia rained down deadly missile and drone strikes on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the ceasefire on energy infrastructure is "done". (AP: Alex Brandon)

In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Mr Zelenskyy said Ukraine's patience had run out.

"The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," he said.

Mr Zelenskyy also made clear he believed changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which have curbed Ukraine's ability to use them to pilot its drones, were a policy decision.

"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Mr Zelenskyy said.

In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Mr Trump.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Mr Musk wrote.

Biggest rift with Washington

By walking away from Mr Trump's demand, Mr Zelenskyy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Although Mr Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries.

At the weekend, Mr Trump said the strikes "damn well better stop".

Russia ignoring 'energy ceasefire': Zelenskyy The Ukrainian president says if Moscow wants Kyiv to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, as demanded by Donald Trump, then it should stop hitting key infrastructure.

Mr Trump has long had a testy relationship with Mr Zelenskyy and berated him in the White House in February 2025.

But his sharp turn against Kyiv in recent days has little precedent.

He first angered Ukraine last week by abruptly lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and then called on Ukraine to replace Mr Zelenskyy.

Over the past several days, Ukrainian officials have reported that they have not received the usual warnings from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles, which rely on US satellite detectors.

Mr Trump has denied withholding intelligence. Mr Zelenskyy said the failure to provide the warnings had been presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch.

President Donald Trump and Starlink CEO Elon Musk. (Getty Images, Kevin Dietsch)

Refinery supplying Moscow hit

Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia.

Mr Trump, under pressure to lower fuel prices, especially for diesel which has reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices.

US President Donald Trump denies withholding intelligence on Russia's ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region south east of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5 per cent of Russia's refinery throughout, helping supply the capital.

Regional governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukranian drone attack had caused a fire at the refinery.

Damage was being assessed and emergency services were at the scene.

A Ukrainian official confirmed that Ukraine had hit a Russian refinery overnight in response to Moscow's heavy ballistic missile and drone attacks this week that violated the energy truce.

In the latest attacks on Ukraine, three people were killed and six wounded in the central region of Kirovohrad overnight, as Russia launched more than 500 drones.

State-owned energy company Naftogaz said a gas extraction facility in Poltava was damaged and operations were suspended.

The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts.

It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was still ongoing to do so.

Reuters

World.title: Quick hits: Walsh vomits after try, Ponga shines then suffers in epic duel
World.content:
Australia and New Zealand have set a high standard for the 17th edition of the Rugby League World Cup, opening the 2026 tournament with an all-time classic.

Young Kiwi Casey McLean defied gravity, and debutant Aussie Jack Bostock won the match for the Kangaroos,

Meanwhile, a vomiting Reece Walsh and a broken-armed Kalyn Ponga produced one of the great fullback duels.

Here are the quick hits from the opening match.

1. McLean defies gravity in all-time finish

Casey McLean is Kiwi superman.

Aussies win, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

After a towering bomb from Jahrome Hughes was batted back by Ronaldo Mulitalo, Isaiah Papali'i threw what could best be described as a one-handed chuck, collected by McLean on the blind side.

With no space to work in, and Kangaroos halfback Mitchell Moses smothering him while directing him towards touch, McLean went airborne.

Somehow, seemingly in slow motion, as his body hovered horizontally over the sideline, McLean grounded the ball in the corner.

ABC Sport expert commentator Luke Lewis described it as "one of the best finishes you will see in this game."

And just four minutes into this World Cup, a contender for try of the tournament was born.

2. Long-range intercepts put Kangaroos on top

The Kiwis dominated the first half at the Sydney Football Stadium.

The New Zealanders had 59 per cent of the ball, made 300 more metres running, and had 66 fewer tackles.

But they went into the break level after the Kangaroos scored two 90-metre intercept tries.

The first Kangaroos score came from debutant Jack Bostock, who rushed out of the defensive line to grab a looping pass by Kiwi halfback Jahrome Hughes.

If that ball got over his head, it would have been a try for the Kiwis. But the Australian winger took the ball cleanly, broke the grasp of a Kiwi, and ran for the goal-line.

Incredibly, an almost identical play happened for Australia's other winger Tom Trbojevic on the other side of the field.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean gave a pass meant for his unmarked winger, but Trbojevic stuck his arm in the way and caught the footy.

Trbojevic then showed the speed he was known for at the start of his career, beating the cover tackle attempt of Kodi Nikorima and streaking away.

3. After first half denial, Ponga breathes fire

The duel of the opposing fullbacks was one of the most hyped heading into this game, featuring two of the most electric talents in the game.

Kalyn Ponga was a standout for the Kiwis, before leaving the game with a suspected broken arm. (Getty Images: Matt King)

And it produced everything fans could hope for.

Kiwis' custodian Kalyn Ponga came into the tournament off the back of a breathtaking season for the Knights, while the Kangaroos' number one Reece Walsh was considered a somewhat controversial selection, preferred over the Roosters' Clive Churchill medallist James Tedesco.

After being kept relatively quiet for most of the first half, Ponga burst to life on the left, dancing, darting, and taunting the Kangaroos.

He slipped past Staggs and tried to sidestep Walsh, who produced a scintillating try-saver, bundling Ponga into touch.

It was one for the purists, in shades of Scott Sattler's tackle on Toddy Byrne in the 2003 NRL grand final.

Ponga shook it off after the break, and the Kiwis debutant was on the end of some slick passing from the Kiwis for a straightforward finish for his first try.

His second was better, a 40-metre vintage Ponga effort.

With his shorts pulled halfway down his legs, he still managed to power past Walsh with a classic step, sending the sizeable Kiwi contingent in Sydney into delirium.

4. Walsh plunders then chunders, Ponga goes off

The Kangaroos were staring down a rare defeat to their arch-rivals in this arena, when Walsh responded to his opposite number's heroics, and left the Kiwis in his dust.

Reece Walsh struggled to re-gain his composure after scoring his try. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Deep in their own half and trailing by six, Bostock slipped a clever flick pass behind his back, and the Broncos superstar swooped.

He swerved past defenders, running 60 metres to go over in the corner.

But he gave everything in the effort, and as he prepared to take the conversion, he was interrupted by his exhaustion.

He threw up and was unable to take the kick, with Lattrell Mitchell stepping up instead.

Walsh continued to dry retch, and looked completely spent. But he managed to keep it together (and inside) to stay on the field and see out the game.

But it was a horrible end to the game for Ponga; his night ended early with a suspected broken arm — a huge blow for the Kiwis' title hopes.

Ponga had nursed his left arm after a tackle on Cam Munster early in the second half.

He stayed out there, but appeared to hit his arm again in a collision with teammate Hughes in an attempt to tackle Walsh.

5. Bostock hat trick

Jack Bostock had already made his mark on international rugby league with his 90-metre intercept try in the first half.

But he was not done scoring, and it proved a match-winning performance.

His second try came in the 57th minute, with the Aussies trailing by six points.

Kangaroos five-eighth Cam Munster put up a pinpoint kick for Bostock to chase.

The Australian went up against his Dolphins teammate Jamayne Isaako, beat him in the air, and scored a fantastic try to help level the scores.

But Bostock had an even better effort to win the game.

Down by two with less than four minutes to play, it was Munster again who put up a high kick for Bostock to chase.

Isaako was in a much better position this time, and appeared to have caught the footy.

But Bostock ripped the ball out of the Kiwi's arms, in turn, ripping the game away from New Zealand.

World.title: Northern Ireland politician jailed for child sex offences
World.content:
The former leader of Northern Ireland's largest unionist party has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for historic child sex offences.

Jeffrey Donaldson, 63, was one of Northern Ireland's best-known politicians until his arrest two years ago.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Police: Triple Zero (000) if it is an emergency

Kids Helpline: 1800 551 800

Headspace:1800 650 890

ReachOut: au.reachout.com

Bravehearts: 1800 272 831

Lifeline: 13 11 14

1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

He was convicted in June of one count of rape, four counts of gross indecency and 13 indecent assault charges involving two girls between 1985 and 2008.

He had denied the charges.

Donaldson led the Democratic Unionist Party, the biggest party in favour of keeping Northern Ireland in the United Kingdom, from 2021 until 2024.

He resigned as leader of the conservative DUP after his arrest, and gave up the seat in the UK House of Commons that he had held since 1997.

Donaldson was convicted in June of one count of rape, four counts of gross indecency and 13 indecent assault charges. (AP: Peter Morrison)

Judge:'Catastrophic descent into disgrace'

Judge Paul Ramsey said that the ex-politician had undergone a "catastrophic descent into disgrace."

He sentenced him at Newry Crown Court, south of Belfast, to 11 years for offences against one victim and four years for the other, to run consecutively.

"There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort," the judge said.

During his trial, Donaldson denied all the allegations against him. He said that he was "crystal clear" that he did not rape one of the girls when she was a child decades ago.

A van carrying Donaldson leaves the Newry Courthouse after a jury found him guilty of historic sex offences earlier this year. (Reuters: Cathal McNaughton)

Donaldson's wife, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, was found to have aided and abetted her husband's offences for witnessing the abuse and doing nothing to intervene.

Because of mental health issues, she faced only a fact-finding hearing that could not result in a conviction.

The two victims testified that Donaldson groped them when they were around primary school age.

The older of the two, referred to in court as Complainant B, said he raped her.

Donaldson testified that the rape "just didn't happen."

Eleanor Donaldson was found to have aided and abetted her husband’s offences. (Reuters: Damien Eagers)

Complainant B said that in the 1990s, years after the abuse, Donaldson apologised to her "for what had happened in the past."

Donaldson testified that he had apologised to her for making her feel uncomfortable.

Donaldson wrote a letter to Complainant A in 2020 to say he regretted the "hurt, pain and distress" he caused.

He claimed that the letter did not refer to sex abuse allegations but other behaviour.

Donaldson's lawyer, Kieran Vaughan, said at a pre sentencing hearing that his client had achieved "significant things in his life."

"These convictions obliterate all those achievements he has made in his life," he said.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Sailors missing as two ships set ablaze in Romanian Black Sea
World.content:
Multiple sailors are missing after a fire broke out on board a ship off the Black Sea coast on Thursday.

Rescuers were searching for seven missing crew from one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight inside Romanian territorial waters.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, but declined to say whether they were Russian.

"Two air drones hit them," Mr Dan said.

"There will be a reaction from the Romanian state."

Recent attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea are Russian attempts to destabilise the eastern flank and weaken support for Ukraine, Mr Dan added after a meeting with NATO's Secretary General Mark Rutte.

The incidents follow drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria over the past 10 days.

Crew members have been rescued after drones struck two vessels in the Black Sea off Bulgaria. (Reuters: Petko Momchilov)

Ships attacked in the black sea

At least 23 sailors were lost from those strikes, which, unlike the latest incidents, took place just outside NATO's territorial waters.

The two ships hit overnight were both anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the canal leading into the Danube River.

The river is a major shipping route used by Ukraine, as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports.

Romania's naval authority said it received an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.

Black Sea tanker attack off Sochi An attack by "unmanned boats" on a Liberian-flagged tanker off the coast of the Russian Olympic city of Sochi sparked a giant "fire of oil", Russian authorities say.

Seven of its 12 crew were missing, and five were rescued.

"At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves," the interior ministry said in a statement.

On Wednesday, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J also caught fire.

Romanian authorities initially said it was not clear whether it had been attacked. All its crew were safe.

Romania shares a border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube.

It has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years.

Both Wine Trader and Yara J caught fire near the mouth of the Danube River's Sulina Canal leading to the Black Sea, where ships often anchor due to weather delays.

Increasing attacks on Black Sea shipping connected with the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months have threatened to cause a global food crisis, as both countries are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.

"We're looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told a security conference in Warsaw earlier this week.

" It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence. "

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said EU leaders would discuss on Thursday a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea.

Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Review ordered after man dies waiting two hours for ambulance
World.content:
Reviews are underway after two Queensland patients died in separate incidents while waiting for medical care.

A 53-year-old man who was experiencing chest pains called Triple Zero (000) to his property in the Brisbane suburb of Annerley on Saturday night.

Paramedics arrived two hours later and found the man dead inside the residence.

The Queensland Ambulance Service has confirmed a review into the matter has been launched.

"The death of a patient is a tragedy, and we extend our condolences to their family and loved ones," a QAS spokesperson said.

On Tuesday afternoon a man in his 80s was under the care of paramedics while waiting for a bed at Mater Private Hospital for approximately three hours.

Upon being admitted he went into cardiac arrest.

The man had a "do not resuscitate order" and died shortly afterwards.

In a statement addressing both matters, Health Minister Tim Nicholls extended his condolences to the family and loved ones of the deceased.

He said the cases would be reviewed "as will always happen when these types of tragic events occur — to ensure all procedures and protocols were followed".

The latest Queensland Health performance data shows ambulance ramping is sitting at 42 per cent across the state's 26 top public hospital emergency departments.

World.title: Story of young woman accused of witchcraft wins $100,000 book award
World.content:
Margaret River-based author Bernice Barry has won the $100,000 ARA Historical Novel Prize for her book about a woman being pursued by a witch-hunter, The Names of a Hare.

It is the story of an unnamed woman living in Cornwall in the 17th century, a time when witches could be burned at the stake.

Barry's protagonist is the daughter of a priest, taught by her housekeeper from a young age about natural cures and magic. She also learns she has a special power of her own where she can float above her body and travel great distances.

When someone shares her secret, she is accused of witchcraft and forced to flee.

Barry, 73, was born in Cornwall and moved to Australia 25 years ago. She says winning the Historical Novel Prize is validating after 15 years writing for a mostly Western Australian audience.

"My books have been bestsellers in WA, but I don't sell a lot of books," she says. "It's a fairly niche area I've been writing in: the stories of forgotten women, history, botany.

" To be acknowledged in this way means the world to me. "

The judges, chaired by publisher and editor Linda Funnell, described Barry's writing as "work[ing] like a spell, building slowly and imperceptibly, attentively describing the natural world and the lives of rural folk in a time of great historical turmoil".

"This is a novel of quiet power that lingers in the mind," the judges said.

Bernice Barry describes The Names of a Hare as about love, home and hope. (Supplied: Fremantle Press)

The ARA Historical Novel Prize, awarded by the Historical Novel Society Australasia to novels set more than 50 years ago, is one of Australia's richest literary prizes.

The prize also awards $30,000 to a book for younger readers. Meg Caddy won this year for their young adult novel A Flash in the Dust about two young people escaping from Fremantle Asylum.

Wayne Marshall won the $5,000 Readers' Choice Award for his novel Henry Goes Bush, which turns the story of Henry Lawson's banishment to Bourke in 1892 into a surreal odyssey.

Barry says the most important thing about winning the top prize is the opportunity for "my little book to get to more readers".

"That is the reason I write," she says.

"It feels like a magical connection [with the reader]. It's the magic of words; the magic of sharing a story."

Writing a neurodivergent protagonist

In The Names of a Hare, the unnamed narrator is at the end of her life, looking back and sharing her story and what she has learned.

Writing the book was an opportunity for Barry to do the same.

The Names of a Hare is the product of meticulous research into C17 recipe books and languages. (Supplied)

"I wanted to convey some of the things that have been on my mind for many years," she says.

When living in England's Midlands and feeling homesick for Cornwall, Barry started to write a short story. More than 30 years later, those pages became the prologue of The Names of a Hare.

But the inspiration for her protagonist goes back even further, to being nine years old and reading RD Blackmore's historical novel Lorna Doone.

She recalls being fascinated by a minor character, who was based on a real woman and dubbed Mother Meldrum.

"I wondered about this old woman who was a healer from Cornwall," Barry says. "Nobody knew her name, and they were afraid of her, but they needed her."

Barry's protagonist, also unnamed, is a neurodivergent woman who avoids eye contact, flinches from touch and is averse to loud noises.

September's best books The latest new releases from some of the world's biggest literary stars, including Emily St John Mandel, RF Kuang and Kate Atkinson, are among this month's best books.

They are qualities borrowed from her own experiences.

"Life was difficult for me as a young woman because I knew I was different," she says.

"I was strange, I was weird, and I spent a lot of time masking. I spent a lot of time thinking it was all my fault.

"I would never have talked about those things until probably two or three years ago, and I wouldn't want anyone else to go through life hiding something that is so discomforting."

It was not something Barry initially set out to include, but when she was about 10,000 words into the manuscript, she realised what she was doing.

"I was thinking, 'There must have been women like me in the 17th century,'" she says.

"It must have been very hard, where people would just look at her and say, 'She's different; she must be a witch.'"

Why witches?

Barry's novel is one of a spate of recent books exploring ideas around magic and witchcraft, including Lucianne Tonti's Good Witch and Kaz Cooke's Spooky Ladies.

They are being released as more young women try out "witchy" things like manifestation, crystal-collecting and solstice rituals.

Barry suggests this interest may stem from young women feeling confident to speak out about misogyny — the same social ill that fuelled the witch trials that form the backdrop of The Names of a Hare.

"I wonder if we'll ever be free of it; of that way of viewing women that makes some people feel women take away their power," she says.

That way of viewing women is something she describes in the novel.

"Having the skill to remove pain and restore good health, that's power, and power in the hands of a woman is not a thing men can swallow easy like a slippery syllabub," she writes.

Barry sees that renewed sense of confidence, paired with "witchy" rituals, as part of a cycle she also recalls from her early adulthood, when she was a student in London.

"The late 1960s and early 1970s was a time when there was a similar wave of confidence and a united feeling of women being able to speak out and do something about [misogyny]," she says.

Barry also wrote the novel Sarah Evans, about an 18th-century convict, and two books about botanist Georgiana Molloy. (Supplied: Fremantle Press)

That united feeling is also in the novel.

"It's about the steadfastness of women and friendship; the way we always turn up for one another," Barry says.

Still, the author would prefer for the reader to decide for themselves if her unnamed protagonist is a witch or not.

"Was this woman a witch or was she someone who had a natural ability for healing?"

Washington: US President Donald Trump says the Pentagon will no longer live-stream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, after the announcement faced bipartisan criticism and Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it. Trump said on social media on Thursday (US time) that publicly airing the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan”. Nidal Hasan in an undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff’s Department. Bell County Sheriff's Department via AP But, he continued, “any very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”. The Pentagon has said Hasan’s execution is scheduled for December 3.



“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump said. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.” The announcement earlier this month from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public – and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be live-streamed – prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalisation. The Pentagon on Thursday declined to elaborate beyond Trump’s statement. The plan was scrapped a week after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced there would be a livestream. Bloomberg When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen”.



“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately live-streamed, I’m not going to be watching it.” Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. The head of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops had condemned the Trump administration’s decision to live-stream Hasan’s execution, with Archbishop Paul S. Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”. Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, voiced similar sentiments. For his part, the president has defended his decision to approve the use of a firing squad, but had for days distanced himself from Hegseth’s announcement that it would be public. “Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said on Friday when asked about the live-stream. As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: “He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”



Related Article Opinion

Death penalty I was in Florida when Ted Bundy was on trial. My mother was right about his, and every, execution Michelle Griffin Federal Bureau Chief Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on November 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunisations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted, “Allahu akbar” – Arabic for “God is great” – and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot. Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defence during his 2013 trial. Hasan was left paralysed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair. Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behaviour at trial, he may not want to. The US military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was executed by hanging.

World.title: ‘Lot of discomfort’: Ponga has suspected broken arm as Walsh, Bostock break Kiwi hearts
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Lot of discomfort’: Ponga has suspected broken arm as Walsh, Bostock break Kiwi hearts Christian Nicolussi Updated October 16, 2026 — 2:08am ,first published 10:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Kalyn Ponga played around 20 minutes with a suspected broken arm, Reece Walsh was nothing short of phenomenal while Jack Bostock bagged a hat-trick on debut in one of the most memorable World Cup games – ever. The international rugby league tournament kicked off in fantastic style with a Kangaroos’ 24-22 victory in front of 41,255 Sydney fans on Thursday night. Loading The No.1 battle between Walsh and Ponga was worth the admission alone into Allianz Stadium, with both men producing some breathtaking plays in attack and defence. Ponga, who was making his debut for the Kiwis, bagged a double, including a try that featured him skip past Cameron Munster, then stand up Walsh on his way to the line.



Walsh then returned serve when he somehow made Ponga and Jahrome Hughes miss him simultaneously before he ran 60m to hit back for the Kangaroos. Walsh also denied Ponga late in the first half when he looked destined to score. Reece Walsh was outstanding for Australia in their World Cup opener against New Zealand. Getty Images Australia coach Kevin Walters defended picking Walsh ahead of Roosters grand final hero James Tedesco for the opening Cup game. Based on Walsh’s effort against the Kiwis, you have to wonder how Tedesco gets a start at the pointy end of the tournament. Ponga, sadly, came from the field with just over 10 minutes remaining, with New Zealand coach Stacey Jones confirming his star back had broken his left arm.



“It’s a possible fracture of the arm, but he’s going to go for scans,” Jones said. “He played about 20 minutes [with the injury], he carried on and toughed it out. “He couldn’t catch a ball or anything like that – he was in a lot of discomfort.” Ponga is seen speaking with Munster post-game in a sling. Getty Images Skipper James Fisher-Harris added: “He’s a tough bugger, eh. He obviously has a lot of pride in the black and white jersey and didn’t want to let his teammates down. I’m feeling for him.”



Considering Cronulla, NSW and Kangaroos’ hooker Blayke Brailey was back from a broken arm in less than a month, there remains an outside chance Ponga is back on deck for the Kiwis who lost no admirers. They will also get Ponga’s Newcastle teammate Phoenix Crossland back from suspension in time for the finals. Walsh had tears in his eyes when the Australian anthem played, and came up with the special moments when his teammates needed him. Jack Bostock celebrates with Latrell Mitchell. Getty Images New Zealand dominated for longer passages, with the Kangaroos’ five tries coming via two intercepts, two Bostock leaps, and some Walsh magic. After Walsh scored, he dropped to his knees and vomited, something he is often captured on TV cameras doing before kick-off. “He’s a vomiter, he’s a chucker,” Walters said of Walsh.



“Because he’s not an endurance athlete, he’s a power athlete, and the amount of running that he did, he had some big efforts there a couple of times back to back. “We had to relieve him from his goal-kicking duties. He took an eternity to line that goal up, and then he couldn’t kick it anyway. He’s alright in there now, and he’s pretty happy. It was his first game back in a long period, it was a very good effort.” Walters confirmed Tedesco would return against Fiji next Sunday in Brisbane, and he was simply overlooked for Walsh because of the gruelling finals campaign he had featured in for the Sydney Roosters. Chooks premiership teammate Sam Walker would also play in the halves with Tom Dearden, with Munster to have a spell, and Mitch Moses forced off the field two minutes into the second half with a cork to the outside of his right leg. Australia half Mitchell Moses was replaced after suffering a calf injury. Getty Images Bostock, who becomes a free agent on November 1, did nothing to hurt his market value with three tries, but an even better offload for Walsh to score.



“I don’t think I’ve seen a better debut game from a winger, or any Australian player – he was in everything,” Walters said. Both teams will have the weekend off before returning to camp, with the Kiwis returning home to face the Cook Islands in Christchurch. World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Proteas swing the axe as ‘Rolls-Royce’ Rabada firms for return against Australia Daniel Brettig Updated October 15, 2026 — 10:59pm ,first published 7:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Gqeberha: South Africa have swung the selection axe, dropping Tristan Stubbs and taking the wicket-keeping gloves away from Kyle Verreynne, as they consider recalling spearhead Kagiso Rabada for the second Test on Sunday. Stubbs and Verreynne were both exposed by Australia in the opening Test of the series, losing their wickets at key times in both innings as the hosts were guilty of poor shot selection under sustained pressure from Pat Cummins and company. Kagiso Rabada at South Africa training in Durban last week. Getty Images In particular, Stubbs’ drive at a tempter from Cummins and Verreynne’s vague dab to edge Matt Renshaw to slip were critical moments in the fourth innings as the Proteas tried desperately to scramble for a draw. Ryan Rickelton, who also had a poor game opening the batting, will move into the wicket-keeping role, with the possibility of moving back down the batting order.



South African coach Shukri Conrad has included Matthew Breetzke in the 17-man squad, after he clattered a hundred against Australia in the ODI series that presaged the Tests. Breetzke has a top score of 13 from two Tests, one each against Bangladesh and Zimbabwe. Related Article Australian cricket ‘I don’t like it’: Aussies shut down Pollock’s pink-ball proposal “That his ODI form is as hot as it is gave him an inside lane, and more importantly the attitude and the character Matt has will go a long way,” Conrad said. “With ‘Ricks’ taking the gloves, there are decisions to be made whether he does move down the order or he can continue opening the batting. “We’ll have a look at what the conditions are like – the weather forecast isn’t great for day one. So [there’s] a few things to consider before we look at that final 11. We’ve had an opportunity to lick our wounds and make sure we turn the ship in the right direction now.”



Rabada will train later on Thursday, and is firming to return to the home side’s 11 following his recovery from a hamstring tear. With his high pace, skill and fire, Rabada is arguably South Africa’s best chance of finding a way back into the series. Editor's pick Australian cricket ‘Not all sunshine and roses’: The hidden cameras on Australia’s Test team They will be heartened by the fact that they beat Australia in Test matches at St George’s Park, in the town formerly known as Port Elizabeth, on each of the previous two tours in 2014 and 2018. “It’s going to sound like an excuse,” Conrad said of Rabada. “But when your Rolls-Royce of fast bowlers is not available, and you’ve got to fashion an attack … Hopefully, our Rolls-Royce will be purring down the highway.” Conrad has also pointed out that the South African batsmen will need to show greater perseverance to stay in the middle, having been taught a lesson by Matt Renshaw at Kingsmead.



“We keep talking about the batting because that’s where we felt we let ourselves down the most. Dismissals in batting sit in one of three places – they are technical, tactical or mental,” Conrad said. Aiden Markram needs more support with the willow from his teammates. AP Photo “If we’re brutally honest, a lot of our dismissals sat in the mental corner. Is that an easier fix than technical and tactical? Probably not. So we need to see our guys pull up fresh enough. “Aiden [Markram] showed us in the second innings that there’s nothing fancy about Test match cricket. That single-bloody-mindedness, where I’ve got to bat for a day and a half now, irrespective of what it looks like – some of our batters can take a leaf from his book.” Australian assistant coach Matthew Wade confirmed that Cameron Green was not under serious consideration for the second Test as he resumed batting for the first time since the abdominal injury he suffered in the ODI series.



Josh Inglis, who did spend some time in the nets in Durban, is closer to putting his name up for selection as an option in the middle order. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Homicide detectives are probing the death of a man in Melbourne’s outer north on Thursday evening in what police suspect was a targeted attack.

Emergency services were called to a property in Gypsum Drive in Wollert after reports that a man had been found unresponsive just before 5.30pm.

Police said the yet-to-be formally identified man’s death is being treated as suspicious, and a crime scene had been established.

At this stage, police are investigating if the incident was a targeted killing.

In a statement late Thursday, police said no arrests had been made and the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident would be ongoing.

World.title: Moderate makes Mate of the Month
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

The guerilla editing that resulted in the removal of a Ben Roberts-Smith image by persons unknown from Sue Lyall’s Herald (C8) could’ve been worse, reckons Peter Miniutti of Ashbury: “Instead of opening your paper and finding something removed, you could’ve found an inserted centrefold of Barnaby Joyce. Talk about a page being re(a)d.”

“Like Peter Hayes (C8) I’m tired of the ubiquitous use of ‘influencers’,” says John Lees of Castlecrag. “My suggestion for an alternative description is ‘inflatulancers’ bearing in mind that all we hear from them is a load of hot air!” Paul Koff of Glenhaven finds himself on a similar path: “Because of the trite garbage most of them peddle, we’ve taken to calling them ‘effluencers’.”

“Our Irish chums have a very accurate way to describe influencers,” advises John Elder of South Brisbane (Qld). “Gobshites.”

“Stand aside ‘shevelled’ and ‘gruntled’ (C8),” declares Greg Phillipson of Aranda (ACT). “My wife sends me out in search of ‘gorm’ whenever I accompany her to the shops.”

Philip Aspden of Miranda is currently conducting “experimental English classes at the Dawu Experimental School in Hubei Province, China, with the Herald for company and reading about all the strife in the world, I’m happy to remain ‘mented’.”

A man was found dead in his Brisbane home two hours after he called for an ambulance and was told to make his own way to the hospital.

The 53-year-old Annerley man died on Saturday night, having called Triple Zero complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath.

A man has died after waiting more than two hours for an ambulance in Brisbane. Dominique Tassell

He was categorised as a code IC, which 90 per cent of the time is seen to within 27.2 minutes.

However, the Queensland Ambulance Service called the man back and asked him if he could make his own way to the Princess Alexandra Hospital, as he lived three streets away.

Getty Images In particular, Stubbs’ drive at a tempter from Cummins and Verreynne’s vague dab to edge Matt Renshaw to slip were critical moments in the fourth innings as the Proteas tried desperately to scramble for a draw. Ryan Rickelton, who also had a poor game opening the batting, will move into the wicket-keeping role, with the possibility of moving back down the batting order.



South African coach Shukri Conrad has included Matthew Breetzke in the 17-man squad, after he clattered a hundred against Australia in the ODI series that presaged the Tests. Breetzke has a top score of 13 from two Tests, one each against Bangladesh and Zimbabwe. Related Article Australian cricket ‘I don’t like it’: Aussies shut down Pollock’s pink-ball proposal “That his ODI form is as hot as it is gave him an inside lane, and more importantly the attitude and the character Matt has will go a long way,” Conrad said. “With ‘Ricks’ taking the gloves, there are decisions to be made whether he does move down the order or he can continue opening the batting. “We’ll have a look at what the conditions are like – the weather forecast isn’t great for day one. So [there’s] a few things to consider before we look at that final 11. We’ve had an opportunity to lick our wounds and make sure we turn the ship in the right direction now.”



Rabada will train later on Thursday, and is firming to return to the home side’s 11 following his recovery from a hamstring tear. With his high pace, skill and fire, Rabada is arguably South Africa’s best chance of finding a way back into the series. Editor's pick Australian cricket ‘Not all sunshine and roses’: The hidden cameras on Australia’s Test team They will be heartened by the fact that they beat Australia in Test matches at St George’s Park, in the town formerly known as Port Elizabeth, on each of the previous two tours in 2014 and 2018. “It’s going to sound like an excuse,” Conrad said of Rabada. “But when your Rolls-Royce of fast bowlers is not available, and you’ve got to fashion an attack … Hopefully, our Rolls-Royce will be purring down the highway.” Conrad has also pointed out that the South African batsmen will need to show greater perseverance to stay in the middle, having been taught a lesson by Matt Renshaw at Kingsmead.



“We keep talking about the batting because that’s where we felt we let ourselves down the most. Dismissals in batting sit in one of three places – they are technical, tactical or mental,” Conrad said. Aiden Markram needs more support with the willow from his teammates. AP Photo “If we’re brutally honest, a lot of our dismissals sat in the mental corner. Is that an easier fix than technical and tactical? Probably not. So we need to see our guys pull up fresh enough. “Aiden [Markram] showed us in the second innings that there’s nothing fancy about Test match cricket. That single-bloody-mindedness, where I’ve got to bat for a day and a half now, irrespective of what it looks like – some of our batters can take a leaf from his book.” Australian assistant coach Matthew Wade confirmed that Cameron Green was not under serious consideration for the second Test as he resumed batting for the first time since the abdominal injury he suffered in the ODI series.



Josh Inglis, who did spend some time in the nets in Durban, is closer to putting his name up for selection as an option in the middle order. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Homicide detectives are probing the death of a man in Melbourne’s outer north on Thursday evening in what police suspect was a targeted attack.

World.title: Labour supporters told to harness 'hope and rage' as National voters fear 'handout society'
World.content:
Labour supporters have been told to harness their "hope and rage" this election while National voters say fear the worst should the left bloc take power.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins joined a number of Labour candidates, including his deputy Carmel Sepuloni, Phil Twyford and newcomer and foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters in the working-class suburb of Kelston in West Auckland, in the auditorium of the local girls' high school, attracting a few hundred locals and party volunteers.

In her speech, Walters said Labour supporters had a mixture of "outrage and hope" to the campaign.

"Some of you, like me, will remember going on a march not long after the last election when they cancelled the smoke-free generation for our children - if they win, there will be marches for three years.

"I ask you one thing: bring all that energy, all of that hope and rage that you would put into those three years ahead, bring it now," she said.

Hipkins took the stage donning a lei presented to him on stage by Sepuloni, who has been the MP for Kelston for over a decade.

Labour supporters cheering on leader Chris Hipkins and local candidates. RNZ / Tuwhenuaroa Natanahira

He used his speech to lay into Christopher Luxon - rolling out his party's new attack line claiming Luxon had left people $6000 worse off - and laid out his party's plan to make life cheaper.

Jobs, in particular, got the crowd riled up.

"Those on the other side who currently sit on the treasury benches say it's not the government's job to create jobs, well, they've certainly demonstrated that they don't think it's their job to create jobs.

"Under our government, we achieved record low unemployment despite some of the most challenging economic conditions any government in New Zealand has faced ... we saved people's jobs [and] we've now got a government that celebrates losing them," he said.

Down south, the National party had their own rally on the West Coast.

Leader Christopher Luxon proved a popular figure among the estimated hundred supporters in Greymouth, many clad in royal blue.

After speaking for about 20 minutes, he then mingled with patrons and posed for a number of photos.

About 100 people gathered in Greymouth on Thursday for the National party's West Coast rally. RNZ / Adam Burns

Luxon also heard staunch views from the locals as pre-election tension ramped up.

Property developer Geoff Ball endorsed Luxon but admitted he was "seriously concerned" heading into the election.

"We've got a country that's in trouble," he said.

"I'm not 100 percent confident that National and the current coalition is going to get in. I think it's a big, big problem."

Ball's concerns stemmed from the belief that three years was not long enough for the coalition to boost the economy.

"I think they made a bloody good start, but I personally think they've got a long way to go," he said.

"To me, the country's got to be run like a business. It's not a handout society.

"We used to be a country where we had a reputation of number eight wire, and we get sh*t done. Now we're a country of red tape, bureaucrats, and b*llshit."

National leader Christopher Luxon is flanked by Brett Cummings (L) and Geoff Ball. RNZ / Adam Burns

Local man Brett Cummings had a post-speech one-on-one with Luxon, where he said they discussed "a few things that needed to be tidied up" on the West Coast, particularly around the repeal of regional councils and the overhaul of the Resource Management Act.

"There's a whole lot of changes they've been promising, but it's taking a long time to implement.

"All that land use and stuff, it's a long time ago. Not that long ago in my lifetime, you used to have permitted activities to be gold mining.

"Now you've got to get three consents plus a bond and all the rest of it."

RNZ asked both men to rate the past three years under the coalition government.

World.title: Rugby League: Kangaroos edge Kiwis in World Cup classic
World.content:
In one of the most stunning starts to a sporting tournament, the Kiwis and Kangaroos played out an absolute classic to kick off the Rugby League World Cup.

It was match chock full of barely believable moments, dramatic twists and turns, and superstars stepping up on the biggest stage, with Australia holding on for an enthralling 24-22 win.

Though unlikely to affect the Kiwis semi-final hopes, the loss may come at a different cost, with Kalyn Ponga forced from the field with a suspected broken arm.

It will take something special to top the tournament's opening try as the Kiwis struck first in sensational style.

With absolutely no room to move in the left hand corner, Casey McLean managed a miracle, finding the grass with his entire body forced over the touchline

The Kangaroos replied with a runaway, Jack Bostock snatching a Jahrome Hughes pass out of the air and streaking away to score.

With the Kiwis forcing a line drop out, Reece Walsh sent it out on the full, Jaymayne Isaako slotting an easy two points.

After the Kiwis forced the defending champs again, Australia nabbed another intercept, this time to take the lead as Tom Trbojevic latched onto a McLean ball and fended off a scrambling Kodi Nikorima to go 90.

As the siren approached, the Kiwis bagged another two points as Nikorima was taken off the ball by Katoni Staggs, the centre sent to the bin as a result as Isaako squared the scores 10-apiece at half-time.

On his first international outing, fullback Ponga put the Kiwis back in front courtesy of a deft offload from Isaiah Papali'i.

After an extended period under the pump, it looked as if Ronaldo Mulitalo had stretched the Kiwis advantage after Trbojevic spilled a kick, but the chasers were ruled to be offside.

The Kangaroos relief turned to rapture as Bostock got his second, leaping above the pack to take a towering Cameron Munster bomb and reinstate the stalemate.

It wouldn't last long though after Ponga chimed into the line and sliced right through, standing up Walsh to reclaim the lead for the Kiwis.

But Walsh would respond with a stunner of his own, exploding onto a Bostock offload 80 out, showcasing his blistering speed as he beat both Ponga and Hughes who collided with each other, the Australian full back far too fast for the desperate chase of Joseph Tapine.

That chase proved crucial however, as Latrell Mitchell sprayed the conversion to keep the Kiwis in front by two.

Cue more Kangaroos magic, Munster sending it to the skies, Bostock and Isaako with a clean aerial contest, won by Bostock to complete his hat-trick and put the home side up 24-22 with four minutes remaining.

A final Kiwis assault proved futile as the Kangaroos held on to break New Zealand hearts, but ignite a tournament.
