World.title: Three hospitalised after chemical exposure in Christchurch
World.content:
A commercial building in Christchurch has been made safe after a chemical spill left three people in hospital.

Emergency services were called to a building in Coleridge Street in the suburb of Sydenham about 3.50pm on Thursday.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said seven crews attended and firefighters had to rescue two people from the building.

St John said one person was in a critical condition and two others were in moderate conditions.

FENZ assistant district commander Michael Balmer said crews found a person unconscious.

"On arrival they discovered there were chemicals involved, they made a very snap rescue. The crews did a great job in getting the patient out of the danger area and into fresh air," he said.

"It was a liquid product but it gave off vapours, I believe, that affected the individual and they collapsed inside the building."

Three people were taken to hospital after being exposed to the chemicals. Nathan Mckinnon

The affected business recycles paints, cleaning and waste products, and other solvents.

"We were able to isolate the systems involved so that it wouldn't escalate any further, once the chemicals were isolated power was isolated to that section of the factory," Balmer said.

"We were able to determine that the product wasn't a huge amount but it was safe enough to then hand back to the property representative."

Balmer said the firefighters responded to a difficult situation well.

"You turn up to incidents like that, chemical incidents, and you're going into the unknown really so it's quite a high risk environment. I was very proud of the way the crews responded to that."

World.title: 'Four-headed beast': ACT leader David Seymour hints at potential for coalition with Opportunity
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour says he could be open to a "four-headed beast" coalition with Opportunity to stop a left-wing coalition taking power.

Speaking to a crowd of supporters in Wānaka, he admitted that if Opportunity crossed the 5 percent threshold, a coalition with them to keep the Greens and Te Pāti Māori from running the country "would be a good outcome".

However, Seymour said he felt Opportunity may not be the kingmaker, "despite the best efforts of the media".

National has ruled out working with the Opportunity on multiple occasions.

Leader Christopher Luxon initially stated he would not do business with a party that wants to raise taxes at the end of July.

Following the TVNZ leaders' debate last week, Luxon reiterated he would not work with Opportunity.

"I have been crystal clear with who we could or couldn't work with. I've laid that out from the very beginning of the year. I've been clear about Opportunity," he said at the time.

Last week, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong dismissed the comments.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong is continuing to keep the door open to coalition negotiations with National. RNZ / Blessen Tom

"I don't believe him. Because he would rather be in government than in opposition, I assume," she said at the time.

"There are many things we could work with National on, I think the five bottom lines are realistic for them to commit to."

At the end of September, Opportunity set out its five minimum requirements a potential coalition partner would have to agree to.

The party's bottom lines are giving the Commerce Commission more teeth, regulating lobbying and capping political donations to "clean up politics", developing a 10-year plan to "fix the health system" alongside health professionals, phasing out bottom trawling, and recommitting to Paris Agreement emissions reduction obligations and protecting the Climate Change Commission's independence.

Multiple polls have shown Opportunity poised to decide who will lead the next government.

The latest 1News Verian Poll, released earlier this week, showed Opportunity winning a potential 10 seats in the election.

If that poll's results were replicated at the election, National would get 34 MPs and New Zealand First and ACT would each get 12 - a coalition bloc of 58.

On the left, Labour would get 34 MPs, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori four - depending on how the Māori seats were calculated - and Te Tai Tokerau Party one seat - for a total of 57.

World.title: The Helicopter Line ordered to pay $17,740 over the unjustified dismissal of Mount Cook cafe employee
World.content:
Just two weeks after being ordered to forfeit two of its $1 million helicopters to the Crown for illegal crayfish gathering, The Helicopter Line has found itself in turbulence again.

The Queenstown company has now been rapped by the Employment Relations Authority (ERA) over its unjustified dismissal of former cafe employee Jonathan Lovatt following the closure of its Delta Tasman Cafe near Mount Cook in 2024.

In an ERA decision, authority member Antoinette Baker said The Helicopter Line (THL) "fell well short" of treating Lovatt fairly, and found the company effectively blamed him for the cafe's closure after he allegedly refused to train new staff and take on other duties.

"It ended his employment suddenly for reasons of fault without any evidence of a process addressing those things beforehand."

Lovatt worked as a cafe assistant for THL for eight months in 2024.

His employment was ended in a December 2, 2024, letter from THL director Mark Quickfall.

The letter stated that during Quickfall's previous visit to Mount Cook, he and Lovatt had discussed changing the cafe business model to ensure it could continue operating.

They agreed to wind back the menu and serve coffee, cabinet food and other self-serve items. The model required the support of all managers and staff.

But Quickfall wrote that the acting cafe manager had since told him Lovatt was unwilling to help order food, support the cafe while replacement staff were recruited after two employees left, or train new staff.

"Unfortunately, the situation at the cafe is out of our control and despite extensive advertising it will take time to find and induct staff. We will close the cafe from 5 December," the letter read.

"As per your contract we will pay you two weeks' notice from today. We will also require you to vacate the staff accommodation. We are unable to meet your requirements and are now forced to close the cafe."

The cafe has since reopened.

Quickfall told the authority that Lovatt had been made redundant and said THL had consulted with him through a series of meetings and discussions before the decision was made.

However, Baker rejected THL's claim that Lovatt's dismissal was a genuine redundancy.

She said Quickfall had communicated in the letter that the cafe had to close because Lovatt would not perform certain tasks while the business recruited more staff or help train the new employees.

Quickfall also confirmed in evidence that Lovatt's employment was terminated because he had refused to operate the cafe under the proposed self-service cabinet model and instead wanted to continue serving a menu with food cooked to order.

"Again, this supports that THL was effectively blaming Mr Lovatt for the closure of the cafe rather than perhaps addressing in a more transparent way its concerns that he was not allegedly prepared to change and behaved in a manner now claimed to be problematic about this," Baker said.

There was no evidence there had ever been a "sensible discussion" about those issues between the parties or that a fair process had been followed, she said.

The authority heard Lovatt had told his then acting manager three days before receiving the termination letter that he was "burnt out" and needed to take a sick day, which Baker said was a catalyst for his dismissal.

Baker found that, because the dismissal was not a genuine redundancy, THL was not justified in ending Lovatt's employment. The company was ordered to pay him $17,740, comprising $16,000 compensation and $1740 in lost wages.

In a written statement, a spokesperson for THL said it had operated at Aoraki Mount Cook for 40 years and valued the people who had worked with the company.

"We take our obligations as an employer seriously and are carefully considering the determination and our options. As this involves employment and privacy matters, we are unable to comment further."

The decision comes just two weeks after THL was fined $12,000 and ordered to forfeit two Airbus AS350 helicopters after it was sentenced in the Queenstown District Court for its part in an illegal crayfish gathering operation in 2022.

THL provided flights as part of its collaborative heli-crayfish experience with The Rees Hotel.

A crayfish diver would fly with tourists to a remote South Island location and gather crayfish, which were then given to The Rees Hotel for its dining service.

Under the Fisheries Act 1996, any seafood used as part of a commercial business must be sourced under a valid commercial permit, which neither party had.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: NZ apple sector helps Indian growers to expand orchards under FTA commitment
World.content:
New Zealand's apple industry is sharing the secrets of its productive pipfruit success with growers in India, but assures the efforts will not hurt competition exporting there.

Sector leaders and diplomats have returned from a week in India, where they met with state officials and apple growers in key growing region Himachal Pradesh, known as the apple bowl of India in the western Himalayas.

Here, New Zealand was setting up a centre of excellence, as part of a co-operation commitment under the new free trade agreement (FTA) with India coming into effect on Tuesday next week.

Audio player for " Midday rural news for 15 October 2026 " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/country/1925779%2Fnz-apple-sector-helps-indian-growers-to-expand-orchards-under-fta-commitment

Midday rural news for 15 October 2026 Rural News Download MP3 3m

In addition to bolstering online data and resources, the centre will feature an apple orchard with different apple varieties, a research centre and foster collaboration with New Zealand experts to expand India's domestic production.

The project built on earlier efforts of sending scientists from Plant and Food Research (now under the Bioeconomy Science Institute) to the region again to help growers improve production.

New centres will be established in India for kiwifruit development too.

What's your experience? Let us know by emailing monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

Danielle Adsett, chief executive of industry group New Zealand Apples and Pears, was accompanied by the country's special agricultural trade envoy Nathan Guy on the trip in late September, early October.

New Zealand apple exports will face smaller import tariffs and new quota concessions under the NZ-India FTA coming into effect soon. www.alphapix.co.nz

Adsett said the project was a result of new FTA provisions.

"India should absolutely benefit. For New Zealand, we have been provided with tariff concessions and a quota.

"So that's what we managed to get on the table, and the co-operation plan is what we offered up to get that result."

Adsett said India deeply trusted New Zealand and its expertise, and there was good opportunity to help Indian farmers increase productivity on their orchards.

AFP

She said Indian apples sat in a different market segment to more premium New Zealand apples, that would also be counter-seasonal.

"India relies on imported apples and they've got 1.4 billion people to feed," she said. "And India fundamentally cannot produce enough apples for the demand that they have.

"There are hundreds of thousands of growers in India farming on very, very difficult terrain with very difficult access and fundamentally growing a different variety mix to what we can offer the Indian consumer.

"So I do not see a world of which New Zealand apples would compete directly with Indian apples."

But she said it would not be without its challenges, including access to nursery stock and cold chain issues.

"Very, very old orchards. Very, very big trees that are not producing much at all. So there's a real opportunity to help that shift, but the opportunity obviously will have a lot of challenges alongside."

A bite into the apple

India was New Zealand's fourth largest export market for apples and pears in the year to June, worth around $100 million, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

https://www.mfat.govt.nz/en/trade/free-trade-agreements/free-trade-agreements-concluded-but-not-in-force/new-zealand-india-free-trade-agreement/key-facts-on-new-zealand-india-trade

A recent Ministry for Primary Industries report showed apple exports reached more than 38,564 tonnes in the year to December, according to its Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries report.

But Adsett said they would be close to 50,000 tonnes this year, mostly Royal Gala, which faced the current 50 percent import tariff on top of the sales price.

"So a very, very difficult market to make any margin on. In fact, most of our product struggles to be competitive in that market, due to the nature of the other markets that they import from."

Himachal Pradesh in northern India in the western Himalayas. Susan Murray

The FTA will see new quotas for apples from year one during India's off-season, in the window of April to the end of August.

The first 32,500 tonnes will be subject to 25 percent tariffs, and the current 50 percent tariff would apply for volumes in excess of that.

Adsett said apple exporters would likely exceed that volume next season.

India's import quota concessions would reduce for Aotearoa over the next six years, expanding to 45,000 tonnes at the remaining 25 percent tariff.

Tariffs on pears into India will drop to 16.5 percent over the next decade, with no quota limit.

For kiwifruit, New Zealand exporters would face duty-free access for 6,250 tonnes each year, widening to up to 15,000 tonnes by year six. Out-of-tariff quotas will halve to 16.5 percent.

The FTA will come into effect on 20 October, Tuesday next week.

World.title: Employment Court rules five Calendar Girls dancers were employees, not contractors
World.content:
Five former dancers who worked at a Wellington strip club have won their case, after arguing they were treated as employees despite being employed as contractors.

The former dancers told the Employment Court that because the club considered them to be contractors, they missed out on entitlements such as annual and sick leave, had to pay their own taxes and were not able to work for other clubs or agencies.

During the hearing in June, one of the dancers described the lack of autonomy the workers had over the services being sold.

She said there was an illusion staff could refuse clients, but if they did, there were consequences.

She said she had to perform a lap dance with a client she was not comfortable with and was reprimanded when she refused to remove her g-string.

Another described having to dance on the main stage and rely on tips for payment. The worker said dancers were not allowed to refuse to strip nude and several said the club had set hours that they expected dancers to be there, regardless of whether paying clients were present.

The workers said in practice, they were treated as employees and Judge MS King agreed.

"When the plaintiffs commenced work with Calendar Girls, there was a clear common intention to do so as independent contractors. However, the evidence demonstrates an inequality of bargaining power between the parties, which points away from the plaintiffs being in business on their own account and requires consideration of how the relationship operated in practice."

World.title: A-League star in fiery exchange with reporter over suspension loophole
World.content:
Auckland FC striker Sam Cosgrove has blown up over questions about using a "loophole" to serve out a suspension before the A-League Men season.

Cosgrove was handed a two-game ban after being sent off in the closing stages of Auckland's 1-0 FIFA Intercontinental Cup loss to Saudi side Al-Ahli in August.

Auckland are allowed to play A-League professionals in their reserves side under New Zealand Football's participation agreement and competition regulations.

That includes up to two 23-year-old non-citizens for each match-day squad.

The clause opened the door for the 29-year-old Englishman to serve out his ban in Auckland's recent New Zealand National League fixtures against Wellington Olympic and Miramar Rangers.

In a fiery exchange on Thursday, Cosgrove could not recall the two matches and was bemused when asked if he had any unease or embarrassment over using the "loophole".

Loading Instagram content

"Embarrassment?" he shot back at a reporter.

"Why would the club not push to have a player available and use every power that they have?"

Cosgrove bagged 11 goals in his debut season with Auckland, securing the men's competition golden boot along the way to the club's first championship.

"It doesn't matter, does it? I have technically [served my ban]. I've missed two NPL matches," Cosgrove said.

"If you pick up a suspension in the A-League, you have to serve it in the A-League.

"So technically, in that case, I should be missing the next few Intercontinental Cups, but I'm not."

Auckland FC are the reigning A-League Men champions. (Getty Images: New Zealand Herald/Alyse Wright)

The media conference ended abruptly before the reporter repeated his claim that Cosgrove had not actually served the ban.

"What are you doing here then? Bugger off, if you're going to talk shit," the striker replied.

An Auckland FC minder stated that FIFA, Football Australia and Football New Zealand were "fine" with the way the ban was served.

"You know what football's like in this country, mate? We f***ing work hard to get it good. You bring it down with shit like that," Cosgrove said, prompting a chuckle from the reporter.

"What are you laughing for? We'll just f*** you off. You won't get back here again."

In a podcast episode posted on Tuesday, Cosgrove said he was relieved when news of the rule's workaround became public so he could "finally stop lying about it".

"It was a poor challenge in oppressive heat and late in the game, but the two-game suspension was a little bit harsh," he told The Unused Subs podcast.

"We were trying to get that reduced, and the power of lawyers and legal teams these days, they managed to find a way to sign me up with the Auckland reserves."

The defending champions will begin their A-League campaign at home to Melbourne City on Saturday, before an away trip to face Western Sydney Wanderers on October 24.

World.title: Aussies win all-time World Cup classic, Ponga suffers suspected broken arm
World.content:
Australia has won an all-time Rugby League World Cup classic, with a hat-trick from debutant Jack Bostock earning a thrilling 24-22 win over New Zealand.

The Kiwis, trying to inflict a first home defeat on the Kangaroos in 11 years, dominated much of the game but a trio of long-range tries, including a pair of 90-metre intercepts, lifted Australia to a stunning win.

Kiwi fullback Kalyn Ponga, playing his first match for New Zealand, suffered a suspected broken arm after starring with two second-half tries and putting the Kiwis on the verge of victory.

But Bostock's three-try performance, including the match-winner with less than four minutes to play, sunk the Kiwis.

The Kangaroos have injury concerns of their own, with halfback Mitchell Moses limping off just moments into the second half.

Relive all the action below in the ABC Sport live blog.

World.title: Wallabies show faith in rookie fly half for final All Blacks Test
World.content:
Declan Meredith will start at fly half against the All Blacks for just the fourth time in his young Test career, as the Wallabies make changes for Saturday's final Bledisloe Cup clash at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Meredith, who made his Test debut against France in July, replaces Ben Donaldson in the number 10 jersey.

Donaldson was ruled out with a minor upper leg injury in the wake of the 50-19 thrashing dished out by the All Blacks at Auckland's Eden Park last Saturday night.

Back-up fly half Harry McLaughlin-Phillips will make his Test debut if he comes on as a reserve in Sydney.

He is joined on the bench by reserve scrum half Kalani Thomas, who is yet to play a Bledisloe Cup Test.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

It will be a tough initiation for Meredith, although he will be playing outside Brumbies teammate and scrum half, Ryan Lonergan.

The 27-year-old got his first taste of playing the All Blacks after coming on as a reserve at Eden Park last weekend.

Meanwhile, the Wallabies have moved Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres.

He started on the wing in the Wallabies' past two Tests, but the absence of Len Ikitau (concussion) forced Wallabies coach Les Kiss to shift the ex-NRL star back to the midfield.

He will partner Isaac Henry, who switches from outside to inside centre, while Harry Potter will start on the wing.

Ikitau is a massive loss for the Wallabies, who are also missing Hunter Paisami (suspension) from their midfield options.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted back to the centres for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Elsewhere in the Wallabies' match-day squad, former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead prop, alongside hooker Josh Nasser.

Ross replaces Angus Bell, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa (rested) made way for Nasser.

Hooker Billy Pollard, lock Josh Canham, openside flanker Carlo Tizzano and utility back Filipo Daugunu have returned to the Wallabies' squad as reserves.

Wallaroos lose star for historic 'quadruple header' The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

"We got a clear picture last weekend of where we need to be better," Kiss said in a Rugby Australia statement.

"We've said all along we'll continue to work hard and grow our game, and the squad has been impressive in the way they have prepared this week."

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who retained his place alongside Jeremy Williams in the second row, will appear in his 50th Test.

The Bledisloe Cup Test will cap off a historic "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos play Scotland earlier in the day, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams meet New Zealand and Fiji respectively.

It is the first time all four national teams have featured on the same match-day schedule.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Aidan Ross, Josh Nasser, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter, Isaac Henry, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright

Reserves: Billy Pollard, Angus Bell, Massimo De Lutiis, Josh Canham, Carlo Tizzano, Kalani Thomas, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Filipo Daugunu

World.title: Wallaroos lose star but regain experience for historic 'quadruple header'
World.content:
The Wallaroos have been forced to leave out star fullback Caitlyn Halse for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Halse is unavailable for the WXV Global Series Test due to concussion symptoms.

The 20-year-old's withdrawal is a blow but the Wallaroos have regained experienced winger Maya Stewart, who returns to the starting XV.

Stewart, a 27-Test veteran with the Wallaroos, was named after recovering from an Achilles tendon injury.

Her inclusion sees Desiree Miller move from the wing to fullback in place of Halse.

Wallaroos 'got some work to do' Ending a run of six straight defeats was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

In the forward pack, captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona and Pia Tapsell swap positions in the back row, starting at blindside flanker and number eight respectively.

Eva Karpani and Cecilia Smith have returned to the match-day squad on the reserves bench, which also features fresh faces Allana Sikimeti and Piper Simons.

"We have maintained considerable selection consistency throughout the WXV, strategically strengthening our cohesion and combinations," Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, said in a statement.

"During the WXV we have layered specific areas of our game to build stronger performances each Test.

"We have selected a balanced 23 armed with leadership, power, strength and speed."

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona will play at blindside flanker against Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland.

In their most recent Test, the Wallaroos triumphed 30–10 in Edinburgh late last month.

The two sides meet in Sydney and Canberra (October 23) to conclude their WXV Global Series campaigns.

Saturday's match is part of a rugby "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the final Bledisloe Cup Test, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams are also appearing.

The world champion Australian women's team plays arch rivals New Zealand, while the men's squad faces two-time Olympic champions Fiji.

It is the first time all four national rugby teams will be playing on the same match-day schedule.

Wallaroos squad (1-15): Brianna Hoy, Brittany Merlo, Faliki Pohiva, Kaitlan Leaney, Michaela Leonard, Siokapesi Palu Sekona (c), Piper Duck, Pia Tapsell, Samantha Wood, Waiaria Ellis, Amelia Whitaker, Faitala Moleka, Georgina Friedrichs, Maya Stewart, Desiree Miller

Reserves: Tania Naden, Allana Sikimeti, Eva Karpani, Jemma Bemrose, Emily Chancellor, Lily Bone, Piper Simons, Cecilia Smith

World.title: Australia is the monster that turns World Cup dreams to nightmares
World.content:
Almost a decade ago, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was the last day before everything changed.

Australia's cracking 23-16 win over New Zealand in 2017 didn't just deliver the team its first-ever World Cup final victory on home soil; it was the last major match before the women's game was transformed forever.

The following season, the interstate series moved under the NRL banner, the first NRLW season kicked off, and women's rugby league began to take giant strides.

Australia's 2017 World Cup win was the last game before the women's game changed forever. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

A few players from that watershed moment are still around for this year's Rugby League World Cup, which begins tomorrow in Parramatta, when Australia plays Samoa.

Isabelle Kelly, Kezie Apps and Simaima Taufa are still wearing green and gold; Zahara Temara has switched to New Zealand and will play for the Kiwi Ferns in their tournament opener against Fiji on Sunday alongside Raecene McGregor and Apii Nicholls.

These six exist in a different world from the one they came from, one where the players are now faster, stronger, fitter and more skilful; where pathways have improved, and player numbers have exploded; and where the game has evolved to the point where this should be the last World Cup held simultaneously with the men's tournament because the product is strong enough to stand alone.

The women's World Cup will again be held alongside the men's tournament. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

But the issue heading into the tournament is at the top end of the product, because Australia's dominance has become one of the growing pains the game must endure as everyone else tries to catch up.

Since that win in 2017, the Jillaroos have won 15 of 16 matches. They have not conceded more than two tries in a game since 2018.

In the last World Cup, they won their five matches by a cumulative scoreline of 312-12, including a 54-4 massacre of New Zealand in the final.

Unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign Jessica Skinner once doubted her coaching style was elite. Now she believes it's exactly what the top level needs, and her journey from rural NSW has shaped why.

The last time they played England, they won 90-4, and those four points mark the only try they've conceded to a team other than New Zealand in their past 16 games.

They won the Pacific Championship last year, scoring 110 points and conceding just 12 across three matches, with the Kiwi Ferns copping a 40-8 belting in the final.

State of Origin regulars like Jesse Southwell and Abbi Church, both overlooked for the match against Samoa, can't make this team. A living legend like Ali Brigginshaw can't even make the squad.

The Jillaroos have nine players from this year's NRLW Dally M Team of the Year. In Tamika Upton, Olivia Kernick, Tarryn Aiken, Isabelle Kelly and Jess Sergis, they have the best player, forward, halfback and centres in the world.

Tamika Upton has won three of the last four Dally M medals. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

They are, without question, the best women's rugby league team ever, and they are so much better than everyone else that anything less than a dominant run to the final and a thumping victory at Lang Park will feel like a departure from a predestined fate.

Other teams have improved. New Zealand, which handed Australia its sole loss in recent years in 2023 and went down by just six points in one game last year, has risen highest with the tide.

As the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, they could rise higher still, and their squad for this year's tournament should put them in contention for the final.

Samoa is another side that has improved and could still get better. The Fetu have benefited from the injection of diaspora players like Taliah Fuimaono, Evania Isa'ako and Amber Hall, plus fresh faces like Queensland Origin flyer Destiny Mino-Sinapati and reigning NRLW rookie of the year Mercedez Taulelei-Siala.

Samoa will be making its World Cup debut. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

They are a vision of what is possible for the expansion of women's rugby league and beneficiaries of the improved pathways leading to the NRLW.

It will take time, because we are talking about change that can take a decade or more to become apparent, but the benefits are there for all to see in the men's game.

The women's game is on the same path; they're just not as far along. This is a brave, dangerous side with a real future, one which is easy to see unfolding before us.

One day a team like Samoa might be able to give the World Cup a real shake. But not these days.

The Samoans are currently 53.5-point underdogs against the Jillaroos in tomorrow night's match. They lost to them 60-0 in the corresponding clash last year.

Even that was nothing compared to the 90-4 belting England copped in Las Vegas last year, an eye-popping result that showed just how lopsided things had become.

England was humiliated in its last meeting with Australia. (Getty Images: Ethan Miller)

The English will get a chance at revenge in Perth next week, and they're a much better side than the one that travelled to Nevada.

Roosters backrower Jasmin Strange is a welcome addition, and they have a core of NRLW players, including North Queensland's Fran Goldthorp, Canberra forward Hollie-Mae Dodd and clever Newcastle playmaker Georgia Roche.

If they can keep things respectable against the Jillaroos, that will be progress.

That gap can close as more top-level talent filters through the ranks, for England and everybody else.

But it will take time to run the Jillaroos down. And because the women's game is semi-professional, it's unlikely to happen as rapidly as it has in the men's game, meaning progress could take a decade or more.

New Zealand shape up as the only side with a realistic chance of taking down Australia. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Until then, there is no choice but to keep going.

Every nation will have a moment. Some will have more than one because there will be glories outside of absolute victory. Fiji will make its World Cup debut and Papua New Guinea will look to continue its steady progress of recent years.

A semi-final berth would be a major achievement for Samoa and a place in the final would be a shot in the arm for the game in England, so their group-stage clash is the pick of the early tournament matches.

The Kiwi Ferns will fancy their chances of an ambush should they meet Australia in the final, given the Jillaroos will have had a soft run in. They will point out that they are the one in 15-1, and perhaps they will be right.

But at the end lurks Australia, the monster at the end of the dream that turns it into a nightmare. And, just under a decade since the rest of history began, the truth of the pain it is about to inflict is simple.

This is the best collection of players ever assembled in women's rugby league, and if they are at any point over the next month beaten, it will be one of the biggest upsets the game has known.

World.title: The data that shows who won and lost in this year's AFL trade period
World.content:
If footballing dreams are lived out in September, they are first shaped in October and November.

If you nail an off-season it can set you up for years to come. If you stumble it can hurt for even longer.

The 2026 off-season class was one of rare quality. Instead of list-cloggers and fringe players that sometimes monopolise trade chatter, this year's crop is full of proven stars.

Lachie Neale, Scott Pendlebury, Jesse Hogan, Toby Greene, Zak Butters, Rowan Marshall and Ben King all found new clubs, among a host of others. It would be hard to find a trade period with a better combined resume than the one we've just seen.

The 2026 trade period has seen 23 trades and seven free-agency moves take place, with 30 players finding new clubs for season 2027. The dealing isn't done yet, with more picks set to change hands before and during the draft.

While much of football — and football commentary — is about instant gratification, the trade period is often a slower burn. Most AFL grand finals are blowouts well before the final siren, and most trade periods have deals that hang in the balance until the final minutes.

This year the opposite was the case. Little suspense was left by the time the last day rolled around, while the ending to that grand final was one that will be remembered for years to come.

While winners or losers of the off-season often take years to fully work out, the direction each team is taking is usually much clearer after the final trade is called.

Dogs taking a big bite

Each trade period it seems like at least one side pushes firmly towards the present over the future. Last year the Saints were the most aggressive side, bringing in a host of players to hopefully kickstart their resurgence up the ladder.

This year it was the Bulldogs that were the busiest club in the league.

All up the Dogs brought in four new players, the most of any club this off-season. The centrepiece of the four was the move for free agent Zak Butters, but the acquisition of Jordon Butts should be equally important for an often under-siege defensive unit.

There are some slight queries about how Butters will fit alongside Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, but with the Dogs captain turning 32 next year this potentially sets the midfield group up for contention over the next half decade. The Bulldogs' best over the past three seasons has rivalled practically any other side. The time is now for them to take the next step.

But the Dogs may not be the biggest winners of the trade period for next season in isolation. Geelong's acquisition of proven talent in Toby Greene, Jordan Ridley and Rowan Marshall looks like providing the most upside next year, while Hawthorn will also be quietly confident in Zach Merrett and Ben King.

At the other end of the "win now" scale, the preliminary finalist Swans will be forced to retool without Nick Blakey and Joel Amartey, and GWS have made the call to get younger with the loss of Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Kieren Briggs and Lachie Whitfield.

Blakey's big deal

Whispers about a Nick Blakey move became increasingly loud as the off-season progressed. The chatter about his discontent in Sydney didn't abate, and quickly the defender became the focal point of an otherwise quiet second week of the period.

There's a couple of good reasons for that too. It's uncommon that a 26-year-old who is arguably the best player in a valuable role becomes available on the trade market.

In all, no club this century has traded more pick value for a single player than North has just traded for Blakey. The trade takes them out of multiple drafts. If North Melbourne was to win the 2028 premiership, the value of the picks traded would still outweigh what Adelaide traded for Wayne Carey way back in 2002.

Beyond the stated cost above, it also has deprived them of another top draft pick — the likely early 20s they would have received in compensation for Essendon's upcoming bid on Dougie Cochrane.

North Melbourne had hoped to pair Blakey with Adelaide's Nick Murray to bolster its defence, but that fell through at the deadline. It could be a bigger loss than it appears. North's defensive stocks are some of the weakest in the league, and its ability to transition the strongest part of their back half game.

Future failing

As predicted here before the trade period began, most clubs were cautious of the value of next year's draft.

One of the clearest examples was offered by Melbourne early in the trade period in its public negotiations for newly minted Demon Zane Duursma.

"We offered (pick) 47, we also offered a 2027 future two, or 2028 future two," Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb told the media.

That pick 47 is notionally a third-round selection, indicating that the drop in value increases to about a round for the next two drafts, which are compromised by the new Tasmania team being handed high picks.

This was even clearer in the trade that took place between Richmond and Port Adelaide, with the Tigers sending pick 22 this year alongside their round one, two and three picks next year for Port Adelaide's fifth pick.

This reflected the general trend of how picks traded hands. Only clubs who have clear father-son or academy talents seemed to be on the hunt for picks next year, with other clubs pushing for lower selections this year or selections in 2028 instead.

Port Adelaide was the keenest to get 2027 draft picks through the door. That's no shock, given it has up to four tied talents. In fact, every club bar possibly Sydney to invest in next year's draft have prospective father-son or academy talents likely to be selected in the upper reaches of the draft.

Most other clubs were somewhat keen to escape the oncoming chaos, or try to move picks into the (slightly) less compromised 2028 draft. The compromised drafts might also be playing into another trend that has emerged recently.

The past two trade periods have seen a re-evaluation of how clubs see the value of players against picks. Instead of the promise of youngsters, the increasingly uncertain availability of young talent has turned the attention of clubs to proven talent instead.

World.title: Aussie cyclists begin World Championships with silver medal
World.content:
Australia has claimed a silver medal in the men's team sprint on the opening night of the UCI Track Cycling World Championships in Shanghai.

The Australian trio of Leigh Hoffman, Ryan Elliott and Danny Barber finished runner-up to the Netherlands in the final.

It was Australia's fifth consecutive World Championships medal in the event.

"For the final, we made a minor change in strategy," Hoffman said.

Richardson withdrawn from world champ squad British track cyclist Matthew Richardson, who defected from Australian cycling at the end of the Paris Games, has been withdrawn from this week's UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai.

"We just tried to have a little gamble, and it almost paid off.

"We were up to the 500-metre mark, so we definitely gave the Dutch a run for their money.

"It's definitely bittersweet to miss out on the [winner's] rainbow bands, but considering last year was a bronze and this year we have silver, I think this team is on the way up."

Australia won a first-round duel against a British team missing Matt Richardson.

He was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct.

Richardson won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

In other results in Shanghai, Australia's Kristina Clonan, Molly McGill and Alessia McCaig finished seventh in the women's team sprint.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Top gymnastics coach fined after assaulting two female teen athletes
World.content:
A gymnastics coach with more than 30 years' experience has avoided conviction and instead been ordered to pay a fine after assaulting two teenage female athletes.

Over the length of his career, Jamie Glen Cannon, 49, has trained athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, in Cairns, and at Brisbane Grammar School.

Mr Cannon was sentenced in Maroochydore District Court last week, after pleading guilty to four charges of common assault against the two teen gymnasts, each aged between 13 and 16.

Jamie Cannon has coached athletes at clubs on the Sunshine Coast, Cairns and at Brisbane Grammar School over his 30-year career. (ABC News: Alex Papp)

Coach touched athletes

Crown prosecutor Alex Stark described Cannon's behaviour as "a breach of trust, both professional and personal" and tendered an agreed statement of facts about the offending.

The court heard Cannon was a senior coach at a Sunshine Coast club when the incidents occurred in 2022 and 2023.

The two girls were under his supervision as athletes.

One of the assault charges related to Cannon smacking the bottom of a 13-year-old as she performed handstands with other gymnasts at the club.

One athlete's victim impact statement said the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely". (Pexels: Ivan Samkov / CC licence)

Three more offences occurred at the same club, involving Cannon touching and rubbing the inner thigh of a second athlete, aged 15 at the time.

The court heard that in one interaction, Cannon asked the teenager if she wore make-up, told her she was pretty, then put his hand on her inner thigh.

In another, he asked if he could touch the teenager's leggings, and before she could respond, he put his hand on her knee.

The fourth charge involved Cannon approaching the 15-year-old as she prepared to coach a class, standing in between her legs before placing his hands on her knees and rubbing her thighs as she attempted to move away.

The court heard it was accepted that Cannon's behaviour had "no sexual intent".

Gymnast left the sport she loved

The 15-year-old athlete's victim impact statement was read to the court at his sentencing by Mr Stark.

The teenager wrote that the offending led to her "quitting gymnastics entirely".

She described problems falling asleep and how it damaged "many friendships", particularly at the gymnastics club.

"[It] affected the development of a romantic relationship with partners due to fear and sensitivity to certain actions and situations," Mr Stark read to the court.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this story, please contact Owen Jacques at jacques.owen@abc.net.au.

Mr Stark said there was a "vulnerability" in the situation because the teenagers were under his supervision.

He said both teenagers had been clear about their boundaries to Cannon, including the request not to be touched.

"It was really that sense of breach of trust that was at the heart of the impact for both of them," he said.

Cannon declined to be interviewed by police.

The court heard he has not been involved with the sport since being charged.

Decades as a top coach

Cannon's lawyer Ambyr Cousen described how her client had been involved with the sport for 30 years both as an employee and as a volunteer, including as a committee member with Gymnastics Queensland (GQ).

"He has won a number of awards for peer service within that industry," Ms Cousen told the court.

Cannon was working with Brisbane Grammar School as a senior coach in 2019 when he received GQ's Individual Service Award for his service to gymnastics in Queensland.

He also spent more than a decade leading GQ's Men's Artistic Gymnastics Sport Committee.

Ms Cousen also supplied the court with several character references for her client.

Court accepts 'no sexual intent'

Cannon provided a written apology to the court for his actions, and offered to pay $1,000 to each of the victims as compensation.

Jamie Cannon was sentenced on four counts of common assault in the Maroochydore District Court last week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In sentencing, Judge Amanda McDonnell told Cannon he treated "these young, vulnerable girls in a way that they didn't wish to be touched".

"I have no doubt that they looked up to you for guidance," Judge McDonnell said.

" I accept that there was no sexual intent, but that you acted in an overly-familiar way. "

Cannon was ordered to pay a single fine of $2,500 for the four offences, plus the promised compensation.

No conviction was recorded.

Tech.title: Shelly’s new presence sensor simultaneously detects up to ten people without a camera
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Following the launch of its $50 subscription-free security camera last month, Shelly announced another new accessory for smart home automation today that can keep track of multiple people as they move through rooms or large spaces without recording them. The Shelly Presence Gen4 sensor uses mmWave radar technology instead of a camera to detect the presence, motions, and activities of people and pets. It’s available starting today for $84.99 through Shelly’s online store and is expected to hit other retailers like Amazon and Best Buy soon.

The Presence Gen4 can be perched on a shelf or a table using its built-in stand or permanently mounted to a wall to take full advantage of its 140-degree horizontal field-of-view allowing it to monitor spaces up to 650 square feet in size. Installation does require access to a power source for the sensor’s USB-C cable, but the Presence Gen 4 can be easily integrated into several smart home systems including Google Home, Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, and Home Assistant with support for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, and Matter.

Mounting the Presence Gen4 to a wall allows the sensor to detect a larger space, but installation will need to accommodate a USB-C power cable. Image: Shelly

Automations for turning on lights, heating, cooling, or even music can be triggered when a person is detected entering a space, and then turned off again when they leave to conserve power usafe. You can set up to ten independently customizable detection zones so that a lamp only turns on when someone actually sits at a desk, for example, or your home theater only powers up when someone plops down on the living room sofa. You also have the option to include small objects like pets when they’re detected, or adjust the Presence Gen4’s sensitivity so it ignores objects that are low to the ground ensuring automations aren’t triggered while your robovac tidies your floor.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s new Photos app combines your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud galleries
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, overhauling the editor and image viewer, and combining photos and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space. The new combined gallery experience aims to make it easier to manage and view your photos without jumping between apps or devices, while also improving app launch and scrolling performance in Photos.

To combine your galleries in the Windows 11 Photos app, you’ll need to turn on Camera Backup in the OneDrive mobile app on iOS or Android, and follow Apple’s guide to set up iCloud for Windows. Once combined in the Windows 11 Photos app, you can browse by date, organize and share albums, search for specific photos via descriptions or by the people featured in them, and more. You can browse files online or offline, and Microsoft says photos will be available on your device “even when you’re not connected.”

The new Photos editor has been “rebuilt from the ground up,” according to Microsoft, launching 25 percent faster and arranging tools into four categories: Crop, Enhance, Repair, and Stylize. The Photos app now also preserves HDR quality during editing processes and allows you to edit and save HEIC and WebP images without altering their original format.

Here’s an example of the tools you’ll find under the new “Crop” category. Image: Microsoft

Lastly, the viewer has been given a cleaner layout and performance enhancements, launching 15 percent faster and opening HEIC images up to 30 percent faster, according to Microsoft’s announcement. Media type support has also expanded to SVG files. These new Photos experiences are rolling out today as an update for Windows Insiders on Windows 11, with Microsoft expecting a full launch for all Windows 11 users later this year.

Tech.title: How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops
Tech.content:
Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch.

One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy.

“When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says Peter Dawoud, principal program manager at Microsoft.

Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says.

Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which Meta announced last week is coming to Windows at some point in the future.

Getting started with Hermes was mostly a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully.

I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background.

Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version.

Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator.

There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.”

Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.”

Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.”

Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app.

This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles.

“Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud.

One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement.

Fortnite, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. Nvidia and Microsoft are also working with a variety of other anti-cheat providers to make more games available in the future.

Activision’s Ricochet anti-cheat engine, used in Call of Duty, will support RTX Spark at some point in 2027, and EA has committed to getting its Javelin anti-cheat working in Battlefield in early 2027. PUBG will start working on RTX Spark laptops in the first half of 2027, and Riot Games has committed to getting League of Legends and Valorant running on RTX Spark laptops at some point in the future.

Microsoft is also bringing its advanced shader delivery system to RTX Spark. This allows the Xbox app to preload game shaders during download. It’s the same experience that’s been available on Xbox Ally devices, allowing you to download a game, click launch, and have shaders automatically precompiled so you don’t have to sit there and wait to play.

I haven’t run into many game compatibility issues during my testing, even though nearly every game I’ve tested has run emulated. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips just weren’t powerful enough on the GPU side to make gaming a reality, but Nvidia has put a much more powerful GPU inside the RTX Spark.

Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.

The last part of Microsoft’s work on RTX Spark involves Windows features. Surprisingly, Copilot Plus PC features like Recall aren’t available on RTX Spark devices at launch. It’s not clear why they’re delayed, but it sounds like they won’t be available fully until next year. “We are partnering closely with Nvidia to deliver Copilot Plus PC experiences on RTX Spark, expected to first become available to Windows Insiders later this year,” says Adrienne Brewbaker, senior director of Windows marketing.

Microsoft is also working on a new Windows Search interface that will work best on devices like the RTX Spark. The interface is being overhauled to focus on speed, and even includes actions that let you do things like turn Bluetooth on or off right from the search bar. It essentially turns Windows Search into a launcher, a much-needed improvement. “We think you’ll love it,” says Dawoud. “We think it’ll change the way people interact with Windows.”

The pad

I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.

Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

Tech.title: An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

An Israeli ad tech firm worked with spyware companies to infect devices, including at Al Jazeera, by simply showing users an online ad, according to a joint investigation by security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant. It’s the first time researchers have found technical evidence of a zero-click attack — a form of hacking that requires no action by users — delivered through targeted advertising, as reported earlier by NBC News.

The ad firm, called Discover-Tech, presents itself as a typical online advertising agency, but researchers say it actually provides a pipeline for hacking groups to plant malicious ads across the web. It operates a platform known as “Controlium” that allows its spyware partners to “precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking,” according to the investigation. It also allows them to “select a user for infection or profiling” using their IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier.

One of the groups Discover-Tech works with is Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that has been blacklisted by the US government. In 2024 and 2025, Discover-Tech ads delivered Candiru-linked spyware to Al Jazeera, a Qatar-based news network. Researchers say the companies targeted “at least” 45 devices at the news outlet in 2024 and 2025.

Citizen Lab and Confiant call on the advertising industry to ramp up security on their platforms. Google and the Comcast-owned advertising company Beeswax have since removed Discover-Tech from their platforms, while IAB Europe suspended the company from its list of approved vendors, Reuters reports. Researchers also recommend that users at high risk of targeting use ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and regularly reset mobile ad IDs.

Tech.title: Prep your cart before iPhone Duo preorders open tomorrow
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable phone opens for preorder tomorrow, October 16th, at 8am ET / 5am PT, but you don’t have to wait until then to get your order mostly sorted. The company’s product page for the phone now lets you select the color you want, along with storage capacity, carrier preference, and whether you want to set up a trade to make the $1,999 foldable a little cheaper.

Once you enter all of the details, all you’ll need to do tomorrow morning, once preorders open, is to confirm your order. It’ll be sitting in your cart ready for checkout. This will save you some time, and you’ll jump ahead of people who are still customizing their iPhone Duo details.

Not quite a preorder, but close.

There’s a lot of hype for the iPhone Duo, and this system should provide Apple with a good sense of how many customers are willing to put down money before preorders open. For anyone who’s waiting until tomorrow, we’ll have preorder details up on the site at 8am ET sharp.

Tech.title: Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

In hindsight, the post on Instagram should have raised more red flags. The image purported to show actress Mia Goth, just days after filing for divorce from actor and filmmaker Shia LaBeouf, posing in a T-shirt with a pointed message: MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN. To really drive home the point, the song “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)” by Beyoncé was added to the post.

It would have been out of character for the star of Pearl, who doesn’t have much of a social media presence, if any. But the Instagram account that posted it, @miagoth_, had more than a million followers and was marked with a blue “verified” checkmark. Within days, the image racked up nearly 500,000 likes, including from peers in the entertainment industry, despite the page being labeled as a fan account.

The image, as The Verge reported, was AI-generated, posted by an account Goth’s representative said they’d complained to Instagram about before for posting “counterfeit, AI images” of Goth. Meta allows users to purchase blue “verified” checkmarks, even if the account is not run by a prominent figure or isn’t an official page.

“The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Christine Tripicchio, a representative for Goth, told The Verge in an email. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.”

Because of the news of her divorce, the post trickled through the celebrity gossip outlets, and that coverage in turn propagated the post through Google search. Searches for the actress and the shirt triggered an AI-generated overview saying Goth was taking “a clear swipe at her ex, Shia LaBeouf, following their recent divorce filing,” in turn citing the aforementioned blogs. A section in Google search results labeled “Mia Goth turns heads on Instagram by wearing a sassy ‘My ex is my biggest fan’ t-shirt” was featured prominently, along with links to social media posts discussing the image. Instagram eventually removed the account for impersonating a public figure.

There was a moment when everyone, even the rich and famous, was grappling with norms around a new technology. Now, the trough of AI content online is only growing — and it’s not clear if anyone is trying or able to stop it.

AI content depicting female public figures is often overtly sexual. A profile that exclusively posts AI-generated images of Johansson — often with bare feet prominently displayed — included contact information so that companies could advertise on the account, along with links to Patreon and Telegram channels selling subscriptions. The content off-platform used Johansson’s name and (AI) image to advertise adult content. Another account posts realistic AI-generated images of actors and musicians like Millie Bobby Brown, Zendaya, and Grande, always partially undressed or in sexualized positions. Some accounts have their own niche, like “Stranger Things actors getting married to each other.”

After The Verge asked Meta about eight accounts posting celebrity deepfake content, spokesperson Alex Dziedzan said the company had removed some of the accounts. Two of them — the Goth one and the Johansson one — appear to be taken down.

“We do not permit accounts to use someone’s likeness to pose as that individual, regardless of whether the content is authentic or AI-generated,” Dziedzan said in an email.

Taylor Swift is holding a drink, rapping along to Drake’s “Burning Bridges,” expletives and all. “I’m off a [Quaalude]/it make my body tingle,” she sings, wearing the dress from the fateful 2009 VMAs moment. The video is AI, obviously. It has 1.8 million views on Instagram.

“I don’t think her pr team gonna like her saying the N word,” someone commented.

Instagram is filled with videos like this, often inexplicably following very specific formats. A clip of AI Shrek doing the same thing as AI Swift has 3.1 million views. Here’s Steve Jobs, swaggering around to a different Drake song with a bottle of champagne in his hand (371,000 views). There’s also an identical Lionel Messi version (2.1 million views) posted by a different account. Here are Formula 1 drivers Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen lipsyncing to “APT” by Bruno Mars and Rosé (2.9 million views). Another clip shows AI Swift’s wedding to AI Travis Kelce at AI Madison Square Garden.

“ai he wore white tuxedo,” one fan helpfully fact-checked.

In the absence of national right of publicity laws, AI-generated content featuring real people is being litigated on the platform level. (The US’s Take It Down Act, which was signed into law in 2025, specifically criminalizes the distribution of nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated content, and compels platforms to remove it within 48 hours.)

YouTube has likeness detection, perhaps the most robust deepfake monitoring and takedown system. Under the program, YouTube will scan its platform for visual matches for a person — and as of recently, sound-alikes — and allow them to request takedowns of content. Not every takedown request is accepted; the company says it considers public interest, newsworthiness, and consent in evaluating takedowns. The program was initially opened to public figures like celebrities, content creators, politicians, and journalists, but now covers every adult with a YouTube account. In the past, the company has said that the number of takedown requests it receives is relatively small. Creators want to be aware of what’s been posted of them on YouTube, but it often ends up being “fairly benign or additive to their overall business,” Amjad Hanif, vice president of creator products, said in a press briefing in March.

Still images are exempt from Meta’s AI labeling requirement

YouTube spokesperson Jack Malon noted in an email to The Verge that the company’s likeness detection was developed in partnership with the entertainment industry. Malon said that in the first half of 2026, YouTube removed over 95 percent of the videos that were reported through the program for takedowns.

AI-generated content on Meta platforms often has labels identifying it as such. Some content, like realistic videos of people or audio of AI-generated voices, is required to have an AI label. Still images, on the other hand, are exempt from the labeling requirement — meaning that the fake image of Mia Goth wouldn’t have required a disclosure under Meta’s rules. The company also introduced “AI-generated profile” labels that apply to an entire account where the avatar depicted doesn’t exist in the real world after an influx of AI influencer types flooded the platform.

But there is a cottage industry of accounts that pump out AI-generated imagery of real people that the algorithm seems to like. Some of the content isn’t obviously nefarious, just kind of strange: There’s a genre on Facebook, for example, of AI-generated movie premiere videos where the original cast (in costume) walks the red carpet next to actors for a recast version. One profile advertises $29-per-month online courses on how to make money through AI content.

AI-generated celebrity content also has the capacity to truly trick people into thinking it’s real, as in the case of the image (and account) depicting Goth. The specific post that went viral suggested the actress was taunting LaBeouf, who has been accused of abuse by another ex-partner and was filmed in 2015 saying he “would have killed [Goth]” if he had continued to argue with her. The fake image was attention-grabbing, shady, and timely — in other words, perfect for social media virality but a potential liability for the parties involved. The incident illustrates the failures of trust and safety provisions that are supposed to protect against this kind of confusion.

On social media, AI content mingles freely with standard-issue reposts of real images. And even when one page is taken down, there are others that continue to push out content: Another Instagram account — still live — with over 300,000 followers posts a steady stream of pictures and videos of Johansson, which appear to be a mix of authentic images and AI-generated content. One of its most popular posts is what looks to be an AI image of Johansson with nearly half a million likes. There is no AI disclosure, in line with Meta’s rules. The deepfaked Johansson lies on a couch, bare feet displayed prominently. It is not her, obviously — but her fans in the comments either don’t know or don’t care.

Tech.title: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades.

But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them.

Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce.

So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy.

A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.)

Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down.

That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency.

We never voted for an insecure network of cameras on every street corner, and we’re certainly not being asked if we’re comfortable with access to this network being given to police officers with a penchant for abusing it. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. And so far, it’s working.

Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. Lately you’ve been an investigative journalist. You are a witness in Senate hearings. Welcome to Decoder.

Thanks for having me.

I’m a huge fan of yours. It’s just a delight to have you here. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable.

Give us a sense of your background. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock?

I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. I’ve also always been kind of a hacker, or somebody who is that type of person who always takes stuff apart. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. But a lot of times that blends into investigative journalism as well.

With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. About two years ago I started noticing them. I thought they were traffic cameras or something like that. Then I started looking into what they were actually doing and then started looking into things like security vulnerabilities. More than anything, everything that’s happening right now in the public, in the news, has to do with people just figuring out that these have existed the entire time.

A lot of my focus now is on the lack of transparency from the government, because the companies are always going to make money and try to make as much money as they can, especially if it’s from taxpayer money. But in this case, I feel like our government missed it. And that’s where we’re at.

There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate.

When I say “modern,” what I mean is it feels like we woke up sometime in the last year and everything is recording us all the time and everything is watching us and the glasses have cameras in them and Mark Zuckerberg is saying phones don’t have a light, and that is meant to end a conversation.

That’s it. That’s the argument. Phones don’t have a light, no further questions. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. No thank you. We actually don’t want this to happen.” But my personal experience of this is that my political coming of age was the Iraq War and the Patriot Act.

This is the stuff that people were talking about twenty-five years ago — don’t do warrantless wiretaps, don’t make the databases all connect to each other so you can take the metadata and de-anonymize people at will.

What is it about this time that has made everybody so angry? Because we could have been angry twenty-five years ago.

I’m always trying to get people more informed on the information that’s being collected about them every time they go to a website, every time they 

I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. I was never given an option on whether to vote for them or vote for somebody who was in favor of them. It just kind of happened and you know people weren’t told about them. That would be the first thing — that you can still install a separate OS on an Android phone or you could turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth or just leave your phone at home. Whereas now you can’t actually go to the grocery store without somebody tracking your vehicle.

The second thing is that — and this is kind of related to opting in and opting out — I can pay for a new AI smartwatch or I can pay for an Amazon Echo device or something like that, or I cannot. Whereas this way I’m paying for this already. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance.

In some ways it is the same as the NSA, but I feel like it’s much more local now.

You don’t get to go to the town board meeting and yell at the NSA. Although maybe you should. Honestly, that might be good for everyone. There is that part of it, and you’ve certainly been at a bunch of local town board meetings. I’ve watched a lot of videos of you talking to them and helping other people articulate their concerns.

That, to me, is one of the more fascinating aspects of all this. Flock went from a company that was selling cameras to everyone, and the idea that adding Flock cameras would increase the safety of your town went from all but assumed to, “Hold on, we all have a lot of questions,” and now this company is struggling a little bit. They’re losing contracts, they are retrenching, their communication strategy has changed.

What do you make of that? Is that just the power of local democracy in action, or is there something else?

It definitely is democracy in action. That’s the good news. The best news out of anything that’s happened is that with both Flock and data centers, it’s two things that have made people actually look up who their mayor is and who their city council members are and show up to meetings and then get involved in those local politics.

Because those local politics affect your life way more than national politics. They just don’t make the headlines. We’re not as involved. Your day-to-day following what Donald Trump is doing is likely not going to make that big of a difference other than what you argue about over Thanksgiving. Whereas local politics, that’s straight up, in the next year, going to have a big effect on your life.
