Tech.title: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
Tech.content:
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee, is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year. The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.

The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device.

The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.

Image Credits:Amazon

Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.

For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.

Image Credits:Amazon

All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.

To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.

In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)

With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.

Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.

Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights.

The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.

All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app.

The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

Tech.title: Citizen Lab says governments are abusing online ads to hack people with ‘zero-click’ spyware
Tech.content:
Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.

The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”

Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link.

The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.

Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code.

While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.

Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps. But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.

Image Credits:Citizen Lab (screenshot)

The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside s.”

Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.

The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.

The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection.

Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action.

“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.

Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

Tech.title: Figma announces new features to define how agents work on its platform
Tech.content:
Design platform Figma announced a new Markdown-based editor to help define a company’s design, bring in design and code libraries, and integrate with the Payload headless content management system during the company’s first Config event in India. Through some of these features, the company aims to provide a definition for its own and third-party agents to adhere to a brand’s design rules better while creating with AI.

The company debuted a new feature called Figma Specs, which is a markdown editor that lets users define their design language in a simple way. The document can serve as a reference for teams and agents while designing in Figma. Specs can exist as a standalone file in Figma or can co-exist within the canvas. Apart from acting as a text editor, users can reference other Figma elements, such as elements on the canvas, and embed FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.

What’s more, teams can bring in more context about design, including design libraries, code libraries, and guidelines to manage context for the design system. Agents can also refer to this centralized system to adhere to rules.

Image Credits:Figma

In the past week, the company made its agent on canvas available to a wider user base. However, given the non-deterministic nature of AI, the company is providing tools to steer it toward more predictable outcomes.

Figma also made its code layers feature available to users in open beta, which adds coding to designs on canvas for more interactive prototypes. The company announced this feature in private beta back in June. At its India event this week, the company is making the function available in public beta to let more users test it out. Users can also ask the agent to turn a design into code or change a part of the code to iterate on a prototype.

Image Credits:Figma

“We see Figma as the place where software teams come to decide what they build and ship. And so for that, I think one of the key things to keep in mind about what AI has changed and what it made available is the ability to build,” Figma’s chief design officer Loredana Crisan told TechCrunch. “There are 17-times more lines of code being produced today than in the past. But when you’re looking at releases, only 1.3-times more releases. A lot of that code actually is not necessarily built to ship, but really built to discover what the product is. It’s built to design.”

The company said it is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code, Dia, Grok Bot, and Indian AI startup Sarvam.

Last year, Figma acquired open source headless CMS Payload. Now, the company is integrating it with its Figma Make product for generating dynamic websites and directly managing content. The company said that Payload’s downloads have increased sixfold in the last 12 months.

The company opened its first office in India late last year with sales, partnership, go-to-market, and product support functions. Figma said that the country is its biggest market in terms of users outside the United States. The company noted that the platform works with 40% of India’s top 100 companies listed on the Bombay Stock Exchange.

Tech.title: Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis
Tech.content:
Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

“There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that’s somewhat potentially conservative,” Goldie said on stage. “So we don’t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don’t know, you won’t see the sun anymore.”

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans to focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

Image Credits:Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

“I think the way everything is shifting is that humans bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI,” Goldie said. “And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that’s something that recursive does for chip design.”

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, “donut-shaped” arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

“If it takes six months or a year or two years to design a new chip, then you really have to be extremely selective about the chips that you design,” Goldie said. “But if you can design a chip in like a week, and then say for manufacturing, you can design custom chips for all sorts of different types of applications in like space and AR, VR, and biological computing, it makes sense financially to do that, and we can be more energy efficient.”

Tech.title: Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV
Tech.content:
“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”

Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.

The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.

Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”

“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.

We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”

Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.

Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”

Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.

When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.

“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

Tech.title: Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Tech.content:
If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.

Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.

Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads, doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.

The company’s cofounder and chief product officer Tanyella Leta tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”

Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”

Tech.title: Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy
Tech.content:
As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.

In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”

The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.

“In a world where there is no shame, it's hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn't involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”

The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress, but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions, but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.

Tech.title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
Tech.content:
On Thursday, researchers from The Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto revealed a worst-case scenario found in the wild: spyware silently infecting targets as they browse past ads in their daily digital lives.

Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk.

“AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. “Someone who gets hacked like this would not see anything amiss. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.”

The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.

During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.)

Tech.content:

The name suggests exactly what they are: a type of string light designed to stay up all year instead of coming down after the occasion you hung them for, whether it's the holiday season or a big party that inspired you to deck out your front porch.

Whether these lights are truly “permanent” is up to you, since you can choose to anchor them to your home with either screws or adhesive. My favorite affordable set is from Cync ($117, 100 feet)—it's easy to use and install and has lots of great color options.

No matter which set you choose, these lights are made for year-round enjoyment, though they shine best in the holiday season. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck uses hers in the post-holiday season to display her husband’s favorite sports team colors, while I'm currently using mine to backlight the giant spiderweb spread across my balcony for Halloween. We're both looking forward to switching over to Christmas color schemes soon, and you can too after picking up one of our favorite sets below.

Permanent outdoor lights are exactly what they sound like: outdoor lights meant to be permanently affixed to your home, so you don't have to go up and down a ladder every Halloween and Christmas season. Tech.title: Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission
Tech.content:
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?

If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.

We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.

We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.

Tech.title: Over $600 Million in Polymarket Election Trades Took Place After Races Ended
Tech.content:
Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories.

Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform, for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win.

This summer, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates.

Even odder? “Nearly all of it—about $284 million—came from pairs of accounts repeatedly buying and selling with each other,” says former Polymarket trader Chris Park, who now runs the prediction-market forensic analysis firm MSR Decode.

Such a high volume of seemingly pointless back-and-forth transactions has raised eyebrows among experts. “It's obviously some form of volume manipulation,” says Rajiv Sethi, a Barnard College economics professor who researches prediction markets.

When asked about these markets, Shana Bautista, Polymarket’s head of global intelligence and investigations, told WIRED that the team “immediately flagged this activity, investigated, and blocked the accounts from trading.” Polymarket did not respond to follow-up questions about why the accounts were able to trade such a high amount of volume before it took action.

The timing of these trades made things even weirder. Polymarket’s rules stipulated that the Ethiopia market would be resolved in October after the prime minister was formally appointed and sworn in, which meant that it stayed open for several months after Ahmed’s victory was all but a foregone conclusion. For 123 days after the election, bursts of seemingly irrational trading continued, prompting Polymarket users to leave comments like “THIS NOT RESOLVED?” and “fuckkkk.”

Tech.title: Can the Shark Tank Water Bottle Really Keep Drinks Cold for 36 Hours? I Tested One to Find Out
Tech.content:
The universal push for better hydration has produced a seemingly endless supply of water bottles that promise to keep H2O cold for hours, days, even months. Admittedly, “months” is a stretch, but given recent advances in insulation technology, that milestone may not be far off.

Fresh off Stanley’s early-2020s hype, a new water bottle contender, Coldest, piqued my interest with its bold, brazen name alone. The company’s line of bottles and tumblers, which come in a range of sizes, styles and limited-edition designs, was featured on ABC’s “Shark Tank” and promises to keep beverages cold for 36 hours.

The design is reminiscent of Stanley’s mug. Joey Skladany/CNET

Coldest also operates out of my hometown of Naples in Florida (which I didn’t realize until I researched it), and I welcome any opportunity to support a local small business. But did it ultimately live up to its hype, the thousands of positive reviews and the praise from national media outlets?

More from CNET

The test

For comparison, I grabbed my go-to $30 Owala water bottle and filled it with equal amounts of water (three cups) and ice (one cup). This model is a different size and shape than the 46-ounce Coldest, which means the liquid and ice were more condensed in the compartment.

That said, despite the lack of error-free, controlled-environment analysis, the primary goal was to determine whether the Coldest water bottle lived up to its 36-hour promise.

I put Coldest’s claims to the test. Joey Skladany/CNET

The results

After only a few hours, both water bottles delivered refreshing, ice-cold agua, with Owala consistently beating Coldest by a couple of degrees. Using a meat thermometer, here is a breakdown of the reading times and temperatures across 36 hours:

After 3 Hours

Coldest: 52°F

Owala: 50°F

After 7 Hours

Coldest: 54°F

Owala: 52°F

After 15 Hours

Coldest: 57°F

Owala: 56°F

After 18 Hours

Coldest: 58°F

Owala: 57°F

After 24 Hours

Coldest: 60°F

Owala: 59°F

After 36 Hours

Coldest: 63°F

Owala: 63°F

While water certainly remained cool after the experiment concluded, it was by no means teeth-chattering cold. Though I can hardly imagine anyone waiting this long to drink a beverage, it’s still worth noting since this is a major part of Coldest’s marketing claim.

Coldest performed on par with Owala in my chill test. Joey Skladay/CNET

Owala’s water bottle, though smaller in volume, yielded a consistently colder liquid, likely because of its smaller surface area and greater exposure to the stainless steel interior. But after 36 hours, both bottles tied in temperature, giving Coldest a slight edge because of its significantly larger size.

The Verdict

My feelings towards Coldest were essentially neutral. While I appreciate the company’s ability to retain a cult-like following with monthly limited-edition design drops, I didn’t feel its water-cooling technology was any more superior than the models I currently own (including the Owala).

The Coldest bottle kept things chilled, but it comes at a steep price. Joey Skladany

It’s clear that this was introduced to disrupt Stanley’s virality and market share, though I’m not entirely sure if I’d cough up the cash to make it part of my must-have accessory rotation. I didn’t dislike it, by any means, and applaud the founders on their early success, but even loyalty points and an affiliate program wouldn’t incentivize consistent buys, despite my obsession with staying hydrated and color-coordinating my outfits.

Best Reusable Water Bottles We've Tested See at CNET

Those who collect water bottles like Pokémon will certainly think otherwise, as the impressive range of designs can be exciting. They are one-of-a-kind, often glow in the dark, and reflect current seasons and holidays, which is undeniably adorable. If that’s your thing, then great. But if your main concern is quenching thirst, you’re likely thinking less about style and more about substance, so any popular drinking vessel will do.

Tech.title: Europe’s Largest Airline Wants Predictive AI Models to Nip Airport Meltdowns in the Bud
Tech.content:
If there’s one thing that’s unifying across the world, it’s that we can all agree that a canceled or delayed flight is a massive headache at best. Ryanair – the largest airline in Europe by fleet size, global passenger volume and total flights, and the second-largest airline in the world by global passenger volume – has implemented proprietary predictive AI models to help prevent airline disruptions before they lead to widespread cancellations or diversions.

The AI models were developed by Ryanair Labs, the Ireland-based airline’s tech innovation hub launched in 2014, to more quickly and efficiently predict when weather delays, airport curfews and issues with airline crew hours are likely to disrupt passengers’ journeys.

I spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland, the governmental economic development agency, before the International AI Summit in Dublin to discuss how the airline is using these AI models. The goal, Wilson said, is not to replace Ryanair’s core of human operators, but to give his employees advanced tools to manage and handle operational complexities across Ryanair’s 96 operational bases and its more than 3,800 flights per day.

More from CNET

“And that, by making us efficient,” he said, “translates into lower fares, better operational performance — same boring, virtuous circle, you know, ’cause that’s what the airline industry is like.”

Predictive models in practice

Wilson said there are a lot of variables in making sure a plane is in the right place, at the right time: weather, an airplane going out of service, an airport closing to meet curfews, staff and crew showing up.

For instance, say a crew on a plane is about to exceed the hours they’re allowed to work due to a weather delay and they’re not going to make it back to their base, yet are scheduled to work the next day. The Ryanair model is designed to recognize the disruptions this will cause and to take appropriate action.

CNET spoke with Ryanair CEO Eddie Wilson at the Version 1 media briefing hosted by Enterprise Ireland before the International AI Summit in Dublin. Macy Meyer/CNET

“If you know they’re not going to be able to do the flights the next day, there’s no point in waiting for them to come back the next morning for them to tell you that they’re out of hours,” Wilson said. “But if the model is running, it reassigns somebody else to do it, or it may just reassign them to do a flight later the next day, and you pair up the crew in a different way, that’s all.”

AI is starting to take a larger role in airline and airport operations. In September, the Federal Aviation Administration rolled out a trial program for a new system, Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, around Washington, DC, airports, to use AI to mitigate delays and congestion caused by air traffic control staffing shortages. Some carriers, like American Airlines, are now using AI for flight rebooking, while others, like United, Delta and JetBlue, have partnered with third-party weather predictors, such as Tomorrow.io, to use AI systems to address route or delay issues and quickly calculate solutions.

The future of AI in airline operations

Looking ahead, Wilson said he thinks the next major impact AI will have on airlines is in distributing flights. Specifically, as more people adopt personal AI agents – like OpenAI Dots or Meta’s Muse, both introduced just in the last few weeks – he’s thinking about whether a customer tells an agent “book me a flight” and the potential negative, costly impact that the agent books a more expensive flight due to an airline paying to be prioritized by that AI model.

Ultimately, though, Wilson doesn’t suspect that AI is drastically changing the airline industry – at least not rapidly. “Everything changes and nothing changes, right?” he said.

Wilson says that Ryanair’s strategy will be to find “the killer applications” of AI to better serve customers and gain a competitive edge, but, really, the humans who “execute the real stuff in flight” are the key to smooth operations.

“The actual nuts and bolts of our industry won’t change,” Wilson said.

“In the AI world that’s coming, we just see this as a new set of tools for fine-tuning work processes and efficiencies in doing the core model of what we’ve been successful at.”

Editor’s note: Macy Meyer’s travel costs for the International AI Summit were covered by Enterprise Ireland. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Popular Norwegian Kitchen Brand Lands in the US with 7 Sleek Small Appliances
Tech.content:
Wilfa, a Norwegian brand known for kitchen appliances and minimalist Scandinavian designs, is officially launching in the US today with seven new appliances.

Although we haven’t put the new lineup through testing just yet, a few have caught our eye.

Blending and mixing

The Probaker NXT, Wilfa’s most expensive new appliance, features a 7.4-quart stainless steel bowl, 20 speed settings and a hefty price tag of $999.

That is by far the most expensive stand mixer we’ve seen, but we’d love to do a side-by-side comparison with the Ooni Halo Pro Spiral Mixer, which we previously gave high marks to, as they feature similar designs and features.

Other launches include the Powerfuel XL Blender, which is a heavy-duty blender with a Tritan plastic, 67-ounce jug, a digital-knob design and three presets — soup, ice crushing and smoothie — plus an included tamper. The Prostick, an immersion blender with multiple attachments, is the final new blending option.

Best Blenders of 2026 See It

Coffee

Wilfa is also launching three new drip coffee makers and an electric coffee grinder.

Coffee connoisseurs may already be familiar with Wilfa, as we’ve reviewed earlier versions of the brand’s coffee maker and grinder, the Wilfa Performance and the Uniform coffee grinder, in 2023 when both were available in partnership with Lardera Coffee.

The three new drip makers and grinders share similar designs but are expected to differ.

From left, the Zense Alux Coffee Maker ($299), the Zense Alux Thermo Coffee Maker ($349) and the Performance Thermo Coffee Maker ($399). Wilfa/CNET

When we get our hands on these new launches, we plan to run the new coffee makers through their paces as well to see if one, or multiple, can perform well enough to make it on our best coffee makers list.

Tech.title: Xreal’s New High-End Display Glasses Get a Brightness Boost
Tech.content:
The quality of plug-in display glasses has gotten seriously good lately, if you can put up with the idea of resting your monitor on your face. The price for good glasses has been dropping (down to $299 for some notable ones), but the pricier top-end models have advantages.

The new $599 Xreal One Pro Plus glasses, available now, offer a few subtle upgrades to last year’s model. I’ve been trying a pair out and the experience is largely the same, just a bit better (namely, brighter).

The lenses on these wearable displays still stick out a bit. (I also have prescription inserts added on them here.) Scott Stein/CNET

What’s new: Brightness, a few new visual modes

The previous Xreal One Pro display glasses were one of my favorite pairs around, along with the Viture Beast ones. In the past, Xreal’s design was thinner and lighter than Viture’s, but they had a notably dimmer display. That’s been fixed now with the One Pro Plus, which have 1,200 nits of brightness (versus 700 for the One Pro display glasses). There are also a few more visual settings, including “Reading,” which seems to move the virtual display a bit closer.

More from CNET

The One Pro Plus also have a smoother AI 3D conversion mode that turns any 2D image or video (or connected game) into 3D. The effect runs at a smoother frame rate than before, but the conversion still feels imperfect and gimmicky and compromises the frame rate too much compared with leaving it off.

But the rest of these glasses are similar to their predecessor. They still need to be tethered via USB-C cable to whatever laptop, phone or game console you have around, and they still project their displays down from the top of the glasses through half-mirror lenses that make the display feel overlaid in front of your eyes. They’re not any more portable or differently designed than before, and still resemble odd sunglasses. (They do pack up easily into an included case, though.) They have the same onboard chip that can pin displays in place when you turn your head, along with the same ability to change the size and perceived distance of the virtual display, including widescreen modes for connected computers.

The included nose pads are slightly more comfortable, and the arms can still bend at different angles for a proper fit.

Connecting to Steam Deck is still my favorite thing to do with these types of glasses. Scott Stein/CNET

Wearing the Xreal One Pro Plus

I’ve been wearing the One Pro Plus with prescription lens inserts while writing this story on a MacBook, and the differences are subtle. But I appreciate the extra brightness, and the electrochromic dimming seems to block out room light even better. Together, those improvements make the glasses much more effective in brightly lit rooms or outdoors.

I also watched some of the indie horror movie Buddy on my iPhone, and the more vivid display made the glasses feel like a more effective personal cinema.

I played Star Wars Galactic Racer on Steam Deck with these on my face, too, and had a blast. The display is crisp and vivid, although after swapping back and forth with the Viture Beast, I prefer the Beast slightly for its larger-feeling display.

The audio on the speaker arms sounds fine, but isn’t any better than the Xreal One Pro’s audio. When I wear them, I prefer to use AirPods for audio.

The Xreal One Pro Plus (left) versus the Viture Beast (right). The Beast glasses are clearly a bit chunkier. Scott Stein/CNET

I liked the Viture Beast for their bright, micro-OLED display and their stepped-up screen resolution, which has an aspect ratio that works better for gaming (1,900×1,200). The 1,250 nits on the Beast are pretty close to Xreal One Pro Plus, though.

My issue is that Xreal has so many display glasses options now that it’s getting confusing, including a pair made with Asus, a more affordable pair released earlier this year and a mixed reality computer-glasses system called Xreal Aura that was made with Google, costs $1,279 and is arriving later this fall.

With the One Pro Plus, Xreal has made the best display glasses I’ve ever worn next to Viture Beast, and their smaller on-face feel is more comfortable. But if you’re looking to see what glasses tech has in store next, you might want to see what the Xreal Aura offer. I’ll be reviewing them soon.

Tech.title: The $2,000 Duo: Who Is Apple’s First Folding iPhone Actually For?
Tech.content:
Apple’s first swing in the foldables market, the iPhone Duo, has already made a huge splash before it’s even available to buy.

The foldables segment has been overrun by Android devices, and all eyes have been patiently waiting for Apple to make its move. And the Duo’s design confirms the popularity of Samsung’s Galaxy Fold 8 and Google’s original Pixel Fold: Shorter and wider seems to be the sweet spot, as opposed to the more traditional taller folding phone designs we see with something like the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

But this is Apple we’re talking about, and the iPhone Duo is more than just an iOS version of the Galaxy Fold and Pixel Fold — it has a lot going for it. We had a lot of things to say about it during our hands-on with the device, and while personally, it seems like the best foldable I’ll never buy, it certainly will be delivered into the pockets of some discerning customers who want the Apple level of polish (or who can’t stand green message bubbles).

More from CNET

So who needs the iPhone Duo? Who is it best suited to? We know that the latest iPhone 18 Pro Max is for photography enthusiasts and those who want the best battery ever in an iPhone, but the Duo doesn’t provide that. It’s an oddly-shaped but good-looking device that fills a new space in Apple’s lineup.

Is the iPhone Duo actually for anyone in particular? There are a few crowds that are more likely to gravitate toward this foldable over others. Your grandparents likely aren’t going to run out and grab the Duo, but here’s who likely will.



Early adopters, power users and professionals

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

There are likely plenty of Apple fans who have been waiting for its first foldable, but a lot of people also likely won’t pick up a first-generation device, preferring to wait until the second or third version so that Apple works out any kinks. (On the other hand, Apple has patiently waited and watched the foldable market, so its first swing might not feel like a first-generation foldable full of finicky foibles at all. It’s probably going to be great.)

But there will be some early adopters and tech enthusiasts who won’t care and plan to get this phone anyway.

Power users and those looking essentially for a foldable iPad Mini are going to love the iPhone Duo. You’ll likely be able to resize apps side by side, similar to how you would on any iPad, making it a dream for those who want an iPad experience with an iPhone form factor that fits right in your pocket. Still, we’ll need to see just how well multiple apps work on the inner screen simultaneously. It might not be as elegant as you’d get on an iPad, but it’s close.

The other group that might really want to get their mitts on the Duo is the professional crowd. The larger inner screen makes way for easier work apps that would be more cumbersome than even the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Editing Excel or Google Sheets spreadsheets, Google and Word docs, checking emails and sending work chats will be a far smoother experience on the wider display. Throw in a wireless keyboard, and you might have a pocket iPad-like productivity suite of your dreams.

Fashionistas

Apple products are synonymous with style, and this is a crowd that will happily gravitate toward this phone.

The new “it” item will be in the pockets of celebrities and content creators who want to make sure they’re seen with Apple’s newest device. It’s also an expensive phone, like all foldables, making it a status symbol that maintains the cool and pretentious vibe that Apple products give off.

The sexiest Kindle replacement

The iPhone Duo has a typical but useful foldable feature of showing a preview of what the rear cameras are shooting to help with selfies. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Avid readers may also want to pick up the iPhone Duo, since it’s virtually the perfect e-reader size. Not only that, but you’ll also get access to the App Store, which doesn’t limit you just to Amazon’s Kindle Store or e-reader apps.

That type of flexibility on top of the power of iOS and the A20 Pro chip makes this a killer Kindle or e-reader replacement. While it is very expensive to replace a Kindle, its style, form and functionality would make it a worthy consideration for some people.

Who isn’t the iPhone Duo for?

If your priorities are camera features, battery life and durability, your first choice shouldn’t be the iPhone Duo. What you’re looking for is the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It checks all of those boxes, and you shouldn’t be swayed by the novelty of the Duo.

It’s not that the Duo isn’t alluring, but it’s both nearly double the price of the latest iPhone 18 Pro handsets and likely significantly less durable. The iPhone Duo costs about as much as a new iPhone 18 Pro and an iPad combined.

Like most foldables, the iPhone Duo doesn’t ship with issues, just compromises. That’s something that really needs to be considered when making your purchasing decision. This device is a marvel of engineering, wrapped in luxurious style, but 90% of people spending money on new phones are not going to buy this one.

Tech.title: Vitamix’s First Juicer Is Now Available, and It’s a Home Run
Tech.content:
When a company enters a new product category, I’m always skeptical. So when Vitamix, a brand known for its blenders, announced its first-ever cold-press juicer, I had reservations. But I got a first look at the product and can say that this juicer lives up to the Vitamix name.

Available for purchase on Thursday, the MaxExtract Cold Press Juicer uses slow-masticating technology to extract juice from fruits, veggies and leafy greens.

The MaxExtract is easy to operate

Assembling the juicer took less time and effort than I expected. Then, all you have to do is chop your produce into 2-inch pieces, throw them into the juicer’s 5.3-inch hopper (which can hold a surprising amount of ingredients) and let the MaxExtract handle the rest in minutes. There’s also a hole on top where you can add more ingredients, but even if you open the hopper, the juicer will stop working. This is a great safety feature.

More from CNET

The light-up front dial makes it extra simple. Turn it to the on position to start the juicing process, to the off position when it’s done and reverse it when there’s a clog. However, I haven’t experienced a clog after making several batches of juice.

The dial has a light behind it. A nice touch. Anna Gragert/CNET

It comes with everything you need

The MaxExtract includes a pusher to push ingredients down, a cleaning brush, pulp and juice containers and two strainers: a fine-mesh for less pulp and smoother juice and an easy-clean for more pulp but an easier clean, as the name suggests. Both filters produce lovely juices, but I prefer the fine-mesh one for less pulp in the final product.

I especially appreciate that the juice container includes measurements on the side.

The juice container also has a handle, making it easier to pour the liquid into a glass. Anna Gragert/CNET

All detachable parts are dishwasher-safe

I love that all the detachable components are dishwasher-safe on both the top and bottom racks. The pulp outlet can also be opened to make removing pulp and cleaning even simpler.

As someone who has never used a juicer, I have to say that the MaxExtract has converted me. It creates a smooth, fresh-tasting juice and takes any effort out of the process, including cleanup.

One of the most satisfying parts is watching the pulp emerge. Anna Gragert/CNET

Size is to be expected

The user manual lists the MaxExtract as 17.7 by 8.5 by 7.7 inches and 8.14 pounds. However, you can remove the hopper and chamber from the base if the full unit is too tall for your cabinets.

By comparison, the MaxExtract is narrower and shallower than the $599 Nama J2 Cold Press Juicer, which measures 17.7 by 9.8 by 9 inches and weighs 12.1 pounds. CNET’s best budget juicer, the 11.14-pound $88 Hamilton Beach Easy Clean, is shorter but wider and deeper, measuring 15.31 by 13 by 9 inches.

Before purchasing any juicer, make sure it will fit in your space. Anna Gragert/CNET

Vitamix MaxExtract availability and price

Available in black or white with a glass front, the MaxExtract is $500. You can buy it on Vitamix.com or Amazon, and it comes with a five-year limited warranty.

Tech.title: Apple Maps Gets a Ticket to Austin for the F1 Grand Prix
Tech.content:
If you’re headed to Austin, Texas, for next week’s Formula 1 United States Grand Prix, you won’t want to miss the city’s other highlights – if nothing else, you’ll need to find good barbecue. Apple is adding another dimension to the Texas capital by applying its Detailed City Experience treatment in Apple Maps, including the Circuit of the Americas track where the race is held each year.

Apple enhanced Maps’ Austin layout with detailed 3D day and night renderings of landmarks such as The Paramount Theater, Sixth Street, the Texas State Capitol building and Terry Black’s BBQ. Navigation improvements include streets with lanes (including bus and bike lanes) marked and more accurate elevation.

The race venue marks the track’s turns, shows 3D versions of the grandstands and pit building, as well as the admission entry points. It also includes flourishes such as the stars-and-stripes design of the runoff areas. (But not the World’s Largest Cowboy Hat, alas, which is still being constructed for the event.)

More from CNET

Enhancements to Apple Maps include race track details, notable areas of the venue and 3D versions of landmarks in the Austin area.

Apple, which is the official US broadcaster for F1 races on Apple TV, previously applied the Detailed City Experience glow-up to Monaco, which hosts one of the most storied F1 races of the entire tournament (several top racers call Monaco home), as well as the Albert Park Grand Prix Circuit in Melbourne.

The improvements to Apple Maps aren’t solely visual additions – the app on the iPhone is also an invaluable guide for getting directions and finding places of interest.

For instance, those attending the F1 race can get directions to COTA and see where roads have been temporarily closed or redirected for the event. But it will also guide you to the section where you’re seated and help you find race-specific areas such as bathrooms and first aid areas.

Although the F1 race is a big reason for visiting Austin, it’s just one of many things to do in the state’s capitol. For that weekend and the rest of the year, Apple has created a new curated guide by country music singer-songwriter Dylan Gossett. You’ll find the race track (where Gossett once worked), as well as his favorite bar, the Armadillo Den, and his favorite guitar store, Moon Music Pro.

The Austin improvements to Apple Maps are available now on Apple devices and on the web.

Tech.title: YouTube Rolls Out New Labeling System for AI-Generated Music
Tech.content:
Streaming your daily tunes is about to come with a bit more clarity. YouTube has expanded its labeling system to mark AI-generated songs on YouTube Music. As AI music continues to flood streaming apps, the service’s latest move aims to keep listeners informed about what they’re hearing and whether it was produced by humans. These labels will eventually appear on the main YouTube app as well.

“Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music,” YouTube said through its official blog on Wednesday. “As these tools evolve, our listeners have told us they want transparency when they’re hearing an AI-generated track.”

The labels in question will appear on songs that YouTube identifies as created primarily with generative AI, based on its own detection tools and music partners. It’s not clear how much AI must be featured in a track to qualify for this label.

More from CNET

Labels marking music as AI-generated are rolling out on YouTube Music and YouTube. YouTube

A YouTube spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

YouTube’s decision to mark AI music is the latest move to clarify the growing presence of AI-generated tunes across the music streaming landscape. Earlier this year, Apple Music unveiled a suite of tools to identify AI-generated content, saying new Made with AI labels will roll out by year’s end. Spotify now includes AI Personas, which help people confirm if musicians are actually people making human-made music.

Other streaming apps like Tidal, Bandcamp and Deezer have all made moves to crack down on the AI music boom.

Earlier this year, Deezer released a report stating that AI-generated music accounted for 44% of all new music delivered to its platform. Apple Music previously stated that over one-third of the tracks uploaded to its service are “100% AI.” Forbes reports that AI-generated music could be an industry worth billions of dollars by 2028.

The Recording Industry Association of America, International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences and the performers union SAG-AFTRA came together earlier this summer to push for a two-tiered labeling program to mark AI-produced songs as either AI-Generated or AI-Assisted.

“Fans want to know whether and how generative AI has been used in the music to which they listen,” IFPI CEO Vikki Oakley and RIAA CEO Mitch Glazier said in a joint statement. “Given how important human artistry and authenticity are to music lovers all over the world, these labels will provide an immediately understandable and easily scalable approach to transparency.”

The line between human and AI-generated audio is rapidly blurring. At least having a labeling system in place will let you know if you’re nodding your head to a banger made by a human or through other generative means.
